Haranath Rakshit, Rajkumar Bhandari, and Subhasis Banerjee present a light way to refresh encryption keys for small Internet of Things devices. Static shared keys are cheap but risky: they get reused, allow replay attacks, and never expire. Their 2025 protocol, DSEKP, derives a fresh AES-GCM key for each session using a standard key derivation function, with a one-step handshake to prove both sides agree.

They ran it on an ESP32 sensor node talking to a Raspberry Pi 5 edge server through an MQTT broker, over more than 6,500 packets per setup. Speed and reliability nearly matched the static baseline. Session setup cost about 27 percent extra once, and packets grew by about 10 percent, in return for per-session isolation and replay protection.
arxiv-2511-03024:
Fabian Levican-Santibanez and Pedro Montero classify a family of algebraic varieties that admit a large additive symmetry. A variety is additive if the additive group of the same dimension acts on it with an open orbit, and uniquely additive when that action is the only one of its kind. Their 2025 paper covers smooth Fano toric varieties, a class built from fans of cones, in dimensions up to six.

The classification was done by computer, with fine detail given through dimension four. It extends an earlier list of threefolds by Huang and Montero. The engine is a new Macaulay2 package, AdditiveToricVarieties, for working with such group actions. The math rests on Demazure roots of the fan, which control when actions exist. They also prove every Picard rank two case is additive.
arxiv-2511-03324:
Tom R Hepworth, Simon L Cornish, and Philip D Gregory chart routes through the crowded state space of ultracold molecules. Each spin state of such a molecule splits into many fine levels, leaving hundreds of possible jumps between two spin states. Picking the best path through that maze is slow work for experimenters today.

A simple heuristic joined with graph theory finds near-best state sets and paths quickly. The method balances speed of preparation against how true the final state stays. The team also studies small networks where several couplings act at once and some states stay isolated. Cleaner state control supports quantum chemistry, simulation, and computing with molecules. The graph view turns a bewildering level jungle into a map that can be searched.
arxiv-2511-03924:
Ekin Ugurel, Cynthia Chen, Brian H Y Lee, and Filipe Rodrigues ask whether personal traits can be shown from mobility signals to help transport planners use passively gathered travel data. Links between movement patterns and traits such as age, income, or household structure are weak, inconsistent, and often fail to transfer across settings.

Higher-order measures from directed mobility graphs capture trip sequences, travel modes, and social co-travel, and they beat baseline features. New metrics and visual tools compare how sure a model is with how right it is, supporting honest uncertainty. A shared framework that predicts several traits together beat single-task models, most with limited data or shifted test periods.
arxiv-2511-04124:
Giorgio Morales and John W Sheppard present decomposable neural symbolic regression, a method that explains a trained opaque regression model by turning it into readable math expressions. Plain symbolic regression often chases prediction error and returns bloated or wrong formulas.

A multi-set transformer drafts one-variable skeletons showing how each variable moves the opaque model's response. Genetic search selects strong skeletons, genetic programming merges them while keeping structure, and coefficients are tuned last. Tests under set, varying noise check whether the recovered formulas track the true links rather than merely fitting points.
arxiv-2511-04224:
Yurij V Kalyuzhnyi, writing alone, offers a simpler scheme for computing traits of associative fluids whose particles are strongly anisotropic in shape, a long-standing challenge for Wertheim's multi-density perturbation theory. The method joins thermal perturbation theory with the interaction site model for molecular fluids due to Chandler and Andersen.

A primitive model of Laponite suspension, a clay system proposed recently, serves as the demonstration case. Phase behaviour and percolation traits are worked out with the new scheme. Fast computation for highly anisotropic bonded particles matters well beyond one suspension, since such models appear across soft matter where shape and bonding act strongly.
arxiv-2511-04324:
Eugenia Pyurbeeva and Ronnie Kosloff write an engineering guide to quantum dot thermal machines. These devices exchange particles continuously between hot and cold reservoirs, with a quantum dot as a narrow energy filter. Theory shows Carnot efficiency can be approached when passive heat flow is suppressed, and experiments have already reached a large share of that limit.

Practice, the authors stress, rewards maximum power, efficiency at maximum power, and low output noise over peak efficiency alone. Internal dot dynamics shape all three through few parameters: overall conductance and three asymmetries of the dynamics. Those parameters tell engineers which quantum states to build, improving performance beyond the simplest spin-degenerate transmission level.
arxiv-2511-04524:
Seungjoo Baek and his co-author propose bulk theories for two-dimensional minimal models. One family is supersymmetric, the other is built on W_N algebras. Both extend earlier work by Gang, Kang, and Kim from 2024.

Each model is matched to a Seifert fibered space over a sphere with three special fibers. The 3D-3D correspondence then realizes the bulk theory from that geometry. For unitary cases, the bulk flows to a gapped phase holding the chiral model at its edge. Non-unitary cases flow to a twisted topological theory, tying geometry to abstract algebra.
arxiv-2511-04724:
Thomas Chillery leads fifteen authors testing a prototype neutron detector for deep-underground studies. The target science is the s-process, a slow neutron capture chain that builds heavy elements. The array pairs an EJ-309 liquid scintillator with six helium-3 counters around it.

Tests ran at the FRANZ facility in Frankfurt using a lithium proton reaction. Neutrons spanned fifty to seven hundred twenty kiloelectronvolts in energy. The team's lowest detectable neutron energy came out at one hundred sixty-three kiloelectronvolts. Coincidence counts match simulations, supporting a larger array now under construction for a key magnesium-forming reaction.
arxiv-2511-04824:
Kosei Horikawa leads six authors studying how AI coding agents refactor real software. Tools like Codex, Claude Code, and Cursor now act as autonomous teammates on development tasks. Refactoring, improving code structure without changing behavior, is a core maintenance job.

How agents refactor in practice, and how they compare with humans, was largely unknown. The team mines agent-made refactorings across real open-source Java projects at scale. Their study weighs usage patterns and code quality effects together. The findings give engineering teams early evidence on where agent refactoring helps and where oversight stays essential.
arxiv-2511-04924:
Ziyang Yuan leads nineteen authors introducing Nuclear Ptychoscopy for phase-sensitive nuclear spectroscopy. Knowing a nuclear response needs both its amplitude and its phase. Phase retrieval was shown possible in time-and-energy spectra.

Ptychography, borrowed from coherent imaging, exploits redundancy across overlapping measurements. Their framework adapts those algorithms to rebuild the full complex response function. Three rebuild schemes fit three test situations. One uses a known analyzer response, one works blind, and one folds in extra constraints. Richer response data would sharpen how X-ray light probes nuclear transitions. The schemes are presented as complementary tools rather than rivals.
arxiv-2511-05124:
Felix Divo and co-authors present QuAnTS, a data set for answering questions about time series, a field that has drawn far less work than image or text questions. Text can open dense numeric records to users and aid choices.

QuAnTS asks many kinds of questions about human motion, given as tracked skeleton paths over time. Models track the moving joints and reply in words. The set is built to be hard, so scores show real skill at linking numbers to language. It gives builders a shared test for time-aware question systems.
arxiv-2511-05224:
G. Lombardi and co-authors test how squeezing a crystal along one axis changes the anomalous Hall effect in Mn3Ge, a frustrated antiferromagnet with a hexagonal form. Tunable traits in such materials could serve in new spin-based devices.

X-ray tests show the crystal's axis ratio shifts in a straight line with strain along one axis, and the crystal is much stiffer along the other. That straight-line shift mirrors what pressure from all sides does. The Hall response under one-axis strain gives a clean knob for probing how lattice change steers electron flow in this magnet.
arxiv-2511-05524:
Ruiying Chen describes EviBound, a guard system for AI research agents that claim work is done when it is not. Such agents may mark a task complete even when files are missing, numbers clash, or code failed to run. EviBound blocks a claim unless machine-checked proof backs it up.

Two gates do the checking. One gate reviews the plan and its success rules before code runs. The other checks the outputs after the run, using stored run records and required files. On eight test tasks, a prompt-only setup let every false claim through. EviBound let none through, with only a small rise in run time.
arxiv-2511-05724:
Mariane Souza-Gomes and co-authors simulate inertial waves inside the Sun and other stars. Such waves were recently detected in the Sun through helioseismology, but what excites them and what they do to solar plasma and magnetism is poorly understood. The team uses global computer simulations to watch them start and evolve.

First they check their setup on a rigidly rotating sphere, where an imposed wobble excites neighboring wave modes as theory expects. Then, with realistic differential rotation switched on, they find the waves grow mainly through baroclinic instability. High-latitude vortices spin backward near the poles, while weaker Rossby waves appear at the equator. Stronger shear lets the polar modes stir stresses that can move angular momentum.
arxiv-2511-06224:
Anmar Kareem and Alexander Aue test whether classic time series tools can forecast Bitcoin prices. They compare four models: ARIMA and SARIMA for price trends, plus GARCH and EGARCH for volatility, the size of price swings. Daily Bitcoin data from 2010 to 2020 supplied the test bed, with the last tenth held back for scoring.

Models were judged by error measures and information criteria that reward accuracy and simplicity. ARIMA gave the strongest short-run forecasts of log prices. EGARCH fit volatility best because it captures lopsided responses to shocks. Even with Bitcoin's extreme swings, the authors find classical models still useful for short-run forecasting.
arxiv-2511-06324:
Lukas Flajsman and colleagues grew thin films of erbium-substituted yttrium iron garnet and measured their magnetic and structural behavior. The material pairs the low magnetic loss of yttrium iron garnet with erbium's light emission in the telecom band. That mix suits hybrid devices linking microwaves to light, including quantum signal conversion.

Films with a range of erbium levels were grown by pulsed laser deposition on garnet substrates. Careful measurements confirmed clean single-phase growth with sharp interfaces throughout. More erbium lowered the saturation magnetization and widened the resonance line through added damping. Lightly substituted films stayed close to pure material behavior, keeping the low-loss traits that optomagnonic uses need.
arxiv-2511-06424:
Amit Vaisman and co-authors speed up image compression that uses diffusion models without any training on the target image. Zero-shot diffusion compressors have improved lately but remain notoriously slow. Their starting point, DDCM, compresses by picking noise vectors step by step from reproducible codebooks so the denoiser rebuilds the target picture.

Turbo-DDCM blends many noise vectors at each denoising step, cutting the number of steps sharply, and pairs that change with a better encoding protocol. Two flexible variants follow: one favors regions a user marks as important, and one targets a chosen quality level instead of a file size. Experiments place the method among the practical leaders.
arxiv-2511-06524:
Haihui Gao and colleagues stabilize an unknown linear system using only recorded inputs and outputs. The plant is a continuous-time system with several inputs and outputs, and no model equations are available. Recent output-feedback methods lean on special realizations but demand a uniform observability index, a strong assumption many systems fail.

Their key move reinterprets Kreisselmeier's adaptive filter as an observer for a stabilizable non-minimal realization of the plant. Filtering the collected experiment data through it produces a linear matrix inequality whose solution is the feedback gain of a dynamic stabilizer. The result covers a broad class of multi-input, multi-output systems without the observability restriction.
arxiv-2511-06624:
Soumyadip Patra and colleagues show that every Bell inequality hides a standard version untouched by a standard data cleanup. Bell tests probe whether nature admits local realistic descriptions, and raw data often carries faint signalling that analysts project away onto the no-signalling set before judging results. Whether that projection distorts the verdict matters for device-independent uses.

For any setup with several parties choosing among binary-outcome measurements, a canonical form of the inequality exists whose violation the projection leaves unchanged. The team derives a general closed formula for the projection, far cheaper to evaluate than older procedures. Non-standard versions of interest for particular uses fit the same generalization.
arxiv-2511-06924:
Simone D'Onofrio, Sergei Odintsov, and Tiziano Schiavone test an exponential version of f(R) gravity, a modification of general relativity, as a system for dynamical dark energy. The model behaves like the standard cosmological model at early times and departs smoothly later. The authors fit it jointly with the total mass of neutrinos, a quantity cosmology can constrain.

A Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis combines cosmic chronometers, the DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation data, the cosmic microwave background acoustic scale, and the Pantheon+ supernova compilation. The exponential model stays consistent with all observations while slightly easing the Hubble tension and the neutrino mass problem compared with the standard model. Its neutrino mass limits are tighter than those of a common phenomenological alternative.
arxiv-2511-07124:
Zhikang Chen and five co-authors stabilize the hidden reasoning of large language models. Chain-of-thought prompting reasons in visible tokens, which propagates errors and constrains expression, so recent work lets models reason in continuous latent space before answering. Those latent trajectories, however, can diverge and contradict themselves, because nothing enforces consistency between steps. The proposed EBM-CoT system calibrates latent thoughts with an energy-based model.

The energy model scores latent thought states, and calibration nudges trajectories toward low-energy regions where steps agree with each other. The base language model itself is left unmodified. Across mathematical, commonsense, and symbolic benchmarks, the system greatly improved both the consistency and the efficiency of multi-step work, suggesting latent reasoning benefits from an explicit consistency check before decoding.
arxiv-2511-07224:
Gabe Hoshino and six co-authors ask whether the Large Hadron Collider can hunt axions through their supersymmetric partners. In the supersymmetric DFSZ axion model, the axino couples at tree level to the Higgs sector. If R-parity is conserved, heavier neutralinos should decay into lighter, mostly axino states with displaced vertices, a distinctive signature. The team simulates a scenario where mostly higgsino states decay to a mostly axino lightest particle.

Using MadGraph event creation and MadAnalysis5 detector simulation with kinematic cuts, they map the experiment's reach. For higgsino masses below one teraelectronvolt, the collider with 140 inverse femtobarns of data can probe axion decay constants below a hundred billion gigaelectronvolts. The reach complements direct detection and astrophysical searches, opening supersymmetric axion models to current collider data.
arxiv-2511-07324:
Andrea Autieri and four co-authors refine predictions for Z boson production at hadron colliders like the LHC. The transverse momentum distribution of the Z is a precision yardstick, but computing it requires adding up large logarithmic effects from radiation emitted before the collision. This work performs that summing with quantum chromodynamics and quantum electrodynamics radiation treated together, a mixed calculation, at next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic order.

Adding the mixed corrections on top of the pure QCD result, the authors find percent-level effects on that spread. Percent-level shifts matter here because Z production is a standard candle for collider physics, used to benchmark detectors and to pull out basic parameters. The paper measures exactly how much the combined strong and electromagnetic radiation changes the expected spectrum.
arxiv-2511-07524:
Bruno Bucciotti, Felipe Figueroa, and Guilherme Pimentel map the heavy states of the open bosonic string. String theory predicts towers of massive particles organized in Regge trajectories, where spin grows with mass. Writing each state explicitly has long been laborious.

Using light-cone quantization, the authors give oscillator recipes for single states and whole trajectories. Transverse oscillators combine into clean rotation representations, and a climbing method adds oscillators step by step from seed states. Composition coefficients follow simple level patterns, yielding closed forms for infinitely many states. The catalog helps theorists test duality and scattering ideas against exact spectra.
arxiv-2511-07624:
Hristo Dimitrov, Viktorija Pavalkyte, and Giulia Dominijanni package motion tracking for non-specialists. Tracking without markers now serves behavior, clinic, and biomechanics studies, yet current toolkits demand heavy skill or fit only narrow tasks. TrackStudio merges proven open-source parts into one guided pipeline.

A simple screen covers recording and syncing, plus automatic pose tracking in two and three dimensions out of the box. Modular design lets users swap parts as needs grow. Labs without programmers can still capture animal or human movement well. Open tracking widens who can run movement studies, from small clinics to field researchers.
arxiv-2511-07824:
Zhiyao Zhang, Zhuqing Liu, and Xin Zhang formalize learning problems with two layers of conflicting goals. Modern systems stack decisions: an upper level chooses preferences or designs, a lower level optimizes within them, and several objectives pull against each other at once. Multi-objective bilevel learning names that structure, but its theory is young.

The study builds theoretical and algorithmic foundations, clarifying when such problems are tractable and how preference guidance at the upper level shapes lower solutions. Many applications, from hyperparameter tuning to policy design, hide this shape. Naming and analyzing it gives practitioners algorithms instead of improvisation when layered goals collide.
arxiv-2511-08124:
Alin Morariu, Jess Bridgen, and Chris Jewell present gemlib, a Python library for building and calibrating stochastic epidemic models. Deterministic outbreak models are simpler, but random state transition models capture chance events that matter in real epidemics. Their cost has kept them out of fast pandemic response work, despite their clearer interpretation.

Gemlib splits a model into three ingredients that fully define it and drive the computation. Simulation uses Gillespie and tau leaping methods, while Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers connect directly for calibration. Built on JAX and TensorFlow Probability, the library uses modern hardware so modelers can focus on structure and assumptions during an outbreak.
arxiv-2511-08324:
Pier Luigi Silvestrelli and co-authors use density theory to compare sliding in bilayers of transition metal dichalcogenides, layered materials valued as solid lubricants. Easy shearing between layers makes these compounds slick, and van der Waals forces dominate the grip between layers. Fourteen bilayers are studied, from molybdenum and tungsten compounds to vanadium, tantalum, titanium, hafnium, and zirconium variants, plus two mixed pairs.

Van der Waals corrected calculations confirm those forces supply most of the interlayer binding, though functional choice shifts exact numbers. Most bilayers bind more strongly and show greater surface corrugation than the molybdenum disulfide reference. A few, including titanium and zirconium sulfides, slide more easily, and links to electronic traits are explored.
arxiv-2511-08624:
Andrés Ledesma and Karo Michaelian ask around which kinds of stars carbon-based life is most likely to start. Their lens is non-equilibrium thermodynamics: life begins, on this view, when ultraviolet light drives molecules into ordered structures that dissipate energy.

For Earth-like planets around star types from hot O stars to cool M dwarfs, they compute surface photon fluxes in helpful and destructive ultraviolet bands. They then track how fast basic molecules build up under different decay rates. Sun-like G stars and their F and K neighbors give the highest molecule levels within weeks to months. Quiet M dwarfs fare far worse, and flaring ones damage the surface. The authors conclude life most plausibly starts around F, G, and heavy K stars.
arxiv-2511-08824:
Yi Yang and twenty co-authors caught a supernova in the act of breaking out of its star, and measured the shape of that breakout with light polarization. The nearby type II supernova 2024ggi was observed by spectropolarimetry starting only about one point two days after explosion, earlier than such measurements usually begin.

The polarization reveals a well-defined symmetry axis for the shock breakout itself. The same axis persists in the hydrogen-rich envelope that appeared once the ejecta swallowed the surrounding circumstellar material. A single stable axis running through the whole event favors explosion mechanisms that act coherently on large scales, whether neutrino reheating or jet power drives them. How massive stars launch their death shock has puzzled astronomers for decades, and this geometry is a fresh constraint.
arxiv-2511-09124:
Ryan Babbush and eight colleagues from the Google Quantum AI team lay out what it will actually take to make quantum computers useful. Their perspective separates promising paths from hard hurdles. They organize the road into five stages, from early theoretical studies of quantum advantage through compilation and resource costing for real machines.

Two middle stages get flagged as both essential and under-resourced: naming concrete problem instances where quantum advantage should appear, and tying those problems to genuine real-world uses. The essay also weighs criteria for a compelling advantage demo, the help AI itself might give this research, and how code translation changes as early fault-tolerant machines arrive. Each stage mixes scientific goals with social roadblocks, and the authors are frank about both.
arxiv-2511-09424:
Henrique de Oliveira and Jeffrey Mensch characterize when an inattentive decision-maker's information costs take a clean closed form. The agent has rationally inattentive preferences over menus of acts, meaning information is valuable but costly to process. The question is which extra assumptions force the cost into that form, depending only on beliefs before and after learning.

Two axioms, Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives and Ignorance Equivalence, turn out to be necessary and sufficient. The cost must also meet a mild smoothness requirement the authors define. Reading the problem as Bayesian persuasion, the same axioms characterize solvability by a unique hyperplane. When costs stay fixed across priors, the axioms yield costs of that same form everywhere.
arxiv-2511-09724:
Yunqian Cheng and two co-authors upgrade a floor-plan-based indoor localization system. It works where GPS cannot, using only a phone camera and a map. The earlier PALMS system needed a stationary scan and was limited by smartphone LiDAR's short range and by ambiguous indoor layouts. Emergency response and assistive navigation motivate something better.

PALMS+ reconstructs scale-aligned three-dimensional point clouds from posed photographs. A monocular depth foundation model supplies the depths, and convolution matches layouts against the floor plan. It outputs a probability distribution over position and orientation. On benchmark and campus datasets it beat PALMS and F3Loc at stationary localization with no training. A particle-filter version tracked real trajectories more accurately too.
arxiv-2511-09924:
Hu Zhang, Zhien Dai, Zhaohui Tang, and Yongfang Xie propose MDMLP-EIA, a forecasting model for time series built from multilayer perceptrons rather than attention. Perceptron models are lean and robust, but they can lose weak seasonal signals, run short of capacity when channels multiply, and fuse channels poorly. The design answers each weakness with a named mechanism.

An adaptive dual-domain seasonal module separates strong and weak seasonal parts and fuses channels with little noise. An energy invariant attention focuses on different feature channels while keeping total signal energy constant, which fits the decompose, predict, and rebuild pipeline. A dynamic rule scales neuron counts with channel count. Across nine benchmark datasets, the model reached state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2511-10024:
Ayush Sahu, Richa Arya, Sergio E. Jorás, and Karim H. Seleim study warm inflation, a version of cosmic inflation where the inflaton stays coupled to a radiation bath. Their model uses a quartic potential and a dissipation coefficient built from two terms that dominate at different scales. The early term governs the large scales seen in the cosmic microwave background, while the second term grows key at small scales.

Inflation then runs in two stages: a strongly dissipative first phase producing a red-tilted spectrum matching microwave background observations. Then a second phase, with a blue tilt, amplifies small-scale power enough to form primordial black holes. The authors vary phase durations and dissipation strength to map the spectrum, and check the model against swampland and trans-Planckian conjectures from quantum gravity.
arxiv-2511-10224:
Udvas Das, Binayak Dutta, Satyabrata Jana, Debabrata Pal, and Sasanka Roy study witness sets in polygons, a visibility concept from computational geometry. Two points in a polygon see each other when the segment between them stays inside. A witness set is a set of points such that every point of the polygon is visible from at most one of them. Finding the largest witness set is the problem, in continuous and discrete variants.

The authors give a polynomial-time method for the discrete variant in general polygons. For monotone polygons they discretize the continuous problem, generating a candidate point set that must contain a large witness set if one exists. That yields an exact method and also an approximation scheme with strong guarantees for the monotone case, building on earlier work on monotone mountains.
arxiv-2511-10324:
Matteo Taffetani and Matteo Pezzulla build a theory for thin elastic shells that change shape under non-mechanical stimuli, such as growing tissue or swelling matter. Large deformations, rotations, and incompatible internal strains are the norm in such systems; the eversion of the Volvox embryo is their motivating example. Starting from a fully nonlinear 3D model, they derive a reduced 2D morphoelastic energy for naturally curved shells.

Earlier morphoelastic theories covered flat plates; this one handles curvature and stimuli acting through the thickness. Two matter laws, incompressible Neo-Hookean and compressible Ciarlet-Geymonat, show how compressibility and curvature steer snap-through and global shape change. Applications include everting spherical shells and vesiculation in living systems.
arxiv-2511-10824:
Inga Girshfeld and Xiaohui Chen build a regression method for data whose inputs and outputs are whole probability distributions. Standard approaches lean on a single global transport map or on linearizing around a tangent space. Those choices can restrict what the model can express and warp the geometry, especially in several dimensions.

Their Neural Local Wasserstein Regression works locally, in analogy with kernel regression. Kernel weights built from the Wasserstein distance focus each estimate near a reference distribution, while neural networks parameterize the transport maps so they can adapt to complicated geometries. Training uses DeepSets-style architectures with Sinkhorn-approximated losses and a greedy scheme for choosing reference points. On synthetic and image-based tasks, the method captured nonlinear distributional relationships that existing methods missed.
arxiv-2511-10924:
Lise Waldek, Brian Ballsun-Stanton, and their colleagues ask when scholars may use hacked data with a clear conscience. Their case is research on far-right violent extremism online, where leaked files can show groups that hide from open study. Rules made for older kinds of research give little firm guidance here.

Through the case, the authors show the doubts that such work raises for safety, consent, and harm. They argue that ethical use is possible in some settings, but only if scholars keep weighing those doubts at each step. The study offers a careful path for others who face the same hard choice with leaked data.
arxiv-2511-11124:
Tuochao Chen, Bandhav Veluri, and their colleagues present AV-Dialog, a spoken dialogue system that listens and watches at the same time. Voice-only systems falter in noisy rooms with many speakers, giving off-topic replies and awkward turn-taking. Seeing the speaker's face gives cues that sound alone cannot supply in such settings.

AV-Dialog uses sound and vision together to track the target speaker, judge when a turn ends, and form apt replies. Training mixes solo, synthetic, and real dialogue data in stages. Tests show fewer transcription errors, better turn-taking, and higher human ratings than sound-only models, which points to richer agents for real noisy rooms.
arxiv-2511-11424:
Simon Badger, Matteo Becchetti, and their colleagues compute one hard part of a precision prediction. The process is top-quark pair production with an extra jet at a hadron collider. The order is next-to-next-to-leading in quantum chromodynamics. The part computed here is the double virtual part. It comes from two-loop amplitudes, with infinite terms subtracted off.

The finite rest is extracted in exact form. The extraction uses evaluations over finite fields. A basis of special functions carries the result. The team then builds the summed interference with the tree-level amplitudes. They release a C++ library ready for use in physics studies. New techniques evaluate the special functions by direct numeric integration. They perform well across the full phase space.
arxiv-2511-11524:
S. K. Steensen and thirteen co-authors tackle a practical headache in materials computing: density functional theory codes each speak their own input and output language, so results are hard to compare or reuse. Workflow tools such as AiiDA, PerQueue, Pipeline Pilot, and SimStack all face the same translation problem.

A common input and output standard lets those tools convert jobs into one unified schema that runs across codes including CASTEP, GPAW, Quantum ESPRESSO, and VASP. As a test, the team computes open-circuit voltages for several battery cathode materials and documents where energies from different engines disagree. The standard is a step toward results that others can check and build on.
arxiv-2511-11824:
Zhongping Dong and four co-authors present SOTFormer, a deliberately minimal transformer that tracks a single object and predicts its short-term path in one unified model. Occlusion, scale change, and drift over time break the temporal coherence real-time perception depends on.

Constant memory is the design constraint: a ground-truth-primed memory and a burn-in anchor loss stabilize identity from the start, and one lightweight temporal attention layer refines features across frames. Detection, tracking, and trajectory forecasting share the same end-to-end framework with fixed graphics memory. Results on a Mini-LaSOT benchmark subset test whether minimal machinery can hold identity as reliably as heavier stacked encoders.
arxiv-2511-11924:
Yongkang Huo, Fulvio Forni, and Rodolphe Sepulchre present a neuromorphic control design built from one motif. The motif is the rebound winner-take-all circuit. It is scaled from cells to whole systems. Brains mix discrete choices with smooth tuning with ease. Built controllers usually force a pick between the two styles.

Winner-take-all state machines supply the discrete side. Excitable biophysical circuits supply the smooth tuning side. Both are described in one physical modeling language. Rhythm generation and decision making share one event-based frame. A snake robot's nervous system shows the design in action. It shows versatility, robustness, and modularity in one build.
arxiv-2511-12324:
Naomi Fokkens and Fei Xue show a new route to flipping a perpendicular magnet reliably without an external magnetic field, a key step for spintronic memory. Standard schemes need explicit symmetry breaking to make the switch deterministic. Their idea uses higher harmonics of spin-orbit torque, the twist exerted on magnetization by a current.

Expanding the torque in vector spherical harmonics reveals extra fixed points away from the equator, and those points allow clean reversal when the higher harmonics are strong enough. First-principles work on the Weyl ferromagnet PrAlGe supports the picture: its band structure and strong spin-orbit coupling make the higher terms sizable, while the usual terms stay weak.
arxiv-2511-12424: Montserrat Vite proves a result about extremal divisors on the Hilbert scheme of points in the plane. That scheme is a space that describes finite sets of points. She takes point counts of two specific triangular forms. For those counts, being extremal is preserved under residuality. That operation passes between a divisor and its residual pair on the scheme.
arxiv-2511-12724:
Nazmiye Alemdar, Hürmet Fulya Akız, and Halim Ayaz develop connectedness ideas inside soft topology, a framework where sets come with a parameter attached. They define a soft version of the usual topology on the real line and use its interval to define a soft path. With paths in place, they define soft connectedness and soft path connectedness, study how the two notions relate, and show both survive under soft continuous mappings between spaces.

The paper then follows these properties into soft topological groups, where the group operations and the topology must fit together. It closes by building the category of such groups, naming its morphisms, and proving the category is symmetric monoidal, a structure that supports well-behaved combinations of objects. The contribution is foundational: it extends familiar topology language into the soft setting and gives later work a checked set of definitions and preservation results.
arxiv-2511-13024:
Aneesh Sivasankaran and eight co-authors simulate what black hole winds do when galaxies collide. Using the SMUGGLE model plus refinement that follows black hole feedback down to tens of parsecs, they compare merging and isolated galaxies, with and without the winds. The comparison spans three galaxy types: Milky Way analogues, gas-rich Sbc galaxies, and Small Magellanic Cloud analogues.

Feedback and merging amplify each other most in the Milky Way-like systems, where winds grow stronger as the merger thickens the disks. In the vigorously star-forming Sbc mergers, the winds matter mainly after star formation fades. The sharpest surprise concerns small galaxies: their clumpy medium knocks low-mass black holes off center, wandering kiloparsecs away, starving them of fuel and feedback.
arxiv-2511-13124:
Changxi Chi and six co-authors predict how a single cell's gene expression will shift under a drug or genetic perturbation, without ever seeing the same cell twice. Sequencing destroys the cell, so data are inherently unpaired: control cells and perturbed cells are different cells. The authors model the trip from one population to the other with a Schrödinger bridge. The entropy-regularized optimal transport process that finds the most plausible stochastic path between two distributions, conditioned on each perturbation.

Earlier bridge approximations inferred the coupling between source and target by modeling both directions, which is ill-posed. This work pairs cells with minibatch optimal transport instead, directly guiding bridge learning, and trains two bridges jointly, one for discrete gene activation states and one for continuous expression levels. The pairing makes the approximation scalable and more precise.
arxiv-2511-20324:
Prieto-Montañez and Selvaggi separate two look-alike surfaces that share a derived category. Their 2025 paper studies Gushel-Mukai surfaces and Fano fourfolds. Derived equivalence means two spaces share their sheaf categories. Isomorphism is the stricter notion of being the same. K3 surfaces can differ on exactly that line.

Very general dual Gushel-Mukai surfaces give the example. They are derived equivalent and L-equivalent simultaneously. Yet they are provably not isomorphic to each other. Fourier-Mukai transforms realize the categorical sameness. The argument builds on Kuznetsov and Perry's framework. Attention then shifts to Fano fourfolds of K3 type. A family of them carries two natural decompositions. Two splittings divide their derived categories differently. A duality relates the two splittings. A question by Bernardara and co-authors is answered. Same category does not force same shape. Categories remember less than the spaces themselves.
arxiv-2511-20424:
Krasnov surveys flat superconducting junctions as building blocks for future electronics. His 2025 review covers planar Josephson junctions. Standard junctions stack two superconducting layers like a sandwich. Planar ones sit side by side in a single plane. That simple geometric change alters their physics deeply.

Planar geometry boosts sensitivity to magnetic fields. It also improves impedance matching for terahertz devices. The flat layout allows drastic miniaturization of components. Recent highlights include junction-on-cantilever sensors for magnetic imaging. Those sensors reach super-resolution in scanning measurements. Vortex-based memory cells store bits in swirling currents. Programmable superconducting diodes steer current in one direction only. The review also lists requirements and open challenges. Semiconductor electronics keeps hitting power and heat walls. Data volumes near 200 zettabytes sharpen the search for alternatives. Planar junctions are positioned as one enabling technology.
arxiv-2511-20824:
Nour G. Al Hassanieh, Alex H. Barnett, and Leslie Greengard present in 2025 a fast way to compute how waves spread from many sources in open space. Direct calculation grows quadratically: each source must be checked against each target at each time step. Their scheme splits the wave field into a local part handled directly and a smooth history part tracked on a Fourier grid. Truncating the wave kernel in space keeps the grid part stable.

The payoff is steep. Work drops from quadratic in the number of sources to near-linear, with a grid term set by the highest frequency present. The team runs it on up to a million sources and targets. Accuracy reaches six digits. Because the method needs no artificial absorbing boundaries, it suits scattering problems in acoustics and optics where waves must leave the scene cleanly.
arxiv-2511-20924:
Weronika Jakubowska and colleagues present in 2025 GaINeR, a way to store a 2D image as a continuous neural function that a user can still grab and edit. Classic implicit representations map each coordinate to a colour through a network, giving crisp reconstruction but no handles to grab. GaINeR scatters trainable Gaussian blobs over the image. For any pixel, it gathers the K nearest Gaussians, blends their learned embeddings by distance, and lets a network turn the blend into colour.

The Gaussians give the picture explicit geometry. Dragging them in space produces semantically consistent, photometrically coherent edits, warping content rather than smearing it. Because the blobs behave like discrete physical entities, the representation can couple to physics engines for animation and dynamic effects. The authors report state-of-the-art 2D reconstruction quality while keeping the representation continuous. Code is public, aimed at interactive and physically aware image tools.
arxiv-2511-21224:
Ruofeng Feng, Jack R. C. King, and Steven J. Lind present a smarter way to simulate fluids around awkward shapes in 2025. Their mesh-free framework skips the fitted grid most simulators need and instead computes flow directly at scattered points, rebuilding local polynomial approximations around each one. The new twist is p-adaptivity: the polynomial order, which controls local accuracy, rises or falls at each point as the solution demands.

Feng and his coauthors steer that adjustment with a fresh error indicator built from the local Laplacian estimate, added at minimal computing cost. Tests on standard equations and on a two-dimensional reacting flow through porous material showed the scheme catching sharp, nonlinear regions where high order matters. For the cases studied, the adaptive method saved up to 50 percent of computing cost while holding the target accuracy, beating the fixed-order version.
arxiv-2511-21324:
Zhangchi Chen and Zihao Ye answer in 2025 a question from complex dynamics about when tuned integer sequences can settle into a cycle. The question arose from Astorg and Thaler's hunt for wandering domains, regions that drift forever under iteration, in skew-product maps of two complex variables. Their construction needs an increasing integer sequence where each term equals alpha times the previous term, plus beta times its logarithm, with the error converging.

Astorg and Thaler had shown such sequences exist exactly when alpha has the Pisot property, a condition about how powers of alpha approach whole numbers. Their question: must a certain combination of beta and alpha be rational for the error to converge to a cycle rather than a limit? Chen and Ye prove yes, whenever alpha is an algebraic number. The result tightens the number-theoretic gate through which any wandering-domain construction of this type must pass.
arxiv-2511-21424:
Neeraj Kumar, Ankur Srivastav, and Phongpichit Channuie rebuild black holes without their central flaw and then merge them on paper, in 2025. Ordinary black hole solutions contain a singularity, where physics breaks down. The Simpson-Visser scheme surgically removes it with one extra parameter, and the authors apply that scheme to black holes in anti-de Sitter space, a universe with a built-in negative cosmological constant.

Kumar and his coauthors verify that the first law of black hole thermodynamics still holds for the regularized holes and derive a matching entropy formula. Free energy analysis reveals phase transitions that shift with the regularization parameter. They then collide two equal-mass regular black holes and test the second law: the allowed range for the merged hole's mass first widens, then falls sharply, as the parameter grows. Setting the parameter to zero recovers the standard black hole results throughout.
arxiv-2511-21524:
Rafael de Paula, Claudia Justel, Carla Oliveira, and Milena Carauba map out extreme networks by brute force, in a 2025 spectral graph theory study. Their graphs are k-path graphs, built around a spine path of length k. Two spectra matter. Algebraic connectivity, defined as the Laplacian matrix's second smallest eigenvalue, gauges how hard the graph is to split. The alpha-index, the largest eigenvalue of a matrix blending adjacency and degree information, is the second.

De Paula and his coauthors first generate complete lists of non-isomorphic k-path graphs: all 2-paths up to 26 vertices, 3-paths up to 19, and 4-paths up to 18. Exhaustive searches over those lists identify which shapes maximize or minimize each eigenvalue at every size. Patterns in the winners become conjectures about the structure of extremal k-path graphs in general. The published lists, in standard graph format, give other researchers a ready testbed for spectral questions.
arxiv-2511-21824:
Brown and colleagues simulate the smallest galaxies in the universe, ultra-faint dwarfs, to see how early radiation shaped which tiny halos of dark matter managed to form stars. Their LYRA simulations follow 65 halos at extremely fine resolution, each particle weighing only about 4 solar masses. They test two versions of the early Lyman-Werner background, ultraviolet light that destroys molecular hydrogen, which gas needs to cool and form stars.

Star formation began before redshift 8 in small progenitors. The stronger radiation background shifted the dividing line between dark and star-bearing halos from about ten million to about a hundred million solar masses. So far more small halos stayed dark. Galaxies above about a hundred thousand solar masses in stars barely noticed. Both versions produced a floor near 1,000 solar masses, from systems that formed stars once, then shut down via their first supernovae.
arxiv-2511-22024:
Litman, a researcher at Stanford, revisits equilibrium propagation. A learning rule for neural networks that avoids backpropagation's separate backward pass by comparing a network's free-running state with a gently nudged state where the output is pushed toward the target. The classic theory only justifies the rule when the nudge is infinitesimally small, which makes the learning signal vanishingly weak and noisy in practice, limiting the method's usefulness.

Litman treats network states as probability distributions rather than single points. He proves the classic contrastive Hebbian update is an exact gradient of the free-energy difference for nudges of any size, with no convexity assumptions. He also derives a generalized equilibrium propagation algorithm from the path integral of loss-energy covariances, built for strong error signals. Unlocking finite nudges, the conclusion argues, fixes the signal-to-noise problem that cripples the infinitesimal version.
arxiv-2511-22124:
Santra, Kale, Giacintucci, Bourdin, Jain, Botteon, and Brunetti present the first detailed radio analysis of the giant halo in Abell 2163, a merging galaxy cluster. Combining new upgraded GMRT and VLA observations from 300 to 1400 MHz with archival X-ray data lets them map the halo's structure and spectrum in unusual depth.

The halo emission extends about 3.3 megaparsecs, out to the cluster's characteristic radius, with brightness falling exponentially and the radio spectrum steepening outward. Radio halos are vast synchrotron glows tracing relativistic electrons and magnetic fields in the intracluster plasma. Radio and X-ray brightness correlate with a slope near 0.70 for the halo, and diffuse lobes at the periphery may supply seed electrons, reaching roughly 0.1 percent acceleration efficiency outside. An east-west merger driving turbulence is proposed as the halo's engine, and nonthermal components carry at least several percent of the thermal energy.
arxiv-2511-22524:
Pourali, Hashemian, and Ardeshir-Larijani design an algorithm for linear regression when most data may be sabotaged. In list-decodable regression, only a fraction alpha of samples are genuine, the rest adversarial, so no single answer can be trusted. The goal is a short list of candidate fits guaranteed to contain one close to the truth. Earlier methods needed data arriving in clean batches, or used heavy sum-of-squares optimisation.

Their expander-sketching method manufactures its own batches using lossless expander graphs, sparse networks with strong connectivity, sorting samples into contaminated buckets. Robust aggregation by geometric median-of-means then produces statistics per bucket, and a spectral filtering stage removes directions where adversarial energy concentrates. The result matches the best known guarantees, with list size proportional to one over alpha and near-optimal sample use, running in near input-sparsity time, essentially as fast as reading the data.
arxiv-2511-22624:
Brodutch, Baimetov, Tham, and Delfosse strengthen a lightweight alternative to error correction. Clifford noise reduction, CliNR, is a partial error correction scheme lowering Clifford circuits' logical error rate for modest overhead. Its original version guarantees vanishing error only when circuit size times qubit count times the physical error rate squared shrinks to zero, excluding the largest circuits. The authors apply the scheme recursively, nesting it inside itself.

The recursive version needs qubits growing only like qubit count times a log factor, and drives logical error to zero under the weaker condition that qubit count times error rate vanishes. Simulations confirm a practical advantage: at fixed gate overhead, recursive CliNR reaches lower error rates than the original once circuits are large enough. This is especially so when idle errors are tiny, as with trapped ions. Such schemes may serve near-term utility-scale computing and later complement full error correction.
arxiv-2511-23424:
Alonso Alvarez and colleagues study how a principal should time bonus payments to a risk-averse agent whose effort cannot be observed. In a continuous-time mathematical contracting model over a finite horizon. Unlike contracts with payments at fixed dates, here the timing of sequential payments is itself chosen optimally. And the authors reformulate the resulting nonzero-sum interaction between principal and agent as a mixed control and stopping problem in the paper.

Numerical simulations then trace how the parties' relative impatience and the number of bonus payments shape the principal's value and the structure of the best scheme. A notable finding is that in some contractual environments the principal also optimally offers a sign-on bonus at the very start. Front-loading incentives rather than deferring them, a result the full framework explains through intertemporal incentive and participation constraints in practice.
arxiv-2512-00224:
Von Neumann algebras are the mathematical home of quantum mechanics and much of operator theory. Jananan Arulseelan begins a model-theoretic study of group actions on these algebras in 2025, expanding earlier work. The focus is dynamical systems where a group acts while preserving a weight.

The author axiomatizes continuous weight-preserving actions of locally compact Hausdorff groups on von Neumann algebras. Crossed products, which build new algebras from such actions, are part of the study. Model theory can reveal which properties of these systems follow from simple logical principles, a perspective algebraists are only starting to use. Crossed products turn symmetry actions into new algebras, a construction with many physical uses.
arxiv-2512-00524:
Hierarchical clustering groups data into a tree of nested clusters, a dendrogram. Guangjie Zeng and co-authors present a hyperbolic continuous structural entropy method for the task in 2025. Most existing methods specify dendrograms without any global objective to optimize.

Graph-based methods often neglect graph structure, optimizing on complete or fixed predefined graphs instead. Structural entropy gives a principled global objective, and hyperbolic geometry suits trees naturally. A better objective could produce hierarchies that reflect real structure in networks, from biology to social graphs, rather than artifacts of greedy merging. A global objective gives the clustering a target that greedy merging lacks. Hyperbolic space expands like a tree, which is why it hosts dendrograms comfortably. For folks who sort firms, genes, or posts into trees, the gain is a tree with a point. Each split can be scored, not just drawn by habit or haste.
arxiv-2512-00624:
Hilda asteroids circle the Sun in step with Jupiter, locked in a three-to-two resonance. Alexander Fleming and co-authors study rotational light-curve recovery for these objects in 2025, and predict what a coming survey will find. The Hildas offer a window into solar system evolution, including collisional processes.

The NSF-DOE Vera Rubin Observatory will run the ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time. Knowing how many Hilda light curves the survey can recover helps plan its asteroid science. Rotation periods reveal shapes and spin states shaped by billions of years of collisions in the outer asteroid belt. Light curves encode rotation in brightness dips as an asteroid tumbles.
arxiv-2512-01224:
Ruixiang Feng and a team from a hiring platform's lab present CoSineVerifier in a 2025 paper. Answer verification is widely used in training language models, for curating data, judging evaluations, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. A verifier checks whether a model's answer is right, so its own errors matter.

Prior work built unified verifiers for many reasoning settings. Questions that hinge on computation pose special challenges, like checking algebraic equivalence and using physical constants correctly. CoSineVerifier is a tool-augmented verifier built for those cases. Calling tools to recompute answers could make checking far more reliable in math and physics.
arxiv-2512-01324:
Samuel Young and Kazuhiro Terao work on reading data from argon detectors. These tanks give dense three-dimensional views of particle hits. They back big tests on neutrinos and rare events. Reading the hits now takes long chains of hand-built steps.

Those chains need large sets of labeled fake data and slow tuning. The team offers Panda, a method that learns from the data itself. It distills sensor-level traits that can be reused across tasks. Reusable traits could cut the need for fresh labels each time. That would speed up work for next-wave neutrino tests.
arxiv-2512-01424:
Xusen Hei and co-authors build a test for fixing errors in video reasoning. Large models that mix text and video often err on hard clips. Fixing those errors is key to growth. Past tests did not score that fixing skill in a set way.

Their test, ViRectify, asks models to spot and fix wrong steps in video thought chains. It spans many kinds of clips and errors. Scores show if a model can catch its own slips. That skill matters for safe use in class, work, and media tools where a wrong read can mislead users.
arxiv-2512-02124:
The Flame Nebula region, NGC 2024, is an active stellar nursery where the newest stars still move with the cloud that bore them. Alena Rottensteiner and eight co-authors measure in 2025 the motions of its young stellar objects using infrared proper motions, the slow drift of stars across the sky.

Because these objects formed most recently, their positions and dynamics trace the parent cloud's motion with little distortion. Comparing stellar motion with the gas reveals when the two decouple, a key timescale for how clusters form and disperse. Infrared measurements matter here because dust hides these young stars from ordinary visible-light surveys.
arxiv-2512-03124:
Finding the shape of a molecule from distances is a key task. Michael Souza, Júlio Araújo, John Kesley Costa, and Carlile Lavor study a step in that task in this 2025 work. The step is the ordered covering problem in distance geometry.

The order in which edges are pruned shapes how fast a search runs. That search, called SBBU, is used to find protein structures. The authors study how hard the ordering problem is in theory. Knowing its difficulty helps builders design better tools for protein work, where speed can decide if a method is practical. Better ordering tools could shorten the search for protein shapes from distance data.
arxiv-2512-03224:
Electric signals in brain tissue depend on its fine structure. Halvor Herlyng and co-authors model ion flow in dense reconstructions of cerebral tissue in this 2025 work. Brain tissue is so complex in shape that detailed modeling is a formidable task.

The team needs efficient numerical methods and robust code to handle real cell shapes. Their model covers electrodiffusion, the joint flow of ions and electric fields. Faithful models can explain how signals spread and where models of the brain go wrong. They also guide safer brain stimulation methods. Real tissue shapes, not idealized blocks, decide whether a model matches brain signals.
arxiv-2512-03324:
Long answers from language models need lots of memory. Ngoc Bui and co-authors present a smarter way to keep that memory small in this 2025 work. The key-value cache grows with text length, and self-attention costs rise fast.

Old fixes quantize, offload, or drop entries by rough attention scores, each with drawbacks. The authors keep tokens that last, based on lasting value rather than fleeting attention. Keeping the right tokens could let models handle long documents on limited hardware. That matters for chat and research tools. Token choice is a budget call, since each kept token costs memory through the whole reply.
arxiv-2512-03524:
Self-driving fleets run by competing firms could destabilize traffic. Grzegorz Jamróz, Rafał Kucharski, and David Watling model that risk in this 2025 work. Drivers may switch between individual routing and collective routing run by a fleet operator.

In individual routing, drivers pick routes that minimize their own travel costs. In collective routing, an operator assigns routes centrally to maximize market share. The authors study the dynamics and equilibria of this routing game. Their warning matters for cities planning rules for autonomous fleets. Chaos in routing would hurt all drivers, not just fleet customers, in dense cities.
arxiv-2512-03724:
Vision-language-action models let robots turn camera images and spoken instructions into movement, but their motions can wander. Ziwen Li and a large team diagnose that problem in a 2025 computer vision preprint. They blame a perception field that treats every part of the scene alike, so irrelevant objects distract the robot on the way to its target.

Their answer, PosA-VLA, anchors attention using pose information as supervision during training. The model learns to keep its gaze on regions that matter for the task, aligning instructions with the visual cues that support action. The design stays lightweight and needs no extra segmentation or grounding networks at run time. Across several manipulation benchmarks, the method produced more precise and quicker behaviour. It also held up in varied, challenging environments, suggesting the attention anchor generalises beyond the training scenes.
arxiv-2512-03824:
Galaxy surveys are about to map the universe with unmatched depth, and subtle relativistic effects ride along in those maps. Bartolomeo Bottazzi Baldi and co-authors examine one such effect in a 2025 cosmology preprint: our own motion through space. If analysis ignores how the observer moves, readings of primordial non-Gaussianity, a fingerprint of the early cosmos, can drift.

The team built LIGER4GAL, an updated simulation tool that inserts linear distortions of this kind directly into simulated galaxy catalogues. It reproduces expected clustering while staying accurate on the largest scales. Using it, they created a sample of luminous red galaxies resembling the coming DESI catalogue. They measured its power spectrum with and without those terms. Omitting this motion effect biased the signal by a full error bar in many possible worlds. Careful modelling, they conclude, is not optional for the coming surveys.
arxiv-2512-04024:
Cuprate superconductors are described by model Hamiltonians with several unknown parameters, and matching them to experiment is an expensive inverse problem. V. A. Ulitko and colleagues shortcut it with machine learning in a 2025 preprint. A trained network reads a phase diagram and predicts the parameters that produced it.

The team compared three deep learning architectures, VGG, ResNet, and U-Net, on the task. U-Net, adapted from image segmentation to regression, performed best. It was trained on a large set of phase diagrams computed in mean-field approximation, then validated against diagrams from a Monte Carlo heat bath method. The network predicted every Hamiltonian parameter accurately. Where accuracy dipped, the phase diagram barely changed with the parameter, so the information was not there. That makes failures interpretable, a quality physicists value highly.
arxiv-2512-04224:
Astronomy reaches far beyond telescopes: its skills and reach can serve global goals, if scientists know how to aim them. Joyful E. Mdhluli presents the LEBS Toolkit in a 2025 preprint written for the International Astronomical Union's Office of Astronomy for Development. The toolkit gives astronomers a way to tackle real-world challenges through their field.

It aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and rests on four components. Leadership, Externalities, Breaking Barriers to Entry, and Supporting Functioning Markets and Institutions supply the initials. Using them, scientists can spread accurate information, encourage positive local impacts, and push against monopolistic barriers. The last one targets market efficiency and institutional settings. Mdhluli frames the toolkit as a bridge between scientific knowledge and practical action. It guides the community toward outcomes serving global goals.
arxiv-2512-04424:
Thomas Macleod, Sebastian Oberst, David Powell, and Yan Kei Chiang show how a single sound sensor, paired with a patterned plate, can tell where a sound came from. Finding a sound's direction usually takes bulky microphone arrays that draw heavy power. Acoustic metagratings offer a leaner path: a surface with fine structure that bends sound in coded ways. Their 2025 arXiv paper turns that coding into a direction finder.

Sound hits the grating and lands on one sensor as a compressed pattern. From that pattern, the system works out the arrival direction across a half circle and a full circle. Simulations showed the method holds up under noise and sparse sampling. Bench tests with built prototypes confirmed the idea works in hardware. Against array systems, the single-pixel design cuts hardware sharply while keeping accuracy, a gain for small robots, drones, and hearing devices.
arxiv-2512-04524:
Tianle Hu, Weijun Lv, and Na Han present PSCA, a method for searching across domains when labels exist for one domain but not the other. A photo search tool trained on product shots, for instance, may falter on user photos. Domain adaptive retrieval tries to carry knowledge across that gap. Their 2025 arXiv paper faults older tools on three counts: they align single pairs while ignoring class meaning, trust fake labels blindly, and hash shifted features directly.

PSCA works in two stages. First, a set of fixed class prototypes builds class-level links between domains, pushing classes apart while tying matches together. Later stages check fake label quality with geometric cues before trusting them. Cleaner features then feed the hashing step that makes search fast. The authors report stronger cross-domain search than prior tools. Such gains help catalogs and archives where new collections arrive without labels.
arxiv-2512-04724:
Brennan Hughes, Christoph Bruder, and Tobias Kehrer study swarmalators, model agents that both move together and tick in sync, like birds that flock and fireflies that flash as one. Each agent has a position and an internal phase. Past work forced the phases from outside. Their 2025 arXiv paper instead applies a pseudo-force that pulls agents toward the center of their spread through their positions alone.

Under that inward pull, the swarm shifts its collective state. Splintered and restless phase-wave patterns give way to a still, anti-synchronized order. The agents settle into crystal-like arrays, each ticking against its neighbors. To grade that crystallinity, the team built an order parameter from the Fourier transform of the positions. The result links centering forces to pattern choice in active matter. It may inform designs for robot swarms that must form ordered arrays on cue.
arxiv-2512-04924:
Weijian Zhang, Prateek Chennuri, and Hashan Weerasooriya present a single-photon LiDAR simulator that is both faithful and fast, breaking a standing trade-off. Such sensors count individual photons to build three-dimensional maps, prized in darkness and fog. Simple Poisson simulators run quickly but misstate photon statistics. Sequential simulators are exact yet painfully slow. Their 2025 arXiv paper rebuilds the core statistics with a Markov-renewal process.

The new formulation predicts, in closed form, the mean and variance of registered counts under detector dead time, the blind interval after each catch. A spectral truncation rule keeps the covariance math cheap. Proof of the process's shift-invariance then extends one pixel's model to whole histogram cubes through a precomputed lookup table. The team reports cubes indistinguishable from the slow sequential ground truth, at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2512-05124:
Christoph Dahl takes a fresh, information-based look at Kaprekar's routine, the number game where you sort a number's digits downward and upward and subtract. Repeated, the process famously funnels four-digit numbers to a single fixed point and three-digit numbers to another. Dahl asks a broader question: how does the whole state space drain toward these attractors, and how does the picture change with the number of digits?

He enumerates every state for three through six digits and builds what he calls entropy funnels from how the population spreads across attractors over the steps. Despite the exploding number of states, typical distances stay small and disorder drains fast before a slow tail. Grouping numbers by shared digits, then by simple gaps between digits, he shows the routine becomes nearly predictable from gap features for three digits, but the trick fades as digits are added.
arxiv-2512-05224:
Miguel de Oliveira Guerreiro presents NVLang, a typed language for the actor-based systems that run telecom and messaging infrastructure. On the BEAM virtual machine, programs like Erlang's achieve legendary reliability with millions of concurrent connections, but actors exchange free-form messages checked only at runtime. A mistyped message then becomes a production failure. NVLang aims to catch protocol errors at compile time without giving up the model's simplicity.

Its key idea is that algebraic data types naturally encode an actor's message protocol. Each actor declares the sum type of messages it accepts, and typed process identifiers carry that protocol with them. Typed futures make request-reply exchanges safe. Extending Hindley-Milner inference to track protocols, the compiler rejects programs that could send a wrong message. NVLang compiles to Core Erlang, interoperates with the ecosystem, and comes with soundness proof sketches — well-typed programs cannot violate actor protocols.
arxiv-2512-05524:
Chinthani Sugandhika, Chen Li, Deepu Rajan, and Basura Fernando teach scene-graph models to understand videos with help from vision-language models. A spatio-temporal scene graph lists the objects in a video and how their relationships evolve: who is holding what, who approaches whom. That gives downstream systems an interpretable scaffold for captioning and question answering. Current one-stage models have two weaknesses: their learnable queries start out semantically blank, and they classify relationships from vision alone.

Their framework, VOST-SGG, initializes queries from two sources at once, separating what to attend to from where to attend, so the queries arrive semantically grounded. A feature bank then fuses visual, textual, and spatial cues drawn from a vision-language model for relationship classification. On the standard Action Genome benchmark the method reaches state-of-the-art performance, evidence that borrowed commonsense from big multimodal models repairs both weaknesses at once.
arxiv-2512-05824:
Hafsa Akebli, Adam Shephard, Vincenzo Della Mea, and Nasir Rajpoot built an AI agent that predicts a key mutation in low grade gliomas, cancers of the brain's support cells. The mutation, in the IDH1 gene, splits these tumors into groups with different outlooks and treatments. Their Multimodal Oncology Agent combines a vision tool that reads tumor tissue images with reasoning over clinical and genomic records, enriched by PubMed, web, and OncoKB searches.

The agent was scored on nearly five hundred patients from a public cancer cohort, against clinical and tissue based baselines. Without its vision tool, the agent already beat the clinical baseline, so its record based reasoning carries real signal. Fused with the tissue features, it reached the best score, ahead of either source alone and ahead of their simpler fusion. Mutation clues hide in both the image and the record, and outside knowledge helps pull them together.
arxiv-2512-05924:
A De Vita, V Polewczyk, G Panaccione, and G Vinai report that soft X-rays can partly heal the surface of a fragile magnetic crystal. The material, vanadium triiodide, is a layered van der Waals crystal prized for its magnetic and orbital behavior. It is also hygroscopic, drinking moisture from air and degrading. Two X-ray spectroscopies tracked the damage and the repair.

Fresh and aged crystals alike show the surface decaying into vanadates. Shining a high flux soft X-ray beam on the aged surface reverses part of the harm: the chemical and electronic fingerprints move back toward the clean crystal's. Restoration by the measuring beam itself is double edged. It offers a way to refresh samples, and warns that the probe is an intervention. Both lessons matter for building with it.
arxiv-2512-06224:
Mohammadhossein Mohammadisiahroudi and four co authors review work on speeding up a core math tool with quantum computers. Interior point methods solve large planning and learning problems, such as how to route goods or train a model, by walking a path inside the set of valid answers. They are fast in theory, but each step can cost a great deal on dense, huge inputs.

Quantum versions try to hand the heaviest linear algebra steps to quantum hardware. The review tracks how these hybrids deal with noise, error, and badly scaled problems, using tricks such as step by step fixes and rescaling. The authors also set out their own near exact version, which builds and solves the key system on the quantum side while updates stay classical. They argue it scales as well as theory allows, pointing to where quantum help may first pay off.
arxiv-2512-06324:
Donghyun Park, Junhyun An, Taehyoung Kim, and Jisu Kim build a test for whether a signal repeats in cycles, based on the shape of its path. When a time series is unfolded into space by a delay method, a repeating signal traces a loop, while a non repeating one does not. Shape based tools can spot the loop, but users need to know how much to trust the spot.

The team first proves the loop claim in strict form, and shows the unfolded path keeps a stable margin that protects its shape. Next, they resample the data to build error bounds around the shape summary, with guarantees that hold as data grows. On top sits TopPT, a formal test whose error rates can be kept in check. Trials on fake data and on heart and breathing records show the method finds true cycles with few false alarms.
arxiv-2512-06524:
Saekwang Nam and four co authors give a soft robot finger a sense of touch that sits away from the surface doing the touching. The finger uses the Fin Ray design, a ribbed structure borrowed from fish fins that wraps around objects. A hinge joins the soft finger to a rigid sensing block. When the finger presses, its bending travels through the hinge to a crossbeam studded with marker tipped pins, in the style of a known vision based touch sensor.

A camera inside watches the pins shift, and a neural network reads the pattern to report where contact happened and how deep it pressed. Tuning the pin layout and hinge angle gave fine accuracy, and sensing held up across many indenter shapes. In a pick and place trial with uncertain positions, the touch feedback clearly improved placement accuracy. The design is light and easy to scale.
arxiv-2512-06924: Milad Alshomary and co-authors present IXAM, an interactive tool for explaining how a model decides who wrote a text. Authorship models based on word embeddings can be accurate yet opaque: they output a name without showing their reasons. IXAM lets a user explore the model's embedding space directly and build an explanation from writing style features, zooming from broad traits down to fine detail. In a user study, people found these self-built explanations more valuable than ready-made stylistic ones.
arxiv-2512-07024:
I Sebastian Buhai builds a theory of why workers doing similar jobs earn such different wages, and why people keep moving between jobs. Standard search models take the ladder of job offers as given, which leaves them unable to explain both pay spread and mobility at once. In Buhai's model, the quality of each worker-firm match drifts randomly over time. Workers choose how hard to search while employed and when to quit, while firms set wages that depend on the match state.

The whole labor market settles into a stationary balance, framed as a mean field game, where the spread of match states shapes everyone's outside options. Matches survive only while their surplus stays above a threshold the model determines. Buhai proves such a balance exists and is unique under standard conditions, then computes it numerically against real evidence on job durations, wage growth, and mobility.
arxiv-2512-07624:
Yongbo Yu, Jari Peeperkorn, Johannes De Smedt, and Jochen De Weerdt wrote this 2025 paper on forecasting business processes. Managers often want to know how a process itself will change over time. Process model forecasting tracks the links between steps as those links rise and fall.

Earlier tests found that custom models barely beat simple statistics on this task. The link data are sparse and vary a lot from one process to another. The authors try time series foundation models, large networks pretrained on generic series. They test the models untuned, and again after fine-tuning. Even untuned, the foundation models forecast with lower error than models trained from scratch. Fine-tuning helps only a little, and the gain can vanish on small or complex logs. Ready-made use, they conclude, is a strong default for such data.
arxiv-2512-07824:
Rabe Abdalkareem wrote this 2025 software engineering paper on what developers borrow from the crowd. Platforms like Stack Overflow let programmers share and reuse hard-won experience. That sharing speeds work and shortens time to market, many studies agree.

What reuse does to software quality is far less studied. Basic questions, like what developers actually take from these platforms, lack answers. Abdalkareem runs several large-scale empirical studies to fill that gap. Stack Overflow and the npm package ecosystem supply the evidence. Reused knowledge does help practice, above all through reused code snippets. The help comes with costs that projects feel for years. Dependency overhead grows as borrowed packages pile up. Maintenance effort rises alongside that overhead. The findings feed data-driven advice for quality assurance teams. Continuous integration is examined as one line of defense. Used well, it can raise productivity while saving team resources.
arxiv-2512-07924:
Shant Baghram wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on searching for alien technology in gravity's glare. A Dyson swarm is a cloud of structures harvesting a star's or black hole's light. Around a primordial black hole, such a swarm would bend light in a telling way.

Gravitational microlensing watches a foreground mass brighten a background star. A swarm's parts are partly opaque and shift around at random. That restless cover would modulate the smooth lensing curve over time. Baghram builds a probabilistic framework for that modulation. Optical depth varies stochastically, and gaps follow their own random spread. He scans the parameter space and maps the resulting transit durations. Infrared excess and its peak wavelength offer a second signature to check. Rates of anomalous events under this model are also worked out.  The work extends the search for advanced civilizations to dynamic signals.
arxiv-2512-08024:
Ethan Levien and Jessica Rattray, applied mathematicians who study cell biology, posted a theoretical study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is cell size homeostasis, the way single cells keep their size steady across generations. They examine a continuous time stochastic model where feedback from cell size to growth and division runs only through size deviations from the cycle path.

In the linear regime, their model reduces to a simple harmonic oscillator pushed by random noise. That form yields closed expressions for size correlations between mother and daughter cells. The authors compare these with measures of size memory over many generations. Their analysis shows that coarse grained correlations can mislead, hiding the true feedback at work. They contrast their model with the common approach that hard codes the coarse pattern instead.
arxiv-2512-08124:
Zijiang Yang, a researcher in financial machine learning, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about managing a cryptocurrency portfolio. Most earlier work predicts the price path of one coin, such as bitcoin, and trades on that alone. Yang instead manages a group of coins together, using how they rank against each other.

At each time step, a neural network predicts the rank of future returns across the managed coins, and the portfolio weights follow those ranks. Backtests on real daily market data from May 2020 to November 2023 covered bull, bear, and flat markets. The method beat existing approaches, with strong risk adjusted returns over the full period. It also held up when transaction fees rose. The study argues that cross sectional ranking, not single coin forecasting, is the more robust way to run a long only crypto portfolio.
arxiv-2512-08324:
Ya Wang, Sargam M Mulay, and Lyndsay Fletcher, solar physicists, posted an observational study on arXiv in December 2025.
