They examine a pair of modest C class flares from June 2012 that produced an unusually strong extreme ultraviolet late phase. That phase, a second rise in warm coronal emission after the main flare, can disturb Earth ionosphere.

Observatory data show the late phase released several times more energy in warm passbands than the main peaks. The source was a sigmoid, an S shaped magnetic structure that never erupted. The flares rapidly energized it inside a complex field, heating its plasma past ten million degrees before it cooled into the late phase glow. Reconstructions suggest the sigmoid formed by reconnection between older J shaped loops. Its cooling ran in fast and slow stages, both led by conduction. Since estimated cooling is quicker than observed, steady reconnection likely kept feeding the heat.
arxiv-2512-08524:
Jawad Ibn Ahad, Maisha Rahman, Amrijit Biswas, and colleagues, computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Multimodal language models need huge parameter counts to align images with words, which makes them heavy and slow to deploy. The team shrinks them by swapping dense network blocks for compact hypercomplex layers, a change of number system rather than a cut in precision.

The swap happens gradually during training, block by block, along a residual interpolation schedule. Light reconstruction and distillation losses make each new compact layer inherit the behavior of the dense block it replaces. Across several vision language models, the compressed versions kept performance close to the originals. At the same time they cut parameters and computation sharply, and answered faster. The authors present progressive hypercomplex substitution as an architecture friendly compression path. It also stacks with ordinary low bit quantization, so the two savings can multiply.
arxiv-2512-08724:
Manos Plitsis and coauthors present a method to uncover hidden social biases in text to image models. Those models produce striking images, yet they often show bias tied to gender, race, and age. Current checks rely on curated prompt sets, which are costly to build and can miss odd prompts that still trigger biased output, even after debiasing work.

Their framework, Bias Guided Prompt Search, generates prompts automatically with the aim of maximizing bias in the images. A language model writes neutral prompts, while classifiers acting on internal model features steer its word choices toward biased regions. Tests on a widely used model and on a debiased model reveal many subtle, previously unreported biases. The prompts found are readable and could be typed by a normal user, making the tool a practical new way to audit image models.
arxiv-2512-09224:
Yuling Max Chen, Bin Li, and David Saunders revisit mean-variance portfolio choice, the classic problem of balancing investment return against risk over time. They add two complications. Prices can jump suddenly, and the investor explores by trying randomized actions, in the spirit of reinforcement learning. The mean-variance goal is also time-inconsistent: a plan that looks best today may not look best later.

Working in an equilibrium framework, the authors solve for the best exploratory policy an investor can commit to moment by moment. The answer is a bell-shaped distribution centered on the classical solution. They then build an actor-critic learning algorithm around that policy, and in simulations every learned parameter settles on its true value. On twenty-four years of real market data, their learned model made money in thirteen of fourteen tests, which they offer as evidence the approach can work in practice.
arxiv-2512-09624:
Victor Janeiro and Radu Saghin extend the theory of SRB measures, the invariant distributions describing how chaotic systems behave over the long term, to non-invertible maps on surfaces. D. Burguet had built them in a related setting. For maps that cannot be run backward, the constructions fail, and the authors adapt them for endomorphisms on the torus.

Their construction produces hyperbolic invariant measures whose conditional distributions along stable manifolds are continuous, a smoothness trait that makes them meaningful. They also maximize the folding entropy, the entropy which accounts for the map's folding, and the authors name them equidistributed inverse SRB measures. For dissipative changes to examples due to Andersson, Carrasco, and Saghin, they obtain existence, uniqueness, and continuity of them as the map varies. They add a statistical trait for the stable potential. The work rounds out the ergodic theory of surface maps.
arxiv-2512-09724:
Nikoloz Gigiberia compares three cosmological models against supernova data from a Bayesian standpoint, asking which description of the universe's expansion the evidence favors. The models are the standard model with a cosmological constant, a variant letting dark energy's equation of state float freely. The CPL model lets that equation of state evolve over time. Type Ia supernovae from the Dark Energy Survey's five-year dataset serve as the standard candles.

Parameter inference is done by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with the No-U-Turn sampler, implemented in NumPyro and analyzed with ArviZ. Model comparison uses Bayes factors computed with the bridgesampling library in R. All three models show similar predictive performance, but the freely floating dark energy variant earns stronger evidence relative to the standard model and the evolving variant. Gigiberia concludes that under the assumptions and data used, that middle model gives the better description of cosmic expansion.
arxiv-2512-09924:
Xinyu Liu leads a large team tackling video editing that requires reasoning, not just style changes. Modern unified video models understand and generate well, yet they fail at edits that demand physical plausibility and causal sense. The authors blame two gaps. Training and test data for reasoning aware editing are inadequate. Also, a model's reasoning skill sits disconnected from its editing skill, so understanding never guides the edit. They define a task, Reason-Informed Video Editing, and build a benchmark, RVE-Bench, to measure it.

Their method, ReViSE, trains the model to critique itself. Instead of an external reward model, the model's own vision language component scores its output during training. That score becomes a differentiable signal that directly refines the generator's reasoning as it edits. On the benchmark, ReViSE clearly beat its fine tuned counterpart on overall editing quality.
arxiv-2512-10124:
Dorian W. P. Amaral and colleagues work out how quantum sensor arrays could detect dark matter that is not a point but a lump. Ultraheavy dark matter, at or above the Planck mass, cannot be an elementary particle. It must be a composite object with real size. Arrays of precision accelerometers have been proposed to feel its gravitational tug as it passes. The authors study such objects interacting through gravity plus a new Yukawa force, and they try three shapes for the lump: a flat topped profile, a Gaussian, and an exponential falloff.

Monte Carlo analysis of the expected impulse signals, against thermal and quantum noise, yields sensitivity projections for a future array. The signal depends in a tangled way on three length scales: the lump's radius, the spacing between sensors, and the range of the new force.
arxiv-2512-10224:
A team led by Ragja Palakkadavath tackles federated learning when each client's data looks different. In federated domain generalization, hospitals, phones, or banks train local models, and a server merges them into one model that must work on clients it has never seen, without pooling private data. Many current methods quietly leak privacy by sharing statistics about client data. Others lose useful local adaptations when averaging models trained on non identical data. The authors fix both ends of the pipeline, in local training and in aggregation.

Locally, a technique called latent space inversion enforces domain invariance across client models while strengthening privacy. At the server, a weight aggregation plan prioritizes the parameters that matter most to each local model's predictions, instead of averaging everything blindly. Across extensive tests, the approach beat leading methods while using less communication, a real constraint for federated deployments.
arxiv-2512-10524:
Sai Bharath Chandra Gutha, Ricardo Vinuesa, and Hossein Azizpour use pretrained diffusion models to solve inverse problems, tasks like rebuilding a clean image from a blurred or partial measurement. A general diffusion model can serve many such problems without retraining, but existing ways of steering it lean on approximations or heavy computation. The authors propose a cleaner route to the most probable answer.

Their variational mode-seeking loss is applied at each reverse diffusion step and provably pulls the sample toward the maximum a posteriori estimate. The loss comes from a fresh view: matching the diffusion model's own belief about the clean image against the belief implied by the measurement. For linear problems it can be derived exactly, with no modelling shortcuts. Their VML-MAP algorithm then restores images across several tasks and datasets, matching quality while cutting computing time.
arxiv-2512-10724:
Alex Hocks and Benjamin Uekermann test a general-purpose coupling library on a climate-modelling benchmark. Earth system models are stitched together from components whose grids do not align, so coupling software must map data between meshes without wrecking accuracy. A recent benchmark by Valcke and others graded the mapping algorithms inside four specialised climate couplers, and the question is whether an outsider can compete.

preCICE was built for coupling in general, with a large community but no climate-specific tricks. The authors describe the preprocessing and postprocessing needed to make the benchmark run at all in preCICE, then report that version 3.3.0 matches the specialised tools overall. Its radial basis function mapping did notably better, with significantly lower errors. For modelling centres, the result suggests a shared, general library is a realistic alternative to bespoke couplers.
arxiv-2512-11024:
Richard Davison and Hanzhi Jiang study how heat and flow emerge in quantum field theories in one space dimension plus time. At high temperature, weak breaking of scale symmetry makes many features of the resulting fluid theory universal. The authors focus on a special pattern in stress correlations called pole skipping, where poles and zeros of a response function cross.

Using holographic models, which represent the quantum theory through gravity in a higher dimensional space, they locate those crossing points. The points lie outside the range where fluid theory is strictly controlled. Even so, resumming the fluid expansion near the light cone predicts exactly where they sit. The same resummation correctly gives the butterfly velocity, a measure of how fast chaos spreads in these theories.
arxiv-2512-11224:
S. Nibedita Swain and fellow authors combine two tricks to stretch quantum key spread over much longer distances. In continuous variable systems, secret keys are encoded in light waves, but loss and noise in fibres normally impose a strict rate limit for any setup without repeaters. Noiseless amplifiers can compensate for loss, while a technique called unitary averaging calms phase noise.

Putting the two jointly in an error correcting relay design, the authors show the combined protocol handles both thermal loss effects and phase swings at once. Crucially, the resulting key rates pass the repeaterless bound, the fundamental ceiling for direct transmission systems. The analysis holds under lifelike settings, including imperfect reconciliation between the communicating parties. The work points toward useful long distance quantum secure links without waiting for full quantum repeaters.
arxiv-2512-12024:
Nuno Macedo and Hugo Pacheco extend the Alloy design language so it can check hyperproperties. A hyperproperty speaks about several runs of a system at once, the form needed for security and concurrency claims. Alloy is a light formal method loved for early design checks, but it could not state such properties natively.

Their tool, HyperPardinus, stretches Alloy temporal backend to verify hyperproperties over relational design models using existing low level checkers. Counterexamples come back drawn at the design level, not as raw traces. Tests on known hard cases with alternating quantifiers show the approach works. Designers can now probe leaks and interference while the system is still a sketch.
arxiv-2512-12224:
Maaz Khan and four co-authors use large language models to hide private details in software data in a 2025 paper. Just in time defect prediction learns from code change records, but those records can leak private facts. Older hiding methods miss how software measures relate to each other, so they trade privacy and accuracy poorly.

The new method groups commits into clusters with like traits. A language model then sets hiding parameters for each cluster. On six projects, from Cassandra to Qt, it reached privacy level 2, beating four graph based methods by 18 to 25 percent on privacy. Its defect scores stayed about the same as before.
arxiv-2512-12324:
Meilin Li and seven co-authors present UniMark, a toolkit for marking AI made content, in a 2025 paper. AI text, images, audio, and video now spread fast, raising trust and legal concerns. Older tools are split by format and rarely support visible marks that rules may require for compliance.

UniMark offers one open source framework for all four formats. It supports hidden watermarking for copyright and visible marking for regulatory needs side by side. A shared engine hides format details from users. Three benchmarks for image, video, and audio give a standard way to test tools. The aim is a more transparent and secure digital space.
arxiv-2512-12424:
Tue-Thu Van-Dinh and five co-authors introduce ViInfographicVQA, a benchmark for answering questions about Vietnamese infographics, in a 2025 paper. Infographics mix text, charts, icons, and layout, so a model has to read text, parse layout, and reason with numbers at once. No benchmark covered this task in Vietnamese before.

The set holds over 6,747 real infographics and 20,409 human checked question answer pairs, spanning economics, health care, education, and more. One task uses a single image per question; a harder multi-image task needs evidence combined across related graphics. Top vision language models showed wide gaps, with the largest errors on cross image and non-span questions.
arxiv-2512-12924:
Gagan Deep, Akash Deep, and William Lamptey build a strict test framework for trading systems based on market microstructure signals. Many published systems overfit past data or peek at future data. Their method combines plain-language hypotheses with reinforcement learning and strict out-of-sample checks.

The framework was run across 34 test periods on 100 US stocks from 2015 to 2024. Results were modest: returns of 0.55 percent a year, a Sharpe ratio of 0.33, and a worst drawdown of minus 2.76 percent. Gains came in volatile years and not in calm ones, and the overall result was not statistically significant. The authors stress honest reporting as the point.
arxiv-2512-13424:
Sebastian Ohlmann and co-authors simulate how magnetic fields grow when two massive stars merge. Strong surface fields appear in about 7 percent of hot OBA stars, and mergers are a leading suspect for their origin. The team modeled a merger of stars of nine and eight solar masses.

The merged star forms a core wrapped in a torus of material from the larger star. Turbulence from two instabilities first breeds small-scale fields. Then ordered swirling flows drive a larger dynamo that builds a strong, large-scale field with intertwined poloidal and toroidal parts. The outcome barely depended on starting separation, resolution, or seed field, supporting mergers as a field source.
arxiv-2512-13524:
Kishan Kumar Ganguly and Tim Menzies ask how little data software engineering research really needs. Much of that field assumes progress takes huge data sets and heavy optimizers. Their paper tests that claim across more than 100 tasks from recent papers, spanning tuning, defect prediction, testing, and cost estimates.

With just a few dozen labels, simple methods reached over 90% of the best reported results. Those methods matched far more complex optimizers on many tasks. The authors frame a data-light challenge for the field and supply a formal model of labeling plus light baseline methods. They also share their scripts and data for open checks by others.
arxiv-2512-13624:
Romain Panis and Bruno Schapira prove sharp bounds for percolation in a half-space in high dimensions. Bernoulli percolation studies random open and closed sites on a grid, and the two-point function measures how likely two points are to connect. They work in dimension above six, at the critical point.

The authors prove an up-to-constant estimate for that function when it is restricted to a half-space. Their result completes earlier work by Chatterjee and Hanson, and by Chatterjee, Hanson, and Sosoe. It also solves a question posed by Hutchcroft, Michta, and Slade. The paper is short and focused: a single bound that closes an open case in high-dimensional percolation theory.
arxiv-2512-13724:
Ayush Noori and a large team present PROTON, a graph AI system that proposes ideas for brain and nerve diseases. Such diseases are the leading global cause of disability, yet most lack treatments that modify the disease. PROTON is a mixed-type graph transformer built to propose testable ideas across molecular, organoid, and clinical levels.

They test it on Parkinson's, bipolar disorder, and Alzheimer's disease. In Parkinson's, it linked risk loci to genes vital for dopaminergic neuron survival and flagged pesticides toxic to patient neurons. In bipolar disorder, it predicted calcitriol, which reversed protein changes in patient-derived cortical organoids. In Alzheimer's, five predicted drugs were linked to lower seven-year dementia risk in records from 610,524 patients, with a minimum hazard ratio of 0.63.
arxiv-2512-13824:
Abhishek Tiwari and Binoy Krishna Patra construct second-order relativistic magnetohydrodynamics with a correlation function approach. Magnetohydrodynamics covers a conducting fluid, here a magnetized plasma. Their frame uses Zubarev's non-equilibrium statistical operator, a tool that yields fluid equations from small-scale physics.

Using total energy-momentum conservation and the Bianchi identity for magnetic-flux conservation, they obtain all dissipative tensors in the medium. The plasma is taken to preserve parity and to be symmetric under charge conjugation. They give Kubo formulas for every transport number that appears at second order. They also extend the formalism to include nonlocal effects in a set way. The study runs 44 pages.
arxiv-2512-14024:
Ian Xu proposes a fast method to invert resampling tests and build exact confidence intervals. Randomization-based inference often inverts hypothesis tests by grid search over parameter values. That is simple but slow, and grid steps can make intervals too wide.

Xu uses the algebra structure of a broad class of test statistics, including ones whose variance estimators depend on the null hypothesis. Writing the statistics as rational functions of the parameter lets him find the exact points where ranks change against the randomization distribution. That yields the exact p-value curve and precise intervals without a full search. For vector parameters, the polynomial terms are stored to build near p-value functions and confidence regions faster. Examples span several published randomization tests.
arxiv-2512-14124:
Boris Mordukhovich, Peipei Tang, and Chengjing Wang give a full account of well posedness in a 2025 paper on composite optimization. Such problems mix a smooth cost with a harder nonsmooth part, and users need to know when small changes in the data cause only small changes in the answer.

The authors use parabolic regularity to define a new second order variational function that governs local behavior. From it they derive a strong second order sufficient condition and several equal forms of a key qualification condition. They link that condition to nondegeneracy, tilt stability, and the Aubin property of KKT systems. The results unify stability and sensitivity theory for these problems.
arxiv-2512-14624:
Rebecca Lewis, Oliver Feng, Henry Reeve, Min Xu, and Richard Samworth study score estimation under shape constraints in a 2025 paper. The score is the gradient of the log density, and estimating it matters for diffusion based generative models and for a new convex approach to linear regression.

They focus on log concave distributions, whose score functions decrease. That shape alone does not give a finite minimax risk, so they define subclasses based on tail behavior and on smoothness of the log density. For smooth cases they pin down the exact minimax rate, which beats what shape or smoothness alone would give. Their bounds come from a locally adaptive multiscale estimator built from a uniform confidence band for the score.
arxiv-2512-14724:
Ethereum's layer-2 rollups promise to relieve congestion on the main network, but whether they actually do, once upgrades and demand are accounted for, is an open empirical question. A daily panel covering 1,245 days, from August 2021 through December 2024, is assembled to answer it.

The panel spans the London, Merge, and Dencun upgrades and links fee and congestion measures to layer-2 user activity, macro-demand proxies, and event indicators. That regime-aware design separates the effect of rollup adoption from the effects of the upgrades themselves. The evidence matters for a live debate about whether scaling through rollups lowers costs for mainnet users.
arxiv-2512-15024:
R. Pablo Arribillaga and a coauthor study fairness in rules that divide one good among people. Each person has preferences with a single best option, and the rule must assign shares of a non disposable commodity. The focus is a relaxed honesty standard called non obvious manipulability, which asks only that gaming the rule not be plainly profitable.

Pairing that standard with full efficiency leads to impossibility results: no rule can have both. Weakening efficiency to unanimity, the demand that a unanimous top choice wins, changes the picture. A large family of well behaved rules then satisfies non obvious manipulability. The study maps the border between what allocation rules can and cannot promise, a basic question in social choice theory.
arxiv-2512-15224:
Séverin Baroudi and three coauthors review how well self supervised speech models serve two tasks built on speaker identity. Models like wav2vec 2.0 and WavLM learn from raw audio without labels, and they have lifted many speech tasks, above all where labeled data is scarce. Speaker diarization, which labels who spoke when, and speech separation, which untangles overlapping voices, have seen far fewer such tests.

The study investigates the quality of recent self supervised representations on both tasks. It highlights gaps in the current literature, which stem from the benchmarks in use. Evaluation datasets lack diversity, and the range of downstream systems tried with these models is narrow. The authors map what is missing so future work can judge these representations fairly. Their survey serves researchers choosing backbones for speaker centered speech tools.
arxiv-2512-15824:
Richard Fox and co authors present state augmented graphs for circular economy triage in a 2025 paper. Triage decides which green path a worn out product should follow: reuse, repair, remanufacture, or recycling. Good triage balances retained value against processing costs, labor, and safety limits.

Their framework is a fixed rule solver over a sequencing graph whose state records the taking apart history so far. Encoding history restores the Markov property. Each choice then depends only on the current state and can be scored step by step. Condition aware utility uses health scores. A worked example triages electric vehicle batteries step by step, valuing parts as taking apart proceeds.
arxiv-2512-16024:
Rishabh Dev Yadav, Shrey Agrawal, and Kamalakar Karlapalem describe a team of carrying robots in an arXiv paper from 2025. Several small robots jointly hold a payload, like movers carrying a table. The challenge is keeping the load level while the ground under each robot tilts in unknown ways.

Each robot carries a piston that can raise or lower its corner of the load. Sensors track the payload's tilt, and a controller mixes an open loop plan with a closed loop PID controller to set each piston height. The design makes no assumptions about the terrain, so it should work on any uneven surface. Tests in simulated worlds with varied, complex ground showed the system holding the payload at its target angle.
arxiv-2512-16124:
Yunfan Zhao studies random sums built on a wandering walk in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. A simple random walk steps left or right on the number line at random. Zhao attaches complex exponential terms to the walk's positions. He studies the size of the sums that result. The size is measured by Lp norms over a circle of phases.

He bounds a central binomial coefficient to start. That estimates how often the walk collides with itself. The walk moves back and forth, which is hard to handle. So he proves a metric domination principle. The energy of a sum over any sparse index set is no larger than over a solid block of the same size. Mixing two norms then gives his main bound. The expected worst-case Lp norm grows at most like a constant times the set size, raised to the power p minus one half.
arxiv-2512-16324:
Mostafa Bella and three co-authors clean up space telescope data in their 2025 paper on arXiv. Slitless spectroscopy, used by missions like Euclid, spreads the light of every star and galaxy in view into overlapping rainbows. The overlap contaminates each spectrum with its neighbors' light, and untangling it is essential for clean science.

The authors propose four new decontamination methods built on two models. A local instantaneous model treats the mixing as a simple linear blend, while a local convolutive model, handled in the Fourier domain, can decontaminate and sharpen spectra at once. Both use direct images from photometers and handle several dispersion directions together. Tests on realistic, noisy Euclid-like simulations confirmed the methods work. Cleaner spectra mean better measurements of galaxy distances and properties across Euclid's huge survey.
arxiv-2512-16424:
Nguyen Xuan-Vu and five co-authors put language models in the chemistry lab in this 2025 arXiv paper. Computer-aided synthesis planning suggests routes to build a target molecule, but older tools shut chemists out of the loop, ignoring expert judgment. Their framework, Synthelite, plans with a language model instead.

Synthelite proposes retrosynthetic steps directly, working backward from the target, and can generate complete end-to-end routes. Chemists steer it mid-plan through plain language prompts, adding constraints on strategy or starting materials. In experiments it adapted its plans to such constraints flexibly, reaching up to 95 percent success rates in both strategy-constrained and starting-material-constrained tasks. It also weighed chemical feasibility while designing routes. The authors present it as a step toward language models orchestrating synthesis planning with humans.
arxiv-2512-16524:
Alcides Buss and Damián Ferraro study a form of niceness called amenability for W-star Fell bundles over a discrete group. Fell bundles are a way to package groups together with algebras, and the question is when such a bundle acts in a well behaved, averageable way.

The authors build a larger bundle that plays the role of bounded functions on the group. They then tie amenability to the presence of good averaging maps at both the bundle level and the crossed product level. Among the payoffs, amenability passes to subgroups, and a bundle is amenable exactly when its parts over a normal subgroup and over the quotient group both are.
arxiv-2512-16624:
Mark Benazet and coauthors from ETH Zurich and Hilti address torque control for battery powered impact wrenches. These tools need fast control updates to track sharp impact events, yet their small built-in chips cannot run heavy predictive control in real time.

Their fix blends two steps. A Gaussian process first improves the tool model from data, and a neural network then copies the costly control rule so it can run in microseconds. Tests in simulation and on a custom test rig show the method keeps safety limits, tracks torque well, and beats standard PID control, making smart control fit on tight hardware.
arxiv-2512-16824:
Amit Jain and Richard Linares present Tiny Recursive Control, a small neural design for optimal control that gains power from repetition, not size. Big controllers with millions or billions of weights do not fit flight hardware with tight power and delay limits.

TRC runs a compact network of about 1.5 million parameters again and again through a two-level latent loop, polishing control sequences by simulating paths and fixing tracking error. More loops cost time, not memory. On oscillator steadying and powered descent with fuel limits, TRC hit near-optimal costs with millisecond inference on a GPU and under 10 megabytes of memory, two orders below language model baselines.
arxiv-2512-17124:
Richard Dawid and Guilherme Franzmann develop a fresh stance on scientific realism for theories linked by dualities, where two models describe the same physics with unlike basic entities. Dualities strain the idea that a theory mirrors one fixed underlying world.

Their proposal keeps realist commitment at the level of full formal structure, while tying ontological commitment, what one says exists, to specific empirical contexts. Borrowing Dennett notion of a theory as a compression algorithm, they split realism from ontology. Against common core realism, which parks ontology in the shared invariant core of duals, their view allows plural ontologies while holding a robust structural realism, tested on quantum mechanics and string theory.
arxiv-2512-17324:
Marine Aulnette, Michael Le Bars, and Patrice Le Gal test a standard ocean equation against a spinning tank of water. The omega equation predicts how fast water rises or sinks inside a vortex, motion that drives upwelling and downwelling in the sea. The team made lopsided surface vortices on a rotating table with layered density, then measured the rise directly.

The equation predicted gentle motion, about 20 micrometers per second, mostly at the vortex rim. Two lab methods agreed with each other but not with the equation: both found speeds near 100 micrometers per second, five times larger. Adding friction terms to the equation closed much of the gap on a test vortex. The fix could sharpen how oceanographers map rising and sinking zones.
arxiv-2512-17424:
Alexandre Anahory Simoes and Leonardo Colombo extend a classic physics principle to systems that lose energy as they move. The Herglotz principle derives motion from a quantity that itself fades over time, which suits friction and damping. They rebuild it on Lie algebroids, flexible geometric stages that cover spinning bodies, fluids, and machines with symmetry.

Out come the matching motion equations, in both local coordinates and a coordinate-free form. Older theories fall out as special cases, from plain particles to spinning tops. The pair also prove balance laws for the fading energy and a Noether-style rule: each symmetry now yields a quantity that drains at a known rate, not a constant. Such drained invariants still help engineers predict long-run behavior.
arxiv-2512-17524:
Louis Gass and Giovanni Peccati study a random field built from the nodal volume of a smooth stationary Gaussian field, rescaled over a large region. Their paper asks what the field looks like in the limit as the region grows without bound.

They prove the rescaled field converges to a standard Brownian sheet. The proof combines a central limit theorem for finite dimensional distributions, drawn from recent work by Ancona and coauthors. It pairs that result with a tightness criterion of Bickel and Wichura, and it rests on new bounds for the field's moments. The result stands in contrast to Berry's random wave model, a classic case in the same area, where the matching tightness step is still an open problem.
arxiv-2512-17824:
Heinz Pernegger and a CERN-led team report first results from CASSIA, a pixel sensor that amplifies its own signal inside each pixel. At CERN's upgraded collider, hundreds of collisions blur into one snapshot, and separating them needs detectors that stamp arrival times as well as positions. Building gain into the pixel itself boosts weak hits above the noise without separate amplifier layers.

The chip, made in a standard 180 nanometer imaging process, carries gain layers under its pixels. First tests map how different pixel designs multiply charge. Turn the voltage low and it runs in gentle proportional mode; turn it high and the same pixel fires in single-photon avalanche mode. One device, two personalities, aimed at the timing trackers future colliders demand.
arxiv-2512-17924:
Viv Atureta, Rifki Priansyah Jasin, and Stefan Siegert share a ready made data set for very short term rain forecasts, called nowcasting. The set holds 1,000 radar image sequences from across the United Kingdom. Each sequence has 20 frames spaced 15 minutes apart, on a 40 by 40 grid with 5 kilometer cells.

Sampling was spread evenly across regions, and clear sky cases were trimmed by a threshold rule. Extra data give date, place, ground height, wind, and storm type for each sequence. The authors add R tools for reading the raw radar format and a worked example that trains a small image network, so others can start at once.
arxiv-2512-18024:
Mithila Mangedarage, Keith Pedersen, and Zack Sullivan build a cleaner way to read the spray of energy in particle collisions. A classic set of measures, the Fox-Wolfram moments, sums up how energy spreads by angle. The moments are all linked, so reading only a few of them throws away shared information.

Their method keeps the full linked pattern while removing noise from sparse sampling, event by event. It also avoids a common shortcut that treats each spray as a set of perfect spikes, which can break a key safety property of the spectrum. Detector shapes and measurement errors can be folded in directly.
arxiv-2512-18224:
W. Andre Perkins and colleagues at the Allen Institute for AI and NOAA build HiRO-ACE, a two stage AI system mimicking a global storm resolving model at a fraction of the cost. Kilometer scale atmosphere simulations capture local extremes well, but cost too much for large regions, long periods, or big ensembles. Both stages train on a decade of output from X-SHiELD, a 3 kilometer model.

The first stage, ACE2S, is a stochastic emulator that runs the atmosphere at roughly 100 kilometer resolution while keeping real rainfall variability. The second stage, HiRO, downscales by a factor of 32, producing 6 hourly precipitation fields at 3 kilometers. The system reproduces extreme rainfall rates through the 99.99th percentile, with average biases below 10% almost everywhere. It generates tropical cyclones, fronts, and convective events from coarse inputs. Decades of regional rainfall take a single day on one H100 GPU, opening ensemble based risk assessment to planners.
arxiv-2512-18324: Sergey Bobkov and Friedrich Götze develop energy bounds for Kantorovich transport distances when the cost of moving mass grows in a convex way. Their main results extend estimates first proved by M. Ledoux for the standard transport distances, widening the range of costs for which such energy controls hold.
arxiv-2512-18524:
Janek Dyer, Jagdeep Ahluwalia, and Javad Zarrin test whether graph neural networks can tell apart the recipes that generate synthetic networks. Knowing which generative model made a graph helps researchers understand real structures, from social webs to infrastructure. Their benchmarking study, posted to arXiv in December 2025, mixes learned message passing with hand-built graph features that stay easy to interpret.

They generate graphs from five families, including Erdos-Renyi, Watts-Strogatz, and Barabasi-Albert, with up to ten thousand nodes and 110,000 edges. Features are pruned by a random forest pipeline, then fed to six network designs. GraphSAGE and GTN reach 98.5 percent accuracy, while attention-based models lag on global structure. A support vector machine using only the handcrafted features confirms that message passing drives the gains.
arxiv-2512-18824:
Mario Piazza and Andrea Sabatini build a logic for reasoning about obligations in a messy world. Real norms conflict, change with context, and rest on incomplete information, which defeats rigid rule systems. Their framework, posted to arXiv in December 2025, is non-modal and proof-theoretic, grounded in default logic rather than possible worlds.

Its key device is the controlled sequent: a sequent tagged with control sets listing what its premises should and should not entail. Separate extra-logical rules encode defaults and norms, and the tags record when each rule may fire, enabling local soundness checks. They prove admissibility of contraction and non-analytic cuts, plus strong completeness for credulous consequence in default theories. Worked examples show the calculus resolving conflicts between duties and tracking obligations that shift as situations change.
arxiv-2512-18924:
Jonquil Z. Liao and Joshua Cape build tests for hidden structure in big data matrices out of ranks rather than raw values. Extreme entries can wreck methods that trust magnitudes, so their Wilcoxon-Wigner matrices use normalized rank statistics, which stay calm under outliers. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, studies these matrices systematically at the meeting point of nonparametrics and random matrix theory.

They prove the leading eigenvalue and eigenvector fluctuate in a Gaussian way, with explicit centering and scaling. That math turns into parameter-free, distribution-free spectral tests for two jobs: finding communities and finding a principal submatrix. Numerical examples show the approach performing well. Because ranks discard size information, the tests trade a little power for a lot of robustness, a bargain many real datasets demand.
arxiv-2512-20124:
Philipp Weder and Annalisa Buffa certify the error made when engineers simplify a model's geometry. Defeaturing strips small features from models to cut cost. Strict estimators already bound the global error that move creates. But users care about set outputs, a stress here or a flow rate there. Global norms are not what they watch.

The paper first gives sound energy-norm estimators for features in linear elasticity and Stokes flow. It extends results known for Poisson's equation. It then gives general estimators for many negative features at once. Both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary cases are covered, for the first time. With the dual-weighted residual method, those become certified estimates for linear outputs of interest. Tests across the three equation families show the estimators at work.
arxiv-2512-20224:
Qijun Qin and a large team present UrbanV2X, a dataset for cars and roadside units that navigate together. It was collected in the Hong Kong testbed for cellular vehicle-to-everything links. Cars carried cameras, LiDAR, 4D radar, UWB radios, inertial sensors, and precise satellite positioning, all synced by an exact time protocol.

Roadside units contributed LiDAR and UWB readings of their own, with calibration data included. The team also benchmarks several navigation methods on the cooperative data. Single cars struggle in dense city streets, where buildings block signals and views. By sharing sensor views between cars and roadside units, researchers can test ways to keep guidance accurate in exactly those hard conditions.
arxiv-2512-20624:
Mazyar Taghavi and Javad Vahidi choreograph ten drones to blanket an area with 6G signal. The drones must work together with only partial views while conditions change, balancing exploration against exploitation. Their approach dresses classic multi-agent reinforcement learning in quantum-inspired clothing.

Variational quantum circuits form the core, with a quantum search method (QAOA) handling combinatorial choices. Bayesian tools, Gaussian processes, and kindred methods model the hidden dynamics of the setting. Training is central while each drone acts on its own, with shared memory and local view grids widening each agent's view. Against PPO and DDPG benchmarks, the quantum-inspired agents learn faster from fewer samples, converge sooner, and cover more area. Scale and stress tests support the claimed balance between exploring and exploiting.
arxiv-2512-20724:
Alexandros Christoforos and Chadbourne Davis return to long text generation with diffusion models, this time betting on sparsity. Such models grow costly in compute and memory as texts lengthen, since each step looks at all pairs of positions at once. SA-DiffuSeq builds in sparse attention, a scheme that lets each position look at only a chosen few others.

A soft absorbing state, shaped to suit the sparse scheme, steadies the model's path and speeds up how fast a clean text is rebuilt. Long-range links between distant words survive the thinning, and the output still reads well. Tests show steady wins over the best prior diffusion models in both training speed and sampling speed, with the largest gains on the longest texts. The target jobs are science writing, large-scale code writing, and long multi-turn chats.
arxiv-2512-20824:
Mohammad Taghi Dabiri and four co-authors design a coordination system for disaster zones, where knowing which areas need help first can save lives. Reports from the ground are often unreliable, sometimes deliberately false, and networks may be down. Their plan uses a public blockchain where users and sensors post time-stamped, location-tagged votes that update a live 3D crisis map.

Digital signatures alone cannot prove a report matches reality, so drones act as flying verifiers. They check locations physically and add their own flags to the ledger. The authors weigh threats such as spoofing, compromised verifiers, and lost connectivity, and sketch layered defenses. One concrete scheme uses retro-reflector sensors placed for clear sight lines.
arxiv-2512-20924:
Andrew Blevins and Ian Quigley test whether drug-discovery models are learning chemistry or learning chemists. They link ChEMBL assay records to publication authors and train a classifier to name the chemist from a molecule's fingerprint alone. It succeeds often enough to matter, reaching sixty percent top-five accuracy across more than eighteen hundred chemists under a strict scaffold-based split.

An activity model fed only a protein identifier and the inferred author probabilities, with no molecular descriptors at all, then matches a baseline that sees the structure. The models are exploiting who made a compound and what that chemist usually targets, a Clever Hans failure mode that inflates public benchmark scores. The authors propose author-disjoint splits and dataset practices that separate chemist intent from biological effect.
arxiv-2512-21324:
Wan Ki Wong, Irwin King, and four co-authors teach a transformer to compress orchestral scores into playable piano music. A piano reduction distills a full score into two staves, a vital sketch for rehearsal and analysis, but skilled arrangers spend hours producing one, and labeled examples for supervised learning are scarce. Their semi-supervised recipe splits the task: trim the music first, then harmonize the skeleton back into idiomatic piano texture, using the ocean of unlabeled classical scores.

Two versions built on MidiBERT, a BERT-style model for symbolic music, show the approach yields practical, realistic reductions needing only small manual touch-ups after. Because the pipeline learns the style of reductions from abundant raw music rather than precious labels, it scales like the data does. Music technologists gain groundwork toward an arranger's assistant: not a replacement for musicianship, but a competent first draft where none existed.
arxiv-2512-21524:
Lichao Wu, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi, and their co-authors present GoldenFuzz, a tool for finding bugs in processors by fuzzing. Fuzzing feeds a system streams of test inputs to provoke failures. Hardware fuzzers have struggled with weak semantic awareness, slow refinement, and the high cost of simulating the chip under test.

GoldenFuzz splits the work into two stages. It first fuzzes a fast golden reference model, a digital twin that follows the instruction set exactly, so test cases refine cheaply. Promising tests then run against the real design. Tests are built by joining carefully chosen instruction blocks, guided by feedback from high- and low-coverage samples. On three RISC-V processors, RocketChip, BOOM, and CVA6, GoldenFuzz beat existing fuzzers on coverage with shorter tests and less computing. It found all known vulnerabilities plus five new ones, most rated highly severe.
arxiv-2512-21624:
Yutaro Tanaka and Akira Furusaki show that the surface of a topological insulator is unstable as it grows. Topological insulators are materials that conduct on their surfaces while insulating inside. Growing clean interfaces matters for devices, yet their surfaces may roughen on their own.

The key quantity is surface stiffness, which measures how strongly a surface resists changes in shape. Ordinary insulators have positive stiffness, so small bumps smooth out. The authors find that the boundary states of a topological insulator push the stiffness negative, so small bumps grow instead. This mechanism is internal, unlike classical growth instabilities driven from outside. They derive a growth equation with the negative stiffness and show the surface dynamics follows the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. That equation is a standard model of spatiotemporal chaos, meaning the growing surface should develop chaotic ripples, not a flat front.
arxiv-2512-21724:
Chao Wu, Ming-Lei Xiao, Jiang-Hao Yu, and Yu-Hui Zheng compute how the effects of hypothetical new physics shift as energy scales change, inside the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. Their target is the full set of four-fermion operators at dimension eight, a large and messy family. They work in an on-shell system, extracting the renormalization group equations from unitarity cuts of bubble integrals.

To avoid redundant equations, the team builds everything from the Young Tensor amplitude basis, which carries the operators' full flavor structure. An algorithm reduces the integrated cuts back to that same basis, keeping the system consistent. Their Mathematica package ABC4EFT implements the method, and the complete dimension-eight results ship as a supplementary output file.
arxiv-2512-22224:
Zeraoulia Rafik, Alvaro H. Salas, and David L. Ocampo present a new special function designed to behave like the error function, a workhorse of probability. Their note supplies an accurate closed form for the function's cumulative distribution, written using Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind together with the error function itself. A series representation built from a Padé approximant adds a second way to compute it.

Numerical checks report accuracy around one part in a million under a quadratic mean norm. The authors show the same approximation strategy carries over to other distributions. They demonstrate it on the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular speeds and on the familiar normal distribution, suggesting a general recipe rather than a one-off trick.
arxiv-2512-22624:
Mohamad Alansari and five co-authors step back and ask how memory should be designed in trackers built on the Segment Anything Model. Memory lets these visual trackers store past frames and stay locked onto an object, and recent SAM2-based methods each tweak memory in their own way, leaving the general principles unclear. The authors compare representative trackers and find most differ mainly in which short-term frames they keep, while sharing one object-centric representation.

They reimplemented those memory methods inside the newer SAM3 and evaluated across ten benchmarks, isolating memory design from backbone strength. Guided by the results, they propose a hybrid memory splitting short-term appearance storage from long-term distractor-resolving storage, into which current policies plug modularly. The system improved robustness under long occlusion, complex motion, and heavy distractors.
arxiv-2512-22924:
Brahim Asfour, Farida Bargach, Yahya Ladghami, Ahmed Errahmani, and Taoufik Ouali ask whether primordial black holes could have formed inside a particular inflation theory. Primordial black holes arise when large density ripples from inflation collapse during the radiation era. They remain a candidate for some or all of the dark matter. The setting here is Higgs hybrid metric-Palatini gravity, where the Higgs-like inflaton couples non-minimally to curvature in the Palatini version.

The team tracks the primordial curvature power spectrum and finds it grows strongly at small scales, the ingredient collapse needs. From the spectrum they compute the mass variance and the fraction of energy collapsing into black holes at each mass, checking both against current limits. Depending mainly on the coupling constant and the number of inflationary e-folds, the resulting black holes can account for all of the dark matter or only a fraction of it.
arxiv-2512-23424:
Jinye Du and a large team present AKG, a multi-agent system that writes and tunes AI compute kernels. Language models, multimodal systems, and recommenders all bottleneck on kernels. Each new chip demands tailored implementations, a treadmill manual optimization cannot match. AKG assigns the stages of kernel generation, migration between platforms, and performance tuning to cooperating agents built on language models.

The system speaks several domain-specific languages, including Triton, TileLang, C++, and CUDA C, so it can target different hardware backends while preserving correctness and portability. Its modular design lets new languages and hardware targets be integrated quickly. Evaluated on the KernelBench suite with Triton across graphics and neural processing backends, AKG achieved an average speedup of about one and a half times over PyTorch's eager-mode baselines. The authors offer it as evidence that agent pipelines can absorb the kernel bottleneck in AI system development.
arxiv-2512-24124:
Advait Gadhikar, Riccardo Grazzi, and James Hensman work on quantization, the compression step that lets large language models run cheaply by storing weights in fewer bits. A stubborn obstacle is outliers, unusually large weights and activations that wreck accuracy when everything is squeezed. Rotating the model's coordinates can tame outliers, and earlier methods chose rotations from data or by expensive search.

Their method, OptRot, learns fusible rotations by minimizing a cheap proxy for quantization error: simply the sum of fourth powers of the rotated weights, with no training data needed. Against the popular GPTQ quantizer it beat both fixed Hadamard rotations and pricier data-dependent rivals such as SpinQuant for weight compression, and it helped activation quantization in mixed settings. A data-aware variant improves further using activation statistics, though at the most aggressive setting both versions trade weight gains against activation losses.
arxiv-2512-24424:
Patryk Michalski and Andrzej Dragan ask whether entanglement can be detected across a black hole horizon. Two quantum wave packets start out possibly entangled. One packet falls into the black hole. Intuition says the two cases, separable and entangled, should look identical from outside. The infalling information seems hidden for good.

The authors show that intuition can fail. Quantum states cannot be localized with perfect sharpness. That fundamental limit leaks a detectable difference. Tools from quantum state discrimination theory quantify the effect. A concrete realization is analyzed in detail. The authors also find which configurations maximize the chance of telling the cases apart. The result is a matter of principle, not a practical detector. In principle, the horizon does not fully seal the distinction.
arxiv-2512-24624:
Borui Du, Yumeng Zhang, Christos Masouros, and Bruno Clerckx study signal design for a wireless system that must sense and communicate at the same time. They use OTFS, a method suited to fast-moving users because it handles Doppler shifts well. Running radar and data together cuts delay, but the best signal plan was unclear.

Their framework jointly designs pilot symbols and allocates power to data symbols under one uniform scheme. They derive a lower bound on communication capacity that allows for channel estimation errors. Readers in wireless engineering get a practical route to lower latency in high-mobility sensing systems.
arxiv-2512-24924:
Ana Mitrasinovic, Marko Grozdanovic, Ana Lalovic, and colleagues report an optical counterpart to the neutral hydrogen cloud FAST J0139+4328, earlier claimed as an isolated dark galaxy. That claim rested on a hydrogen detection and no visible galaxy in a shallower survey. Deep imaging with two telescopes and spectroscopic follow-up of the field changed the picture.

A low-surface-brightness galaxy sits at the cloud's position, so the system is not starless after all. Astronomy readers get a cautionary verification story for dark galaxy candidates. Deeper light can dissolve a dark galaxy claim, which matters for testing cold dark matter predictions about faint galaxies.
arxiv-2601-06624:
Marco Martinelli and two co-authors find a cheap way to grade name linking in a 2026 paper. Name linking is a core step in pulling facts from health texts. Grading it at scale is hard, for two clear reasons they name.

Skilled graders cost a lot, and the text sets are huge in size. Their test case is GutBrainIE, a health fact set on gut and brain. They grade by sampling, which gives a sound grade at low cost. The grade comes with a known margin and a fixed budget of grading hours. Teams need not grade each line to trust the score for the whole set. The plan suits any large text set where skilled help is scarce. It makes honest quality scores cheap enough to use often.
arxiv-2601-06924:
Research by Hedieh Abdollahi and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with isaac newton telescope monitoring survey of local group dwarf galaxies – VIII.. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors present a comprehensive catalog, in the Sloan i i and Harris V V filters. Of long-period variable (LPV) stars in the spheroidal dwarf satellites of the Andromeda galaxy.

Based on a dedicated survey for variable stars in Local Group dwarf systems. Using photometric time-series data obtained with the Wide Field Camera (WFC) on the 2. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07024:
Dario Borrelli wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on graphs that grow by a copy-and-change rule. In such a graph, a node is copied, and some of its links are then lost or kept. The two steps are called duplication and divergence. Borrelli asks how large the biggest linked chunk of the graph can grow.

The copy rule here is paired, so the loss on one side mirrors the loss on the other. As the rate of loss shifts, the graph hits a sharp change point. Past that point, the biggest chunk acts in a new way. Borrelli finds that point by a size-scaling test. The rate at the change sits near the place where a graph count called the Euler characteristic hits zero. That count is known to mark this kind of shift in graphs of set size.
arxiv-2601-07624:
Chris Lambie-Hanson and Pedro Marun study which topological properties survive when a mathematical universe is extended by forcing. Forcing is a set theory method that builds new models with chosen features. A property preserved under forcing stays true in every such extension. Their 2026 preprint answers a question posed by Gilton and Holshouser, in a strong form.

The focus is on games played on topological spaces, including the strong countable fan tightness game. If player II has a winning strategy at a point, the authors show it persists in every set forcing extension. The same holds for the Rothberger game, but not for two related games. Such fine distinctions map the border between stable and fragile properties. Set theorists and topologists are the intended readers.
arxiv-2601-07824:
Piotr Sierant, Jofre Vallès-Muns, and Artur Garcia-Saez compute how magical a quantum state is. Magic, formally non-stabilizerness, measures how far a state departs from the easily simulated stabilizer set. It is a central resource behind quantum advantage. It also probes the complexity of quantum many-body states. Standard measures include stabilizer Rényi entropy for qubits and mana for qutrits.

Those measures are costly to evaluate numerically. Their cost grows rapidly with the number of qudits in the system. Faster computation would let scholars map magic across larger states and devices. Knowing where magic sits helps explain when quantum computers beat classical ones. The paper serves quantum information scientists who benchmark resources. It tackles a measurement problem that limits how magic can be studied at scale.
arxiv-2601-08424: Roohani Sharma and Michal Wlodarczyk revisit protrusion decompositions for graph deletion problems. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies F-deletion, where k vertices are removed so no minor from a finite family remains. Protrusions are well-structured graph parts that kernelization algorithms can shrink safely. The authors derive uniform lossy kernels for reducing treewidth. They also give linear kernels for hitting disconnected minors. Kernels matter because they shrink huge inputs to small cores before exact solving, making hard graph problems practical.
arxiv-2601-08524:
Richard Stiskalek and co-authors revisit the Great Attractor with digital twins of the nearby universe. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses the Manticore-Local simulation suite. The Great Attractor idea has been asked to answer three distinct questions at once.

First, what sources the Local Group's velocity in the cosmic microwave background frame. Second, where present-day velocity streamlines converge. Third, where the Local Group is actually moving to. Separating these questions matters because one attractor may not answer all three. The simulations trace the Local Group's streamline trajectory and dynamical fate, giving cosmologists a cleaner account of our cosmic motion.
arxiv-2601-08624: Mauro Barbieri and Abraham Loeb point out a rare alignment of the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes the object will align with the Earth-Sun axis on January 22, 2026. The angle is exceptionally small, just 0.69 degrees. Such near-opposition geometry offers unique circumstances for observation. Astronomers can measure the opposition surge, a brightness spike at tiny phase angles. They can also measure polarimetric properties of interstellar cometary dust, testing how material from another star system scatters light.
arxiv-2601-08824:
Kenta Kasai works on quantum codes that guard data spread in a sparse net. In plain codes, a known trick links the shape of the net to both good fix work and long safe span. Round loops in the net help on both counts. In quantum codes, a rule that parts must cross at right angles blocks that trick.

Kasai looks for a way past that right angle wall. The goal is a quantum code that keeps the sparse ease of plain codes, yet gains the loop gains that plain codes enjoy. Such a code would fix flaws well and guard data far. A reader in quantum codes gets a new path past a long held bound. It may shape how next codes are built.
arxiv-2601-09224:
Eung Jin Chun gives a joint birth tale for the stuff of space and for the mass we can not see. Space holds more plain mass than star counts can explain. That gap is the baryon asymmetry, why stuff beat anti stuff in the early cosmos. Dark stuff is a next gap, a hid mass that holds galaxies. Two gaps may share one cause.

His tale turns on the QCD axion, a light bit set to solve a deep force ask. Early spin of that field, sped by growth era pulls, can yield both gaps at once. The frame ties that spin to the seesaw path for neutrino mass. A reader in cosmos work gets one cause for two gaps.
arxiv-2601-09624:
Jiali Cheng, Ziheng Chen, Chirag Agarwal, and Hadi Amiri ask why some facts resist being unlearned. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies machine unlearning, the removal of chosen data from a trained language model. Success varies sharply by sample: some items erase cleanly, others persist.

The authors argue the gap is not only about the data. Internal mechanisms in the model can encode and protect memorized content. They take a mechanistic view and propose a circuit-guided difficulty metric. Knowing which items will resist erasure helps firms meet privacy and compliance duties honestly.
arxiv-2601-10524:
Frank Bobe III, Gregory Vetaw, and Chase Pavlick probe why tuned models fail on new data, with phishing hunts as the test. Fine tune steps can make a model top at one task. Yet the same model can break on a slight shift in the data. Why it breaks is oft not clear.

The team use a multi layer probe frame. They fine tune a Llama model and kin on phishing texts. They then test each net form for where skill is lost. The aim is to name the parts that make a tuned model frail. That may guide tunes that hold up more well.
arxiv-2601-10724:
Rishabh Dev Yadav, Viswa N. Sankaranarayanan, and Spandan Roy study control for platoons of self-driving vehicles. A platoon is a line of cars that drive close together under shared control. The road grip each car feels is uncertain and changes with its state. That unknown friction can shake the line's spacing and safety.

The work develops adaptive sliding mode control that copes with state-dependent friction uncertainty. It grows out of Yadav's master's thesis at IIIT Hyderabad from 2023. A shorter version ran at the ICAR 2021 robotics conference. The control design aims to keep each car at its set gap even as grip shifts beneath it.
arxiv-2601-11224:
Barbara Dietz, Dung Xuan Nguyen, and Tilen Cadez study scarred states in billiard systems. Their 2026 preprint sets relativistic cases next to plain ones. A scar is a state that piles up along a classical orbit. The team looks at neutrino billiards and at graphene ones.

A third case uses Haldane graphene billiards for compare runs. In the range near the Fermi energy, the physics is linear. There all three cases share one Dirac equation for light spin-half parts. The authors also sum up scars for the plain quantum case. Those use the shape of a full stadium and a quarter stadium. The side-by-side view shows what the speed of light changes in scars.
arxiv-2601-11524:
L. Schilcher, P. Waldert, B. Kantz, and T. Schreck build a dashboard for patient data. Their 2026 preprint is named Clusters in Focus. Exploring tables to find cohorts is key in biomarker discovery. Feature pairs split patients into groups in many such hunts.

Comparing clusters across many feature pair views is hard. A dashboard must keep detail on demand, simple and robust. The team's tool does just that for tabular patient data. Users can focus on one projection and pull detail as needed. Cohorts can then be checked across views with less strain. The work comes from Graz University of Technology. It aims at clinical data work that stays readable.
arxiv-2601-11724:
Muditha Fernando, Kajhanan Kailainathan, Krishnakanth Nagaratnam, Isuranga Senavirathne, and Ranga Rodrigo work on a hard learning task. A model must learn from few marked cases and still work on new domains it has not seen. This task is called semi-supervised domain generalization in the field.

Their method, named SemAlign in the work, is guided by language. Past work shows two chief risks in this task. One is wrong tags made for unmarked cases. The other is a model that fits its training data too well and fails on new data. The new method aims to cut both risks at once.
arxiv-2601-11824:
A. Brennan, L. Matrà, S. Mac Manamon, and the ARKS team report new views of the debris disk round the star HD 121617. Debris disks are rings of dust and rock left round young stars. About twenty such disks show carbon monoxide gas, split into gas-poor and gas-rich kinds.

HD 121617 is gas-rich, so it is a key case in the ARKS survey. That survey uses the ALMA array to map fine rings in such disks. Fine maps can show gaps and clumps made by unseen planets. The work adds one rich case to that map set.
arxiv-2601-11924:
Ming Shi studies shared bandit tasks where reward data can be spoiled. Many agents pick arms over many rounds and share what they learn. Each reward is a vector, so more than one goal is in play. A foe can spoil the shared data, but only up to a set total budget.

A check step can test some data, but checks are scarce. Shi links how much spoil is used with how checks are placed. The work aims for methods that still learn well under attack. Such guards help shared learning in open, risky nets.
arxiv-2601-12224:
Meng Wei, Kun Yuan, Shi Li, and a large team find surgical tools in video by how they move, from a text brief. Language-led work with surgical scenes could aid smart operating rooms and robot help. The task is to cut out the tool named in words.

Past tools rest on static visual cues and fixed tool names. Those fail on new tools and phrasing. Motion gives a strong extra cue, since the used tool is the one that moves with intent. The team's motion-led method aims to generalize better.
arxiv-2601-12424:
William Dorrell and James Whittington review a puzzle from neuroscience: grid cells. These neurons fire in a neat hexagonal pattern as an animal moves. For twenty years, that pretty code has raised a basic question. What computation does this pattern serve, and why does it take this curious form?

The first answer came fast: grid cells track position as an animal moves. That skill is called path integration. Dorrell and Whittington survey normative theories, which ask what an ideal system should do. Such theories try to derive the grid pattern from a goal, not just describe it. Their review weighs how well that project has worked so far.
arxiv-2601-12724:
Rishabh Iyer works on set functions that come from entropy, a core idea in the theory of data and codes. Shannon entropy is one such function, and it has a clean shape that math can use. But the set of all such entropy based functions is smaller than some had hoped. A newer frame stretches entropy style measures to a wider class of set functions.

Those wider measures have found many uses in the past few years. Teams use them to pick data, to guide learning, and to shift a model to a new domain. Iyer gives hands on forms of them for three classic tasks. The tasks are coverage, facility location, and graph cuts. Clear forms let users plug proven measures straight into real tools.
arxiv-2601-13124:
Donglei Du, Qizhi Fang, Bin Liu, Tianhang Lu, and Chenchen Wu sort the core of a broad class of games where pay offs bend. In game theory the core is the set of splits that no group can beat by breaking off. For straight line games the core is well known.

For bent games the core was far less clear. The team finds a fit loosening of the bent form. With it they give a full mark of when the core holds and what it holds. Their result grows the set of joint games that can be read in this way. It also links to games that spring from opt tasks, a rich source in trade and nets.
arxiv-2601-13224:
Michael Hanus and Steven Libby ease the work of tools that reshape code. Compilers, code probes, and proof tools all walk a code tree and change nodes as they go. To write such walks by hand is slow and prone to flaws. Each tool must loop the whole tree and act at the right nodes.

Hanus and Libby work in functional logic programming, a style that joins two code styles. They give ways to state code reshapes in a more brief and safe form. Their aim is less boiler plate for tool builders. For language tool teams, clean reshape rules mean tools that are more quick to build and more safe to change.
arxiv-2601-13424:
A. Martinez-Mendez and co-authors cut waste in the vast compute pool of the LAGO project. LAGO is a Latin American watch for high energy bits from space. It runs heavy sims on high performance clusters. Such sims eat time, power, and funds, so yield per run counts for both science and green aims.

The team counts where cluster time goes in the LAGO set up. They then tune how jobs are placed and run to lift yield. Their marks are tied to astroparticle sims, which have long runs and big data. For big sim teams, the work shows how yield checks pay off in more science per watt.
arxiv-2601-13624:
A team with Xin Zhang weighs two puzzles in the study of the early universe in 2026. One is cosmic birefringence, a slight twist in the light left from the Big Bang. The twist would link the two modes of that light in a new way. Such a link is a sign of parity violation, a break in mirror symmetry.

The team joins data from ACT, Planck, DESI, and PantheonPlus to set joint limits. They test birefringence next to early dark energy, a brief extra push in the young cosmos. New high-grade sky data make such fine effects worth a fresh look. Joint limits keep one puzzle from skewing the other.
arxiv-2601-14024:
Sergio López-Baños and co-authors boost a hybrid quantum-classical solver for hard planning problems in 2026. Mixed-integer linear programming, or MILP, is used widely in industry optimization. As problems grow larger, classical solvers struggle within practical time limits. Quantum annealers could in principle accelerate some of these tasks.

The problems map to quadratic unconstrained binary optimization instances for annealers. Limited annealer scale currently prevents practical speedups. The team enhances the hybrid Benders' algorithm, which splits a problem into parts. Better splits may bring quantum help closer to real industrial use. The split must be smart, or the gain is lost in extra work. Their tests show where the split helps most and where it does not.
arxiv-2601-14124:
Saad Mankarious and Ayah Zirikly use style transfer to build mental health text data in Arabic in 2026. Synthetic data promises a fix for data scarcity and demographic bias. Existing approaches rely largely on pretrained large language models. Those models may suffer limited output diversity in what they generate.

They may also propagate biases inherited from their training data. The team uses diffusion models for synthetic mental health text instead. Style transfer can recast real text in new voices while keeping content. Fair Arabic datasets could improve mental health tools for Arabic speakers.
arxiv-2601-14224:
Sahel Sharifymoghaddam and Jimmy Lin study where deep search agents should spend their compute in 2026. Deep research agents rely on iterative retrieval and reasoning to answer complex queries. Scaling test-time computation raises significant efficiency concerns for them. The team studies how to allocate reasoning budget in deep search pipelines.

Listwise reranking, which reorders a whole list of results at once, is their focus. They analyze reranking tradeoffs through effective token cost. Their title gives the advice: rerank before you reason. Spending tokens on better sources first may beat deeper thought on poor ones.
arxiv-2601-14724:
Haowei Zhang, Shudong Yang, Jinlan Fu, and their co-authors present a video understanding system in this 2026 paper. Streaming video understanding means answering questions about a video while it still plays. Long streams strain the KV cache, the memory a model keeps for past frames. HERMES treats that cache as a hierarchical memory.

HERMES is a training-free approach, so it needs no new model training. It reuses the KV cache and performs hierarchical management of the video tokens stored in it. Key tokens stay at fine detail, while older ones are compressed in tiers. Readers get stable, efficient inference for long videos, where naive systems run out of memory or forget the plot.
arxiv-2601-15024:
Nipun Agarwal reviews how to keep wireless links private when the listener stays silent. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with massive MIMO, a system where a base station uses a great many antennas. The tech drives 5G and later networks, with big gains in spectrum and energy use.

A passive eavesdropper never transmits, so the station cannot learn its channel. That makes secure links hard to promise. Agarwal surveys the known challenges at the physical layer. He also sets out open research directions for guarding these systems against such silent, hidden listeners.
arxiv-2601-15324:
Mark Wind bolts a memory onto a language model without touching its weights. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with a common problem: adding memory to a pre-trained model usually means changing its architecture or its weights. Prometheus Mind takes a different route.

The base model, a Qwen3-4B, stays frozen. Eleven modular adapters add the memory, at seven percent overhead, and removing them undoes the change. Building the system took four fixes. One finds semantic directions from minimal pairs with no labeled data. Another trains each adapter in stages, since end-to-end training collapses.
arxiv-2601-15424:
Juan Gomez Quispe, Matheus Medina, and co-authors tune carbon sheets to make hydrogen production cheaper. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with graphynes, carbon frameworks that mix two bond types. The mix gives distinct electronic regimes and site-selective reactivity across the sheet.

The team studies the hydrogen evolution reaction, a key step in splitting water. They dope two graphyne forms with boron, nitrogen, or both. Density functional theory and reactive molecular dynamics simulations judge each doped variant in turn. The goal is to control both the reaction's activity and the material's stability.
arxiv-2601-15524:
Ni An, Bhola Nath Saha, and Bidyut Sanki work on curves on hyperbolic surfaces in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their objects are filling pairs. A filling pair is two simple closed curves in minimal position. Cut the surface along both curves, and what remains is a union of topological disks. Nothing else is left over. Such pairs are basic tools in the study of surfaces.

The title names the paper's goal: length minimization for these pairs. Among all filling pairs on a surface, which ones are shortest? The abstract in the record states the definition and little more. Readers should expect a specialist geometry paper with proofs at its core. Short filling pairs give concrete ways to measure and compare surfaces.
arxiv-2601-15724:
Chenglin Li and a large team build video models that use tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-form video remains a hard problem for video language models. Most models reason over uniformly sampled frames. That static approach weakens timing: they cannot pinpoint when things happen. It also loses much information in long videos. The team's system is called VideoThinker. It is built as an agentic VideoLLM.

Agentic tools let the model explore a video adaptively. The tools include temporal retrieval, spatial zoom, and temporal zoom. Guided by a language model, the system picks where to look closer. That mirrors how a person scans a long recording. For tasks like surveillance review or lecture search, active looking beats uniform sampling.
arxiv-2601-15824:
Joan Vendrell Farreny and colleagues at NeuralTrust propose a new security layer in a 2026 arXiv paper. They call it the Generative Application Firewall, or GAF. It is an architectural layer for securing language model applications. Existing defenses are fragmented, they argue. Prompt filters, guardrails, and data masking each guard one spot. GAF unifies them into a single enforcement point.

The model is the web application firewall. A WAF coordinates defenses for web traffic in one place. GAF aims to do the same for generative apps. It also covers autonomous agents and their tool interactions. Agent actions are a new attack surface that old tools miss. For security teams, one chokepoint is easier to audit than scattered patches.
arxiv-2601-15924:
Brainard Philemon Jagati and four co-authors fix learning on skewed class data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep networks degrade badly under long-tailed distributions. A few head classes dominate the training data. Tail classes get very few examples. The model then masters the common and fumbles the rare. Their method is class-confidence aware reweighting, per the title. Training examples are reweighted by class and by model confidence.

Reweighting shifts attention toward what the model gets wrong. Class awareness counters the head classes' bulk. Confidence awareness focuses on uncertain cases. Rare classes matter in medicine and safety, where the rare event is often the important one. Methods that lift tail performance without hurting the head are in real demand.
arxiv-2601-16324:
Rebecca Lopez and coauthors screen student minds with Fitbit data from the plague years. Their 2026 preprint deals with stress in college life. High stress drives high rates of fear and low mood in students. Wear gear gives quiet sense data through the day. Such data could flag ill minds at an early stage.

Past work used few mind tests and few body sense types. The team widens both the tests and the sense types in use. Wide data should give a more true screen of mind state. Early flags could guide help to students in time. The work uses data drawn in the COVID span.
arxiv-2601-16724:
Kevin Fan and Eric Yun study bias in machines that grade essays. Schools now use such tools for tests with high stakes. Tools trained on native speech can grade harshly. Students who learn English as a new tongue may lose marks. Their style traits get read as flaws. Their 2026 preprint seeks a fairer way to grade.

The team uses a learn-by-contrast trick in training. The trick pulls the tool's eye to real skill. It pushes the eye off surface traits of new learners. Fair grades guard life paths like school seats and jobs. This work shows one path to tame such bias in code.
arxiv-2601-16824:
Rongjun Ma, Shijing He, Jose Luis Martin-Navarro, Xiao Zhan, and Jose Such study love chats with AI. Apps now sell AI partners for romance and chat. Folks share deep, private woes with these bots. The risks of that share stay little known. Their 2026 preprint draws on talks with users of such apps.

The talks span first tries, close bonds, and break-ups. Users told what they share and what they guard. They also told who they think holds power in the bond. Their tales show where privacy lines blur with bots. The work can guide safe design for such apps.
arxiv-2601-17124:
