The bacterium is a strain of E. coli that escapes the gut. It is a severe threat to newborns. Its O antigen, a variable coat component, is the leading candidate target for a protective vaccine. Yet nobody has charted its global variety in this age group.

The planned study will fuse two evidence streams. One is published serotype reports from four databases. The other is serotypes predicted from genome sequences in three public archives. Each strain's disease, site, year, and origin will be extracted. The verdict it seeks is strategic: one multivalent vaccine for the world, or regional recipes.
plos-pone-0354524:
Liu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, examine natural killer cells inside triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form that lacks the usual drug targets. These immune killer cells should attack tumors, but in this cancer they often arrive immature and weak. Using public single-cell data, the team sorted the killer cells found in tumor tissue into three subtypes.

One subtype, the strongest killer, was scarcer and weaker in triple-negative tumors than in other breast cancers. Its cells carried more of a brake receptor that switches them off. Signals from neighboring immune cells appeared to set that brake. A second subtype, marked by an alarm gene, was more active in these tumors, and high levels of that gene tracked with worse patient outcomes. The strong subtype's signature, by contrast, tracked with better outcomes. The authors say releasing the brake on killer cells is a concrete target for new treatments.
plos-pone-0354724:
Kelsey Thompson led a team of six authors on this 2026 focus group study of clinicians who treat children with pediatric feeding disorder. In this condition, eating breaks down for medical, nutritional, skill, or emotional reasons. Twenty-five providers in seven groups described their training and daily work across all four areas of the condition.

Training varied wildly between professions, clinics lacked easy access to specialist backup, and everyone wanted fuller yet workable care that honors family views. Thompson calls for earlier teaching, mentorship, and ready evidence-based resources to lift patient care.
plos-pone-0354824:
Gökşen Polat and four colleagues published this 2026 interview study in Türkiye of people whose chronic diseases leave them disabled. Twelve adults holding official disability reports described their daily limits and what they expect from disability services. Recruitment ran through clinics and personal referrals during 2024.

Disability spilled into social, cultural, school, and work life. Although services are a legal entitlement, many participants barely knew what existed or could not reach it. Polat argues the gap is informational and structural, and that fixing awareness and access matters as much as passing laws.
plos-pone-0354924:
Kaiyue Du and colleagues built lifestyle-based risk models for keratoconus, a disease that thins and bulges the cornea. They used records from 711 patients at a Chinese eye center, 275 of them with the disease. Their 2026 study combined standard regression with seven machine learning models. The models were fed demographic and habit data. The team then asked the models to explain which factors mattered most.

Seven risk factors stood out. They included male sex, higher body mass, and less schooling. A more distant childhood home and allergic conjunctivitis counted too. Above all stood rubbing the eyes, harder and more often. The best model sorted patients with fair accuracy. Because eye rubbing is changeable, the authors see a practical opening. Flag high-risk patients early, and coach the habit away before corneas deform.
plos-pone-0355124:
Rogers Kamulegeya and seven colleagues systematically review artificial intelligence models that predict whether tuberculosis treatment will fail, in this 2026 meta-analysis. Failure fuels transmission and drug resistance, so early warning matters. Searching two major databases for a quarter-century of work, they gathered thirty-four studies, most published since 2019, and pooled the accuracy of nineteen of them covering over one hundred thousand patients.

The pooled discrimination looked promising, but the ground beneath it was shaky. Results varied enormously between studies, models performed notably worse in groups including people with HIV, and only a quarter of studies had validated their model on outside data. Just one study earned a low overall risk-of-bias rating, and the analysis detected signs of publication bias. The authors conclude these tools are not ready for routine care and prioritize rigorous external validation in high-burden settings.
plos-pone-0355224:
Rafael Borges and three colleagues examine whether who you have worked alongside predicts reaching ministerial office in Portugal, in this 2026 network study. They scraped the membership of Portuguese governments and parliament over a decade, plus officials' interest registers, and built a network linking people who shared institutional venues. Then they asked whether network position, computed before the fact, screened out future ministers better than chance or a simple career-ladder rule.

It did. Their centrality-based screen caught over half of the in-network ministerial appointments, far above the baselines. Ministers also showed systematically higher institutional reach than colleagues who never made cabinet, with the sharpest gap inside party structures, where ministers scored about double on one key centrality measure. The authors are careful to call the work exploratory, but it suggests appointments flow through relational position, not just résumés.
plos-pone-0355724:
Mirjana Grdinić-Rakonjac and Vladimir Pajković survey more than thirteen hundred licensed drivers in a developing country, in this 2026 case study. They asked about four risky behaviors: speeding, drunk driving, seatbelt use, and phone use. Because crash deaths fall hardest on poorer countries, and because habits differ by road type, they compared men and women separately on high-speed, regional, and urban roads, adjusting for age and experience.

Men were generally more prone to speeding and drinking and driving. Yet women reported significantly more extreme speeding, far over the limit, on high-speed roads, a reversal of the usual pattern, while also buckling up more reliably on regional and urban roads. Both sexes texted and used social media behind the wheel at similar rates, and overall risk awareness was higher than the authors expected. They recommend campaigns aimed at men in cities and at speed among women on fast roads.
plos-pone-0356524:
Pooja Panth and three colleagues studied cancer patients at Bhaktapur Cancer Hospital in Nepal, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. How patients view their illness shapes how they cope, seek care, and keep going through treatment. Panth's cross-sectional study linked those views to resilience, the capacity to bounce back under strain.

The team surveyed patients and compared illness views with measures of resilience. Some beliefs track with stronger coping, while others track with despair. Knowing which views help lets counselors support the beliefs that sustain patients, and gently challenge those that drag them down. In a setting with few support services, that guidance helps staff focus scarce time where it lifts patients most.
plos-pone-0356624:
Alexandra N Sheldon and colleagues reviewed 173 infected artificial joints treated at one center over nearly a decade. All were treated with a joint-saving operation. Surgeons cleaned the implant and kept it rather than replacing it. The team asked which germs doom that approach. Their 2026 retrospective study graded success as lasting eradication without further surgery. It tested fungal, resistant, mixed, and culture-negative infections against the odds.

Two thirds of cases were cured. Fungal infections almost always failed, carrying heavier illness burdens besides. Infections where no germ could be grown were nearly four times likelier to clear. That is a hopeful sign for a frustrating category. Resistant and common skin bacteria also dragged success down. The authors suggest microbe identity should steer the choice between saving and replacing a joint.
plos-pone-0357124:
John Adeleke used Nigeria's 2024 national health survey to ask whether household wealth protects children equally against two kinds of undernutrition. One is stunting, the slow height loss of chronic deprivation. The other is wasting, the rapid weight loss of acute shortage. His 2026 analysis covered more than nine thousand children. It adjusted step by step for other social and geographic factors.

Wealth showed a clear graded link with stunting. Each step up the wealth ladder came with less of it. For wasting, wealth showed no link at all. Adeleke reads the split through one idea. Money buys protection against slow, cumulative harms more readily than against sudden illness or food shocks. Programs fighting wasting, he argues, need tools beyond poverty relief.
plos-pone-0357824: Agrawal and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on sleep apnea using electronic health records. Obstructive sleep apnea makes breathing stop and start during sleep, and it is tied to stroke risk. The team measured how common it is, split by age and sex, along with related conditions. The data set was large and cross-sectional. Clear rates help clinics plan screening for a disorder often missed.
plos-pone-0358224:
Quan Pham Hong leads a team of five designing a neural network that listens for damage in structures, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Bridges and towers betray cracks through subtle changes in how they shake. The warning signs are brief blips in narrow frequency bands. Models that read only the time signal miss the frequency story; models that transform the whole signal lose track of when each frequency occurred. Their network, SpectralTCN, is built to keep both.

Inside each layer of a temporal convolutional network sits a wavelet gating module. It splits the signal into sub bands that correspond to vibration modes. The network then decides how much of each band to keep. Then it rebuilds the signal before moving on. Because wavelets preserve timing and frequency together, a short damage signature keeps its moment and its pitch. The design targets inspection of structures that cannot afford missed hints.
plos-pone-0358424:
Mohamad Kazem Dehghani, Reza Ghasemi-Fasaei, Sajjad Abbasi, and Amin Mojiri wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on plants and pollution. Working with spinach grown in water rather than soil, they study nanoplastics sprayed on leaves. The question is how these tiny plastic particles change the plant's handling of cadmium, a toxic metal.

The responses depend on both time and concentration, so the authors track uptake and the metal's movement from root to shoot under different doses. Cadmium in leafy vegetables is a food safety concern, and plastic particles are now common on farms. Plant scientists and food regulators share an interest in how these two pollutants interact.
plos-pone-0359224:
Sivarama Prasad Tera and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents an explainable AI framework for detecting cancer from skin lesion images. Explainable means the system shows its reasoning, not just a verdict, which doctors rightly demand before trusting software with diagnosis.

Skin cancer caught early is usually curable, so faster and more reliable screening saves lives. An imaging framework that explains itself can also teach, showing trainees which features drove a decision. Dermatologists and medical imaging researchers are the readers weighing whether this framework is ready to support real clinics.
plos-pone-0359424:
Darío López-Delgado and eight colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a review that will gather studies systematically and pool them in a meta-analysis, on infections passed through sex, among women who are pregnant and who are migrants or refugees. Pregnancy plus displacement is a double vulnerability, and infections in pregnancy endanger both mother and child.

The review will gather prevalence figures, how common these infections are in this group, from studies worldwide. Migrant and refugee women often fall outside routine screening systems, so pooled prevalence can expose a hidden burden. Maternal health services designing outreach for displaced women are the audience waiting for this synthesis.
plos-pone-0359524: The PLOS One Staff published a 2026 correction notice in PLOS ONE. It amends an earlier scoping review about coach learning in youth participation sport. A correction keeps the public record straight when a detail in a published paper was wrong. Readers who cited the review can now check what changed. Notices like this are a small but real part of how science fixes its own record.
plos-pone-0359624:
Naim Gheymoumi and four colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies experimental allergic rhinitis, the laboratory version of hay fever's nasal inflammation. The treatment candidate is kynurenic acid, a natural compound made from the amino acid tryptophan, tested for whether it attenuates, or eases, the allergic response.

The authors tie the effect to the AhR receptor, a pathway that keeps immune activity in the nose in balance. A natural compound that calms nasal allergy through this pathway interests drug developers seeking gentler options than steroids. Allergy researchers are the core readers.
pmc-11168924:
Abramson, Adler, Dunger, and co-authors introduce AlphaFold 3, a model that predicts how biological molecules fit together. AlphaFold 2 had already changed the field by predicting protein shapes with high accuracy. Many teams then used it to model proteins and design new ones.

AlphaFold 3 extends that power from single proteins to interactions between molecules. It uses a substantially updated design built around a diffusion approach, the same broad family used in image tools. Predicting how drugs and other molecules bind their targets could speed drug discovery and deepen basic biology at once.
pmc-13191824:
Masaki Shinohara is first author on a 2026 case report of kidney surgery in a child with OHVIRA syndrome. OHVIRA is a rare birth condition. It combines a blocked half-vagina with a kidney anomaly on the same side. Some variant cases have a tiny, poorly formed kidney draining into the vagina, causing constant urine leakage, so removing the kidney is required.

At age five, doctors found the misplaced urine tube opening by vaginal scope and threaded a fluorescent catheter, a glowing tube, backward through it. During keyhole surgery, the glow reliably showed the tube and the small kidney remnant, guiding safe removal. The authors present the technique as feasible and useful for selected children with this condition.
pmc-13195024:
Leticia Gondim Souto is first author on a 2026 veterinary study of platelet counts as a prognostic sign in dogs with cancer. Thrombocytosis means an abnormally high platelet count, and platelets are known to aid cancer progression. In human oncology it marks poor outlook, but its meaning in dogs was little explored.

The authors reviewed one hundred and sixty-six dogs with malignant tumors and high platelet counts. Dogs with moderate-to-severe elevation survived significantly less long than mildly elevated dogs. In mammary carcinoma, higher elevation more than tripled the risk of death, and a similar trend appeared in mast cell tumors. Prospective studies with larger groups are needed, the authors say, to confirm platelet count as a useful marker.
pmc-13195224:
Yunnan Zhang is first author on a 2026 safety analysis of statin use alongside breast cancer treatment. More breast cancer patients now take statins, cholesterol-lowering drugs, during therapy, yet safety data are sparse. The authors mined the United States Food and Drug Administration adverse event reporting system, covering two decades of reports.

Of nearly two hundred and thirty-eight thousand breast cancer related reports, over eight thousand involved statin co-use. Reporting signals ran lower for liver and blood disorders among statin users, but higher for skin, psychiatric, kidney, muscle, and several other categories. Such reporting patterns cannot prove cause, the authors note, but they argue for individualized monitoring and deeper study of the pathways involved.
pmc-13200324:
Chikara Nakagami and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare fatty tumor near a past surgery site. A myelolipoma mixes mature fat with blood-forming tissue. It usually grows on the adrenal glands above the kidneys, so one in the belly wall is extremely uncommon.

Their patient was a 62-year-old man who had chest surgery for a thymus tumor at age thirty-nine, using a breastbone-lifting device. Decades later, a scan for another reason found a slowly growing mass by that device site, in front of the belly lining. Scans showed fat inside, raising worry of a cancerous fatty tumor. Full removal proved it benign. The authors add this tumor to the list for fat masses at old surgical sites.
pmc-13200624:
Li-min Wang and colleagues review cardiac mast cells in heart disease in a 2026 article. Mast cells are immune cells that release inflammatory signals. In the heart they help keep tissue balance but also drive swelling, scarring, and remodeling after injury, with roles that can flip by context.

The review traces where heart mast cells come from and where they sit in cardiac tissue. It covers their part in calming inflammation and reshaping tissue after damage. Animal work suggests they act much like other inflammatory cells, directly and indirectly. Their dual roles could cut both ways in disease. The authors map open questions and possible clinical uses for targeting these cells.
pmc-13200924:
Wenjun Liu and colleagues propose a finer fluid metric for children on continuous kidney therapy in a 2026 study. CRRT slowly cleans blood and removes fluid in critically ill children. The usual removal rate ignores each child's starting overload, so the team coined a clearance percentage: balance removed as a share of the initial overload.

They reviewed 432 children treated at one center from 2012 to 2023. Non-survivors got higher removal rates yet cleared no more overload than survivors. Body weight drove the removal rate strongly. The new percentage barely tracked illness severity or starting overload, making it a cleaner progress gauge. Their three-part framework pairs prescription, safety, and clearance for daily care.
pmc-13201324:
How many operations a surgeon needs before robotic hernia repair becomes routine is the question behind a 2026 scoping review by Francesco Brucchi. The review gathers studies that used cumulative sum analysis, a statistical method for spotting when performance stabilizes, during robotic repair of groin hernias.

Brucchi and colleagues searched five databases and found seven studies covering eight learning curves and 1,361 patients. The point where operating time leveled off ranged widely, from 12 to 138 procedures across the included studies. The authors estimate stabilization after roughly 25 to 35 procedures in structured training, while stressing that the evidence is weak and not a credentialing standard.
pmc-13202524:
Turning a biomass byproduct into a valuable chemical without solvents is the goal of a 2026 catalysis study led by Margi Joshi. The research article anchors a tungsten-rich cluster compound onto zeolite HY and uses it to oxidize levulinic acid into succinic acid with hydrogen peroxide.

The catalyst achieved complete selectivity toward succinic acid at a moderate yield, which the authors present as a first for this reaction setup. Careful tuning of reaction conditions and scavenger experiments revealed a controlled radical pathway that cleaves the target bond while suppressing over-oxidation. The material kept working through four reuse cycles, offering a blueprint for sustainable production of dicarboxylic acids from biomass.
pmc-13234824: Overgaard and colleagues introduce an editorial series on writing scientific articles better. The series targets two linked faults: weak reporting, where key details go missing, and weak method, where the study itself is loosely built. Its stated themes run from transparency and proper presentation to quality improvement and fair peer review. A well-reported study, the editors argue, can be repeated, judged, and used; a poorly reported one cannot, however good its data. The series aims to cut review rounds and raise the share of papers fit to guide practice.
pmc-13237224:
Vamsi and colleagues present HS-RankFormer, a model that rebuilds a full light spectrum from an ordinary colour photo. Hyperspectral images record dozens of narrow colour bands and reveal what eyes cannot see, but the cameras are costly. Rebuilding that data from a normal RGB image is hard: labelled examples are few, and models often fail on new scenes.

Their transformer-based model aims to be both efficient and sturdy across different settings. It tries to keep fine spatial detail while guessing each pixel's spectrum, without the heavy cost of earlier methods. Reliable reconstruction could put spectral imaging into farming, medicine, and inspection using cameras people already own.
pmc-13237424:
Chen and colleagues review how to steer crystal growth in antimony-based solar films. These chalcogenide materials are cheap and promising for thin-film solar cells. Their flaw is structural: their ribbon-like crystals conduct charge well along one direction and badly across it, so the way crystals lie in the film decides performance.

Crystals lying flat create slippery internal walls that block charge flow. Crystals standing upright, the team explains, form clean paths with friendly grain boundaries. The review gathers strategies to favour the upright growth, from seed layers to heat treatments. Mastering crystal direction could lift these films from laboratory promise to real panels.
pmc-13240924:
Ndengue's team in Douala tested how sample handling distorts breast cancer marker readings in a low-resource lab. One breast tumor from a 34-year-old woman supplied fifty tiny samples. Four cohorts varied the fixing recipe, fixing length, and delay before fixing. Estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and Ki67 were scored by staining.

Non-buffered formaldehyde shifted receptor shares slightly, yet Allred scores never changed. Fixing stayed sound up to 48 hours before values fell away. Cold delays hurt most: markers held for about two hours, then declined. The findings reassure labs that cannot always source buffered formalin.
pmc-13241524:
Tóth and Nagy at the Balaton Limnological Research Institute studied how city life affects common reed along Lake Balaton in Hungary. Reed beds dominate the shallow edges of the lake. Artificial light at night proved much stronger along the shore than over open water. The pair measured vegetative and reproductive traits across sites with different urban pressure.

Most growth traits showed no meaningful link to night lighting. Reproduction told another story: brighter shores held less reproductive biomass and fewer flowering plants. Reed growth also started later in the season at more urbanized sites. The authors argue that city influence acts as a selective filter, hitting reproduction and timing harder than bulk growth.
pmc-13242424:
Claire Munsie and colleagues evaluated a community exercise program built for teenagers and young adults who had finished cancer treatment. Their study appeared in Supportive Care in Cancer in 2026. Participants aged fifteen to twenty-seven joined twice-weekly group sessions for twelve weeks at a local facility. A trained exercise physiologist tailored aerobic, strength, and flexibility work to each person, and the team measured fitness and well-being before and after.

Of 127 starters, 93 finished the program and final testing. Aerobic fitness, leg and chest strength, and everyday physical function all improved, and lean mass rose while fat mass and fatigue fell. Quality of life improved across physical, role, and social domains, and no one was harmed by the training. Because the program ran in a community setting rather than a hospital, the authors see it as a model that survivorship services could copy widely.
pmc-13245424:
Miyazawa and co-authors investigated a patterned pufferfish's origins in this 2026 PeerJ study. Mushifugu, a poisonous pufferfish found only around Japan, wears a striking labyrinth pattern unlike its plain or spotted relatives. Biologists had speculated it might be a hybrid, since blending two spotted patterns can produce labyrinth designs. The team compared its DNA with its closest spotted relative, komonfugu, across both coasts of Japan.

Mitochondrial DNA split mushifugu into two regional groups, one in the Sea of Japan and one in the Pacific, with the Pacific group linking toward the relative. Genome-wide markers, though, showed little split between the two mushifugu populations and a clean separation from komonfugu. The authors use demographic modeling to weigh the hybrid story, treating the fish as its own lineage whose pattern demands explanation beyond simple mixing.
pmc-13247224:
Sun, Zhou, Huang, and co-authors describe a camouflage trick for delivering messenger RNA to the lungs, in this 2026 letter in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Inhaled mRNA vaccines could raise immunity right where respiratory viruses enter, but the lung's mucosal barrier blocks the lipid nanoparticles that carry mRNA, and none has finished clinical trials. The team borrowed a component of the lung's own surfactant, the soapy film lining the air sacs.

Swapping the particles' helper lipid for DPPC, surfactant's main lipid, let the particles bind a lung protein that normally recycles surfactant. That binding kept them in the mucosal layer longer and ferried them into and across airway cells. In their tests an inhaled vaccine built this way provoked stronger lung immunity, and the trick also boosted other approved particle designs.
pmc-13248324:
Zhao and co-authors looked for better predictors of cancer drug response in this 2026 Biomarker Research letter. Their patients had advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma treated first with immune therapy plus chemotherapy. The usual marker, PD-L1, alone predicts benefit poorly, so the team stained pretreatment biopsies for several immune cell types.

In one hundred forty-seven patients, high PD-L1 pointed to longer time before the cancer grew. Yet dense PD-1 positive killer T cells pointed the other way, toward shorter control. Combining both markers separated patients sharply, from under four months to nearly nine. The authors propose the pair as a practical guide for treatment choices.
pmc-13249124:
Miller and a U.S. team describe a trial protocol aimed at caregivers who sit too much, published in 2026. Caring for a relative with Alzheimer's disease raises a caregiver's own health risks, and long sitting is part of that load. The twelve-week trial sends text messages built on four behavior change techniques, including goal setting, planning, prompts, and self-monitoring.

The goal is a habit: four hourly walks a day, each adding a modest burst of steps, held for a week straight. Wrist trackers record movement passively while surveys probe whether the walking becomes automatic. Forty percent of the planned sample had enrolled by August 2025, with data collection expected to finish in mid 2026.
pmc-13250224:
Beauchamp and co-authors lay out a trial testing whether activity-based coaching can prevent depression after stroke. Their 2026 BMJ Open protocol targets low-income adults aged fifty-five and older, within three months of a stroke. Poststroke depression affects about a third of survivors and worsens recovery, yet no standard prevention approach exists.

Three hundred fifty volunteers with mild symptoms will be assigned to phone-delivered behavioral activation or to usual care. Trained community health workers will run an orientation, five weekly sessions, and two monthly booster calls. Depression scores over nine months form the main outcome, with anxiety, quality of life, and hospital visits also tracked. The team will share deidentified data and code through a national archive.
pmc-13250324:
Mohmmed Margni and co-authors set out a technique paper in 2026 on treating painful knee arthritis from inside the blood vessels. Blocking overgrown small arteries around the knee can ease pain, and the entry point is usually the groin artery.

Drawing on more than ten years of practice, the team instead enters through a foot artery, checking it first with ultrasound. Guided by live X-ray pictures, they steer a fine catheter into the knee branches using a no-wire method, then reduce the excess blood flow while keeping normal flow. They report faster walking after the procedure, plus lower radiation and dye use, making foot entry a practical option.
pmc-13251524:
Vlasov and Manley review enhancer RNAs, short-lived transcripts copied from the genome's enhancer switches. Their 2026 RNA Biology paper sorts what these RNAs do and how they blur the line between coding and non-coding RNA. Enhancer RNAs are usually destroyed quickly, yet several roles in switching genes on have been proposed.

The review covers current models of enhancer RNA function and the discoveries behind them. It highlights a surprise: some enhancer RNAs contain readable protein recipes, and a few are actually translated. Proteins from supposedly non-coding transcripts tend to be small and may carry their own jobs. The authors argue these findings reshape thinking about how both enhancer RNAs and ordinary messenger RNAs evolved.
pmc-13253924:
Francesca Alfieri and many colleagues test an AI model that warns of kidney injury in a 2026 study. Acute kidney injury is a sudden loss of kidney function common in intensive care. Their model gives hourly risk scores for moderate and severe injury, and was upgraded to cope with missing data.

Past records covered 70,107 ICU admissions in three countries across 176 units, with strong scores above 0.89 on a key accuracy measure. A live test in three European hospitals with 329 patients scored from 0.82 to 0.96. Warnings came about 14 hours early on average, which the authors say could aid care.
pmc-13254424:
Xiaobin Tang and co-authors run a pilot study of facial microbes in rosacea in a 2026 paper. Rosacea is a chronic facial skin disease with redness and bumps. Skin samples from six patients and two healthy controls, across three skin oil types, were sequenced for bacteria and fungi.

Patients showed higher bacterial diversity than controls, at a Shannon index of 2.26 versus 0.71. Fungal communities were almost fully replaced between individuals, a near-complete restructuring. Skin oil content shaped microbial diversity strongly, while bacteria-fungi links were weak. The authors say care may need to target both kingdoms.
pmc-13256224: A short 2026 retraction notice in Open Forum Infectious Diseases withdraws an IDWeek conference abstract by Monirujjaman Biswas on acute viral hepatitis among dengue patients in northern India. The journal says the abstract overlapped significantly with a previously published paper by Jain and others, without giving credit to it. It also says the authorship of the publication cannot be verified. The notice reports no prevalence figures of its own, so the retracted work is described here only by its subject and the reasons for withdrawal.
pmc-13258024:
Michelangelo Fabbrizzi and colleagues present a 2026 study of FEDE, a pipeline for building a digital twin of a human brain. A digital twin is a computer copy that aims to match both the brain's structure and its activity. FEDE combines imaging data, finite-element analysis, a math method for modeling physical structures, and biophysical modeling. The goal is one framework that holds anatomy and whole-brain activity together at fine detail.

The team demonstrated FEDE by building the first brain digital twin of a toddler with autism spectrum disorder. After tuning, the model copied the child's measured neural activity and rebuilt features from whole-brain connections down to synapse timing. It also estimated possible faults in synaptic transmission, the passing of signals between nerve cells, that fit known autism biology. Clinical uses are proposed next.
pmc-13258524:
Piotr Stogowski and colleagues report a gentler way to fix fractures at the top of the neck. Screws joining the first two cervical vertebrae must dodge arteries and the spinal cord. Their 2026 review covers fifty-one patients treated through small incisions with CT-based navigation guiding every screw.

Two hundred twelve screws were placed, and almost all sat in the top accuracy grades. Nobody suffered an artery injury, a new nerve deficit, or hardware failure during surgery. One surface wound infection was the only complication recorded. Operations averaged just over two hours, supporting the navigated route as a safe alternative to open surgery.
pmc-13259224:
Paulina Salazar-Aguilar and colleagues refine how to photograph nerve-support cells growing on plastic scaffolds. Schwann cells drive peripheral nerve repair, and judging their shape on electrospun mats matters for tissue engineering. Their 2026 pilot compares six preparation recipes under a low-vacuum electron microscope, no metal coating required.

Seeding more cells made far more of them visible on the scaffold surface. Marking the seeded side with graphite helped counts and preserved natural star-like shapes. Marker ink, by contrast, seemed to repel the cells. The team also codified a careful way to trace cell extensions in image software, aiding repeatable measurements.
pmc-13260224:
Alim Emre Basaran leads a 2026 retrospective study of swelling around meningioma brain tumors after surgery. This swelling, called peritumoral brain edema, can persist after the tumor is removed and affects prognosis. The single-center study covered seventy-five confirmed meningiomas. Swelling volumes before and after surgery were measured from MRI scans, and tissue staining measured expression of a protein called FOXC1. Statistical analyses searched for independent predictors of how much the swelling shrank.

Higher FOXC1 expression was independently associated with greater swelling resolution, with an odds ratio of 6.36. Larger tumor volume was independently associated with lower resolution, with an odds ratio of 0.25. The authors propose FOXC1 as a possible molecular marker for predicting recovery from swelling after meningioma surgery. They caution that the finding needs validation in larger independent patient groups before clinical use.
pmc-13260724:
Rafael Willems and colleagues present a 2026 prospective pilot MRI study asking whether mRNA COVID-19 vaccination changes brain microstructure in the weeks after vaccination. Twenty-nine healthy adults who had never had the virus were scanned at three points. Scans came before the first dose, one to two weeks after the second dose, and two to three months after it. Both vaccine brands in use were included, giving eighty-five scans in total.

No new or growing white matter hyperintensities, bright spots linked to small vessel changes, were observed. Quantitative T1 values, a measure of tissue microstructure, showed no significant changes within individuals. Deviations averaged 0.1 percent and stayed within normal scan-to-scan variability. One participant's pre-existing spot shrank by one millimetre. The authors report no evidence of structural brain changes after vaccination in this small healthy group.
pmc-13261124:
Keul and co-authors present a 2026 study proposing a new way to read past ocean temperatures from pteropod shells. Pteropods are small swimming snails whose shells can archive past ocean conditions. The team tested lithium-to-magnesium ratios, a thermometer long used in corals, in the species Heliconoides inflatus for the first time.

Shells were collected along an Atlantic transect from 31° N to 38° S, spanning about 15 °C of surface heat. The lithium-to-magnesium ratios fell steeply as heat rose. That link allows heat reconstruction with an average precision of ± 1–2 °C. Seasonal heat changes were also captured from the early-life to adult parts of the shell. The species is widespread and plentiful in seabed layers. The authors present it as a new tool for rebuilding past surface heat.
pmc-13262724:
Pan Kang leads the study behind a 2026 journal article on how high blood sugar worsens vitiligo, a skin disease where immune cells destroy pigment cells. Patient comparisons linked high blood sugar to the disease, but the mechanism was unclear. The team used patient data and a mouse model, and measured small molecules in blood and tissue to find a mediator.

A fuel-cycle product called succinate emerged as the key link. Succinate switched on killer T cells through its receptor, SUCNR1, the authors found. It also pushed skin cells to release signals that draw those T cells into the skin. Blocking this pathway is therefore a possible treatment route, they argue, and succinate may mark disease activity.
pmc-13262824:
Cosmas Zyambo leads a national survey study of HIV treatment adherence in Zambia in a 2026 journal article. Antiretroviral therapy, the drug regimen that controls HIV, works only when taken as prescribed. The team surveyed people living with HIV at 193 clinics across all ten provinces, using a 2023 national survey, and modeled which factors tracked with missed treatment.

Of 5,204 people surveyed, 7.1 percent were not adhering, with higher rates in men than women. Among those not adhering, 60 percent drank alcohol and 22 percent smoked tobacco. Drinking and smoking each raised the odds of non-adherence roughly two to three times. Older age and more schooling lowered the odds. The authors suggest targeted support around alcohol and tobacco use.
pmc-13263224:
Takeshi Yamashita and co-authors report a relapsing neck spine infection in an 88-year-old man in a 2026 case report. The infection, called spondylodiscitis, attacks a spinal bone and its disc, and neck cases are uncommon. Blood cultures found a strain of Streptococcus gallolyticus, a normal gut germ rarely blamed for spinal infections.

A standard 90-day course of antibiotics first cleared his fever, neck pain, and blood markers. Yet symptoms returned on day 174, even though repeat scans showed no clear active inflammation. Doctors resumed oral antibiotics for nine months, reaching lasting remission without surgery. To their knowledge, no earlier case caused by this strain described a return. They suggest longer, patient-matched treatment and long follow-up for such cases.
pmc-13264824:
Katie de Luca led a 2026 commentary on the role of chiropractic care in rehabilitation, the care that restores daily function after illness or injury. About 2.4 billion people live with conditions that could gain from such care. Chiropractors train in muscle and joint health and person-centered care, and the paper argues they can strengthen health systems.

The authors describe chiropractic work after surgery, in sports injury recovery, and in nerve rehabilitation. They show how chiropractors join team-based care, public systems, and hospitals. Gains in low- and middle-income countries and for fair access are weighed. Barriers include uneven laws, low recognition by other professions, and patchy team integration. The paper ends with a call for better training links and advocacy.
pmc-13264924:
Lars Dijk and colleagues published a 2026 interview study on how sudden worsening events shape daily life for people with COPD, a long-term lung disease. Such events were defined by drops in breathing measures, more reliever use, or worse symptoms. The team asked patients in five countries how they spot and handle these turns.

Nineteen patients with moderate to severe disease took part, with interviews right after an event and again six weeks later. Patients described bad days in varied ways, from lost ability to do tasks to needing extra treatment. Events under two days often went unnoticed, while longer ones were usually recognized. Most said they would seek care if needed, but hard-to-get appointments and a wait-and-see habit held some back. The authors link low awareness to under-reporting.
pmc-13267024:
Xinjing Shen and colleagues report a 2026 study of a drinkable drug carrier aimed at scarred liver tissue. Liver fibrosis builds up when star-shaped liver cells switch on and lay down excess matrix. The team loaded a plant compound called morin into tiny oil droplets marked with vitamin A, which those cells tend to take up.

In rats with chemically induced liver scarring, the oral carrier crossed the gut wall intact and reached the liver through the lymph route. Treated rats showed less scarring, less of a scar marker, and lower levels of a key scar-driving signal. Liver function also improved. The authors offer the system as a long-term oral option for fibrosis care.
pmc-13267424: Shah and colleagues' letter on lung blood pressure in chronic lung disease is the subject of a 2026 correction notice. The original letter argued that male sex is linked to severe pulmonary hypertension and worse outcomes in COPD patients sent for a heart catheter test. A publisher's error left the published title incomplete. The correction restores the words Letter to the Editor at the start of the title, marking it as a letter. The notice apologizes for the error. No findings or conclusions change.
pmc-13267924:
Min Xu and colleagues report a 2026 survey of fear of movement after pacemaker surgery in China. Kinesiophobia, an excessive fear that movement will cause harm, can keep patients from rehab exercise. The team surveyed 211 patients at one large hospital in Yinchuan between October 2025 and January 2026. They measured family functioning, pain, worst-case thinking about pain, and movement fear.

About 60 percent of patients showed kinesiophobia. Stronger family functioning went with less fear, less pain, and less worst-case thinking. Pain and worst-case thinking each went with more fear. The chain analysis showed family support linked to lower fear partly through lower pain and calmer thinking about pain, in that order. The authors caution that a one-time survey cannot prove cause and urge follow-up studies.
pmc-13270724:
Manouri Wimalasekera is lead author of a 2026 narrative case study on bringing community engagement and involvement into research in Sri Lanka. That approach, shortened to CEI, means involving local people in shaping and guiding studies, and the work was coordinated by a Sri Lankan research institute between 2018 and 2025.

Drawing on stakeholder activities, workshop results, and programme records, the authors describe how CEI became part of the national research system. Success, they argue, needs tackling structural inequality, matching engagement to local culture, and backing from ethics rules and leaders. They present Sri Lanka's foundation as a model other lower- and middle-income countries could adapt.
pmc-13271424:
Jingyan Zhang is lead author of a 2026 single-centre survey on whether Chinese breast cancer patients would consider corrective surgery. The patients had breast deformity after breast-conserving surgery. They had finished radiation at least a year earlier. Deformity was graded with a standard scale. Willingness meant openness at survey time, not a booked operation.

Among 306 patients, 123, or 40.2 percent, were willing, and 183 declined. In simple analyses, willingness linked to home area, income, travel time to care, deformity grade, and other factors. Those declining most often cited fear of complications or failure, cost, acceptance of their look, or not wanting another operation. Better body image and self-belief motivated those willing.
pmc-13272524:
Konstantinos Ouranos leads a 2026 database study of sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection, paired with very high ferritin in the blood. That pattern is called macrophage activation-like syndrome, or MALS. The authors used the TriNetX database and a ferritin cutoff to define the group.

From 2017 to 2025, 10,169 patients met the MALS pattern, against 214,338 without it. After matching, MALS patients died more often at 28 and 90 days and needed breathing tubes, intensive care, and blood pressure drugs more often. Higher ferritin cutoffs meant worse outcomes, and the drug anakinra showed no survival gain.
pmc-13273524:
Emily Ravenhill and William Farr present a 2026 review of hikikomori, long social withdrawal first described in 1990s Japan. Debate persists over whether this is a disorder, a response to stress, or a coping strategy. Their two-stage review looks at overlap with autism traits and at cultural context.

They find overlap in social talk differences, sensory sensitivity, and narrow interests, though life paths differ. School pressure, family dynamics, and norms in Japan can worsen withdrawal. They also frame withdrawal as sometimes protective, aiding rest and coping. Harm arises when isolation lasts long with no support. They urge flexible, culturally aware help.
pmc-13273624:
Charlotte Naslund-Koch leads a 2026 study of fatty liver disease with fibrosis in patients with psoriasis, a chronic skin disease. The prevalence in this group is unknown and no screening consensus exists. Patients from a Copenhagen skin biobank program were examined with transient elastography, a scan that measures liver fat and stiffness, plus blood markers.

Of 403 patients, 40 percent had liver steatosis and 5 percent had fibrosis. Nearly all steatosis cases fit metabolic dysfunction-associated disease by reported alcohol use. Against the scan as reference, the FIB-4 index and the ELF test performed best, with accuracy measures of 0.92 and 0.90, while a collagen marker scored 0.77.
pmc-13274024:
Carla Bellinghausen and co-authors report a 2026 journal article from the CCHROMO study of long-lasting illness after COVID-19. The study follows patients at a post-COVID clinic with lung tests, exercise tests, and blood samples for up to three years. Its exact causes and course are still poorly understood.

This interim report covers 253 patients across 561 visits, a median of 273 days after diagnosis. Fatigue hit about eighty-five percent, with breathlessness, headache, and thinking problems each near seventy percent. Standard breathing tests were mostly normal, yet over half of visits showed weak breathing muscles and nearly a third showed poor exercise capacity. Links between symptoms, test results, and blood markers were weak overall.
pmc-13276324:
Jennifer Robblee and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on brain size during status migrainosus, a migraine attack lasting more than three days. These long attacks disable patients and resist treatment. Whether the brain itself swells during them was not known.

Eleven participants had MRI scans both during an attack and later at a pain-free baseline. Ten were women, and attacks had lasted a median of about twenty-five days. Total brain volume measured higher during attacks than at baseline. The cortex and deep gray matter trended slightly smaller, while white matter under the cortex trended larger, though neither shift was clear-cut. The authors suggest hidden cell swelling could explain the volume gain. They call for larger studies to pin down the mechanism and what it means for patients.
pmc-13276524:
Ruth Harvey and co-authors report a 2026 journal article testing human immunity to a new flu strain that emerged in 2025. The strain, a subclade K version of A/H3N2 flu, carried many changes in its surface protein, raising fears it might dodge vaccines. Yet the season in Britain looked fairly normal.

The team mapped how the new virus relates to recent strains, then tested blood from two hundred forty-three people in Britain and Norway. Cohorts spanned ages one to over one hundred. The seasonal vaccine, though built for an earlier strain, boosted antibodies against all tested viruses, including the new subclade. People of every age group already showed some reactivity to the emergent virus, with no age band standing out as unprotected. The authors urge including blood profiling in future flu risk assessments.
pmc-13277824:
Fatemeh Sarani Rad leads a 2026 scoping review of digital twin systems for diabetes care. A digital twin is a virtual copy of a patient, updated with real data, that can be used to test or guide treatment. The review mapped studies published up to April 2025 across four databases, screening more than two hundred records.

Twenty-eight studies met the rules. Most covered type 1 or type 2 diabetes and used data-driven or simulation models. Common uses were glucose prediction, treatment control, and decision support. Inputs leaned on glucose monitors, wearables, lifestyle logs, and health records. The review sorts the field by design, personalization, and validation so future builders can see where evidence is thin.
pmc-13278424:
Lisa Graham leads a 2026 pilot study of a handheld device that measures a tiny eye tremor in people with Parkinson's disease. The tremor, called ocular microtremor, is an involuntary eye movement linked to brainstem activity and may be reduced in Parkinson's. Older methods were invasive and slow. The team tested the iTremor ONE device in 33 patients and 31 matched healthy controls.

Repeated measures in patients were highly reliable. Average tremor frequency was lower in patients than in controls, and the measure separated the groups fairly well. Frequency tracked with age in both groups and with speech, facial expression, and gait features in patients. Medication state made no difference. The measure may support screening, with more work needed.
pmc-13279824:
Juliette Vivien and colleagues present a 2026 toolbox paper on DBSsync for Parkinson disease research. Deep brain stimulation devices can now record brain signals for long spans while they stimulate. Such records could reveal disease marks and guide adaptive stimulation, which tunes itself by brain feedback. To find sound feedback marks, brain records must align in time with outside data like motion or heart signals.

Heart artifact removal tools clean the brain signal as a first step. The setup lets labs run multimodal protocols, where many signal types run at once. Precise sync is the base for new biomarker hunts in Parkinson care.
pmc-13281424:
Wajahat Mirza and colleagues pooled trials on wound suction after stoma reversal surgery in a 2026 review. A stoma is an opening that lets waste leave the body after bowel surgery. Reversal closes it, but the wound gets infected in a large share of cases. A suction dressing pulls fluid from the closed wound and may cut infection. Seven strict trials with four hundred twenty-nine patients met the review's rules. The team split results by how skin was closed, gathered or straight.

The review rated proof quality with a standard grading tool. It tracked infection in the first weeks, hospital stay, healing time, and blood loss. Two reviewers screened and scored each trial on their own to cut bias. The authors frame the work as a check on whether suction helps in all closure styles or just some. Their design aims to guide surgeons who face this common, costly setback.
pmc-13281624:
Sunil Thakali and colleagues reviewed eye injections at a community hospital in Nepal in a 2026 paper. The drug, bevacizumab, is shot into the eye to treat leaking or overgrown blood vessels at the back of the eye. The hospital serves a poor area with few resources. The team read charts of patients treated from 2019 to 2022. More than four hundred shots were given to two hundred forty-seven patients. Vision and retina thickness were tracked over follow-up visits.

The swollen center of the retina thinned a great deal after treatment. Overall sight scores, though, held flat across the whole group. Gains in sight did show in four subgroups, covering diabetes swelling, age-related damage, and two kinds of vein block. Most patients needed just one or two shots. The authors say the drug gave real gains even in a low-resource clinic, where repeat visits are hard to secure.
pmc-13281824:
Tobias Sägesser and colleagues built a single-atom probe that scans in three dimensions in a 2026 study. Stray fields from surfaces blur fine measurements and shorten quantum device life. Trapped ions, single charged atoms held in place, are superb field sensors. Past traps could only slide the ion along a line. Their new trap holds the ion with steady fields alone. That frees it to move through a block of space near a metal surface.

The probe mapped still and flickering electric and magnetic fields. It worked from close up to about half a millimeter away. Maps revealed charge patches and the texture of surface noise. By their pattern, the team could tell noise sources apart. The authors say the probe can serve surface science broadly. Any field where surface grit limits tools, from gravity tests to quantum chips, could gain.
pmc-13282324:
Kyriakos Psarakis and co-authors describe a 2026 computer systems paper presenting Styx, a runtime for stateful cloud functions. Cloud functions are small programs that run on demand. Many real tasks also need stored state, strict consistency, and low delay, which current tools handle poorly. Styx organises work as a flowing graph of functions and promises each transaction, a set of linked steps, runs exactly once and in a consistent order.

Three additions cut delay: detecting where a transaction ends, caching function results, and replying before full commit when safe. Styx can also move state between machines to balance load as demand shifts. Standard benchmark tests showed at least ten times the throughput of rival approaches, with near-linear scaling and low delay. Migration tests beat a stop-and-restart method. The authors aim at workflows and microservices that need speed without giving up correctness.
pmc-13282424:
Suey Yee Low and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their study of zoonotic gut parasites in public spaces in Malaysia. The original study surveyed small animal faeces and soil for parasites that can pass from animals to people. Several figures in the abstract, main text, and a table were wrong. The correction replaces them and leaves the study's topic and setting unchanged.

The corrected count is fifty-six positive samples, about seventy-nine percent, not sixty-three. Cat faeces carried parasites more often than dog faeces, at ninety percent against about sixty-five percent. The risk findings also change direction. Lacking a dustbin, not having one, was linked to higher hookworm infection in dogs. Cat samples from apartment playgrounds carried more hookworm than those from residential parks. Soil from dog-friendly parks showed higher odds of one hookworm type than soil from residential parks.
pmc-13284024:
Over half of men awaiting penile implant surgery report strong pre-surgery anxiety in a 2026 survey by Fayez T Hammad and colleagues. Worry may run high due to the foreign device and partner expectations afterward. No earlier study had measured anxiety in this exact group.

A total of 123 men at one institute answered a standard anxiety scale before surgery. Mean age was about 56 years across the survey group. Just over half scored in the clinically significant anxiety range. Past surgical problems and internet searching predicted high anxiety after adjustment. Top concerns were device failure, trouble activating the device, and size changes. Longer consults also tracked with worry.
pmc-13284324:
Fatma M. Talaat and colleagues present GreenAid, a plant disease detection system described in a 2026 research article. GreenAid combines three image models, VGG16, ResNet50, and InceptionV3, and weights each model by its class-level F1 scores. The system pairs the models with a phone app, a web dashboard, and a chat tool for farmers.

On the PlantVillage set of 87,000 images in 38 classes, the combined system reached high accuracy and beat five other ways of merging model outputs. A small phone version kept most of that accuracy while running offline in 127 ms per image on a mid-range phone. The work matters because plant disease causes large crop losses, and small farms often lack fast expert diagnosis.
pmc-13284424:
T. D. A. Stindt and co-authors report a nationwide Dutch cohort study, published in 2026, on local breast cancer return after mastectomy. Even after full removal of breast tissue, cancer can return at the chest site, yet trials often merge local and regional return. The team used the Netherlands Cancer Registry for women treated from 2012 to 2016.

Among more than 22,000 patients split by whether systemic therapy came first, local return stayed low, near 2 percent in both groups after long follow-up. Lower risk linked to screening detection, radiation, and some drug treatments, while higher stage and missed hormone therapy linked to higher risk. The patterns could help tailor follow-up and added treatment after mastectomy.
pmc-13285624:
Diabetes more than doubles the odds of severe dengue and nearly quadruples death odds, Jingjing Lin and co-authors pool in a 2026 review. Dengue spreads fast by mosquito bite while diabetes climbs worldwide, and its chronic swelling and weak defenses may deepen dengue harm. Three databases plus hand checks yielded twenty-seven studies with 734,123 patients.

Patients with diabetes faced clearly higher odds of severe dengue than those without, and higher odds still of dying from it in the pooled results reported here. Both gaps held across the varied study set. The authors urge early flagging and tight watch of diabetic patients where dengue thrives, plus care plans that treat both ills together.
pmc-13285824:
A Shreenivas and a large team of colleagues map HER2 changes across solid cancers in a 2026 real-world analysis. HER2, a growth signal protein, can be copied too often, mutated, or simply present at high levels on tumor cells. Using a huge profiling database, the team asked how these forms line up with each other and with survival.

The set held more than 200,000 tumors with gene data and a smaller group with protein stain results. Gene copies often, but not always, matched high protein levels, and some mutated tumors showed raised protein without extra copies. Patients whose tumors stained strongest lived longest on median, though the edge came mostly from breast and stomach cancers with known HER2 drugs. The mixed picture argues for testing each tumor on its own terms.
pmc-13285924:
Kien Trung Nguyen and colleagues describe late-pregnancy preeclampsia care at a large hospital in Vietnam in a 2026 retrospective study. The blood pressure disorder can turn severe fast and endangers both mother and baby. The team reviewed one year of cases to map how the disease looked, how staff handled it, and which signs warned of poor outcomes for newborns.

The review covered 154 women who gave birth at the hospital between August 2022 and July 2023, and severe disease made up well over half the cases. Older mothers, first pregnancies, past stillbirth, and assisted conception each came with higher odds of severe illness. Every woman with severe disease gave birth by cesarean, and early birth struck more than a third of the group. Birth before 34 weeks stood as the strongest warning sign for harm to the baby.
pmc-13286324:
Tri Budiati leads a 2026 quasi-experimental study of breastfeeding support after caesarean birth in Indonesia. Mothers who deliver by surgery often start nursing late and doubt their milk supply, and local myths feed that doubt. A culture-aware support model was tested against usual care in 116 mothers, with belief in milk adequacy and newborn weight tracked before and after.

Mothers receiving the model gained more confidence in their milk supply than the control group did. Their babies also put on more weight across the study window. After myths and family support entered the math, the model more than doubled the odds of a mother rating her milk as very sufficient. Nurses gain a ready option for coaching surgical-birth mothers through the shaky first days of nursing.
pmc-13286524:
Christina Ping and colleagues run a randomized trial on paid invitations to research through patient portals in a 2026 study. Portal messages recruit cheaply, but the same groups missing from trials also use portals least, so the tool might widen the gap it promises to close. Twelve hundred cancer patients, half from historically underrepresented groups, got a message about a fictitious survey study, with a third randomly offered twenty dollars to respond.

Only about four in ten patients even opened the message, and 13.3% answered with interest. White patients responded at 18%, against 7% for Black patients, and patients over 65 engaged far less than younger ones. The twenty-dollar offer moved nothing: response rates with and without it sat within noise of each other. Portal recruiting, the authors conclude, mirrors the very disparities it was meant to heal.
pmc-13287224:
Martin Pingel and colleagues mapped farming systems across Germany in 2026 so that payments for wildlife-friendly practice can be fitted to local conditions instead of applied uniformly. They grouped districts using land cover, field patterns, farming intensity, climate, and terrain, then refined the grouping with specialists from farming, conservation, and public agencies.

Eight system types emerged, ranging from cash-crop dominated areas to livestock dominated areas and mixed mosaics. Each type carries its own pressures on farmland wildlife, from heavy inputs to loss of varied habitat. The authors outline where tailored schemes could relieve each pressure and note that the grouping method could be repeated in other countries.
pmc-13288724:
Ismail Cifci, Bilal Durmaz, and Esra Meltem Koc test a muscle screen in Turkey in 2026. The screen is the five-question SARC-F. Records covered 396 adults. All were aged sixty-five or more. Two family health centers in Izmir took part. Blood tests joined the screen data.

Risk hit 16.9 percent of the group. Women showed risk more often than men. Older age raised the odds. Female sex and higher body weight also raised them. Lower ferritin tracked with more risk. Lower albumin did the same. When time blocks the screen itself, blood values may help. They can flag patients worth a full check.
pmc-13289224:
Elsa Martins and a large team report a 2026 phase Ib trial of mosunetuzumab given under the skin in systemic lupus erythematosus. Mosunetuzumab is a lab-made antibody that links T cells to B cells so T cells can remove B cells. The open-label study tested safety, drug levels in blood, and effects on immune cells across several centers.

Fifteen adults with active, antibody-positive lupus joined between January 2022 and December 2023. Some got one fixed dose, while others got a small first dose then a larger dose on day 8, up to 60 mg in the highest group. Two people stopped care because of side effects during treatment. No severe cytokine release events or nerve toxicity linked to immune cells were reported, which supports further careful study.
pmc-13289324:
Flávio Fidêncio de Lima headed a 2026 systematic review on whether poor diet links to painful temporomandibular disorders. These disorders cause jaw joint and muscle pain, and interest in lifestyle drivers of chronic pain is growing. The team searched five major databases for clinical and observational work through November 2025, then rated bias with a standard tool.

From 7,760 records, only seven studies passed with low risk of bias for synthesis. Birth and teen diet quality did not predict later jaw pain in cohort work. Cross-sectional work hinted that some eating patterns track with symptoms, and women with muscle-based jaw pain ate fewer key nutrients than controls. One lab test found a flavor enhancer raised pain, while the sole trial found no clear vitamin D benefit.
pmc-13290124:
Plant compounds packed into tiny carriers are reviewed as weapons against drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus by Neha Gupta and a large team in 2026. The bacterium is a leading cause of hospital-acquired infection, and standard antibiotics increasingly fail against it.

Plant chemicals alone disappoint, the authors note, because they dissolve poorly, break down fast, and miss their targets. Loading them into nanoscale carriers fixes much of that. The loaded particles attack on several fronts: they jam efflux pumps, break membranes, make reactive oxygen species, and stop biofilms from forming. Curcumin particles broke MRSA membranes in the studies reviewed, and quercetin in liposomes entered biofilms better than the free compound. Gains also appeared when such particles were paired with standard antibiotics.
pmc-13290624:
Priyanka and colleagues report in 2026 that the gel inside the eye clings to the retina more often in diabetes, though how much sticks does not clearly differ. Their prospective study comes from central India. Vitreomacular adhesion is a normal stage of vitreous separation that may steer how diabetic retinopathy advances.

The team used optical coherence tomography scans at four angles. They measured the share of retinal surface still attached in 68 eyes of 40 diabetic patients without proliferative disease and 50 eyes of 25 matched controls. Adhesion was present in 96% of diabetic eyes against 84% of controls, a significant gap. The attached percentage, though, averaged 65% versus 58% without reaching significance, and early retinopathy stages did not separate either. The authors call for studies in advanced disease with newer scanners.
pmc-13290724:
Each drug in one leukemia family carries its own danger signature, Yong Wang and colleagues find in a study from 2026 of the FDA's adverse event database. Anthracyclines anchor acute myeloid leukemia treatment, but their harms differ by drug and by patient.

Mining reports from 2004 to 2024, the team analyzed 1,079 cases and 3,622 adverse events. Epirubicin showed the strongest heart-toxicity signal, doxorubicin the most pregnancy-related events, daunorubicin blood-vessel disorders, and idarubicin marrow suppression and infections. Most events arrived within 180 days of treatment. Idarubicin's onset ran late in older patients, and timing differed by sex for two drugs. Wang and colleagues argue the distinct profiles should steer drug choice and monitoring in leukemia care.
pmc-13290824:
Speed, prior revision, and mixed germs decide whether an infected hip implant can be saved, Ernesto Muñoz-Mahamud and colleagues report in a long-term study from 2026. Debridement with implant retention is a main option for acute prosthetic joint infection, but reported success swings wildly, from 16 to 92%.

Failure roughly doubled when surgery waited past the first week after diagnosis, when the infected joint was a revision rather than a primary implant, and when infections were polymicrobial rather than single-organism. No other traits mattered significantly. The authors urge fast action while flagging the timing result as needing confirmation.
pmc-13291024:
Abel Trujillo-Ocampo heads a 2026 laboratory study of a calming immune cell type called NKT10, grown from cord blood invariant natural killer T cells. Such cells can steer immune responses toward control rather than attack, yet their medical use in stem cell transplantation had barely been tested before this work.

Single-cell analysis confirmed a distinct NKT10-like group rich in control pathways. In dishes the cord cells slowed other immune cells from multiplying, and in mice they eased graft-versus-host disease, supporting their promise as a cell therapy.
pmc-13291224:
Growing onions in very dry soil takes smart feeding. Abeer Abd EL Moiez Ahmed Bakr leads a 2026 field study in Upper Egypt. Poor soil, scant water, and storage losses cut profits. The team paired organic waste with tiny mineral sprays.

Sugarcane filter mud was spread as organic feed. Sprays held copper or calcium particles at varied doses. Trials ran over two growing seasons. Best yields beat plain controls by a wide margin. Low copper with high calcium worked best. Too much copper with too little calcium harmed plants. Storage quality also improved under good mixes. Balanced pairing is the core lesson for dry farms.
pmc-13291324:

The agent learned by trial inside a physics simulator. No pre-made training set was needed. Repeated runs with varied seeds found the same best design. It took just twelve steps and about three minutes. Rival methods needed far more steps each. Loss fell well below the target value. Stable, fast search is the main win here. Photonics design may gain from such self-driving tools.
pmc-13291924:

The bleeding disorder stems from a fault in the F8 gene on the X chromosome, so females are usually only carriers. Mating a mildly affected male with a carrier can produce daughters carrying the fault on both copies. Their patient bled heavily from minor injuries from puppyhood, starting with swelling after microchip placement at three months.

pmc-13292024:

Otitis media with effusion is common in childhood, and recurrence after tubes fall out worries clinicians. Their August 2024 search covered eight databases under PRISMA guidance.

Tubes alone gave 31 percent recurrence, against 20 percent when antibiotics were added, though the authors urge caution about that comparison. Children who also had cleft palate surgery fared worst, at 45 percent recurrence in the analysis. Year-by-year pooling showed recurrence easing from 39 percent in 2005 to 24 percent by 2019.
pmc-13292424:

Working in senior high schools, they combined teacher interviews, classroom observations, and stimulated recall sessions. The study leans on the Technology Acceptance Model and self-efficacy theory to explain reading and writing instruction.

Positive attitudes also collided with thin infrastructure and scarce time. The authors argue teacher psychology is the missing middle layer between what AI could do and what lessons actually deliver.
pmc-13292924:
Graeme C. Hays leads a 2026 study tracking how green turtles steer across open ocean between nesting beaches and feeding grounds. How sea animals find distant targets far from land has puzzled scientists for over a century.

New tags sent compass headings by satellite during trips over 1000 kilometers that lasted about 27.5 days on average, a span the authors report. Turtles often held one steady heading for long stretches, even when that path drifted off course, then turned to correct it. Steady legs with rare fixes fit the idea that turtles use magnetic signposts or rough maps, rather than constant fine tuning.
pmc-13293824:
Ning-chen Wang and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective cohort study on early breast cancer care. Their focus is why some people who choose breast-conserving surgery later need full mastectomy because tumor remains at the cut edge. Records cover operations from January 2015 through December 2024.

Among 290 patients, 31 needed the larger operation while 259 kept the smaller one. Four traits stood out as independent predictors: low body mass index, disease in more than one spot, larger tumor size, and a ductal carcinoma in situ part. Spotting these traits before surgery could help teams plan better and counsel patients more honestly.
pmc-13294124:
Abdullah, Zulaikha Fatima, and José Luis Oropeza Rodríguez present ApneaSense in 2026, a home-friendly system for spotting sleep apnea without a costly lab study. Standard overnight testing can cost over $6,000 per unit and reaches few people. Their setup fuses heart, oxygen, breathing effort, and motion signals on a low-power Raspberry Pi unit with a phone app for live viewing and telehealth sync.

Validation mixed a public database of 25 people with a clinic set of 61 people. On a held-out group of 17, the EvoApneaFormer model scored near 99.9% on accuracy, precision, and recall across six event classes. Home accuracy reached 96.9%, even with movement and signal dropouts.
pmc-13294224:
Manqi Cai, Xinxin Song, and Jun Tong pool therapy trials for teen borderline personality disorder in a 2026 meta-analysis. Four databases were searched through January 2026 for randomized trials of manual-based therapies in ages 12 to 18. Twelve trials held 844 teens, mean age 15.8 years and 81% female, covering dialectical, mentalization-based, and other structured programs.

Therapy gave small but clear gains for core symptoms, emotion control, and general mental health scores. No clear effect appeared for depressive symptoms or quality of life, though quality data came from just two trials. Variation between studies stayed low and no publication bias showed. Gains are real but modest, so expectations should stay measured.
pmc-13294324:
Yu Huang and colleagues grade two MRI methods for facial pain surgery planning in a 2026 retrospective study. In primary trigeminal neuralgia, a vessel pressing the nerve is the usual target for decompression surgery. Records covered 412 patients whose surgical findings served as truth, comparing vessel angiography imaging, a steady-state sequence called FIESTA-c, and both together.

Surgeons found a culprit vessel in 407 of 412 patients, most often the superior cerebellar artery at 60.68% in the reported share. Simple presence checks scored near 91% for each scan alone and 96.36% combined. Exact vessel matching also favored pairing both scans. Preoperative confidence rises when the two views agree.
pmc-13294424:
Feng Xu and colleagues hunt scan signs of tumor spread through air spaces in early lung cancer for a 2026 study. Such spread worsens outlook even in stage IA disease, yet it is usually confirmed only after surgery. Records for 765 resected patients fed group comparisons and a prediction model, checked in an outside cohort, with tissue and mutation profiles compared as well.

Four scan signs independently flagged spread: high solid share, cut-off airways, pleural pulling, and satellite dots. Model accuracy areas reached 0.823 in training and 0.829 outside in the reported figures. High-risk patients relapsed sooner. Spread-positive tumors favored solid growth patterns and KRAS or ALK changes.
pmc-13295324:
Andrzej Falniowski, Aleksandra Jaszczyńska, and Sebastian Hofman describe a new snail genus and species from the Dominican Republic in a 2026 article. Minute freshwater snails were found in 2001 in the Dudu cenote, a pond formed where a cave roof partly fell in. Island snail life remains poorly studied despite its rich history.

Body features and DNA evidence placed the snails in the family Cochliopidae but apart from every known genus. The new genus honours Robert Hershler, a leading specialist on that family. The snails still live in the same pond today, underlining how much hidden diversity small island waters may hold.
pmc-13295424:

Protein clumps marked by vimentin and ubiquitin piled up near and even inside the nucleus. Boosting the clearing process partly saved cells from death. The authors point to skeleton steadying and waste system support as joint treatment directions.
pmc-13296024:

Half the patients had recovered well by three months, but among those alive at one year, two in five still had notable nerve problems. Little improvement came after the first year. Relapses affected about one in seven patients, while restarting immunotherapy rarely triggered one. Cancer-linked nerve syndromes and early relapse predicted lasting harm.
pmc-13296324:

Comprehension scored highest in the easy format and clearly beat the hard format. Easy text also brought shorter fixations and longer jumps between them, hinting at lighter mental load. Hard text drew the most fixations overall. The authors suggest plain formatting may ease reading for everyone, not just its target group.
pmc-13297424:
Kidney function might one day be read from a light scan of blood serum rather than a chemistry lab, propose Diogo Serrano and colleagues in a 2026 methods paper. They tested whether vibrational spectroscopy can estimate the markers clinicians use to stage chronic kidney disease.

The team prepared 54 serum-like solutions mimicking five disease stages and measured creatinine, urea, and albumin with mid- and near-infrared light. Mid-infrared scans, taken after a simple drying step, predicted urea best, while chosen near-infrared regions excelled for creatinine and albumin, with top models above R2 of 0.9. Classification separated healthy from diseased profiles with AUC above 0.93, supporting point-of-care potential.
pmc-13297624:
A simple ratio from two routine blood tests may warn which heart attack patients risk poor blood flow after stenting. Patients split at a ratio of 48.4 into low and high groups that differed in smoking, cholesterol, and final vessel flow. The ratio predicted reduced flow with an area under the curve of 0.9, close to a related combined index at 0.94 and ahead of either component alone. The authors propose the cut-off as an accessible way to flag patients needing extra vigilance.
pmc-13297724:
Waste fiber from coconut oil production yielded peptides that eased diabetes in mice, report Dingyan Sun and co-authors in a 2026 study. Breaking down coconut kernel fiber protein gave a small fraction, sized 1 to 3 kDa, that blocked the starch-digesting enzyme α-glucosidase by 74.49% in tests.

In diabetic mice the fraction improved insulin resistance and sensitivity to about three-quarters of metformin's effect, repaired liver damage, and calmed inflammation. Docking analysis named three peptides, including FDLPAR, as likely active agents. The material survived digestion well and cut glucose release from bread by over 50%, pointing toward low-glycemic functional foods built from an industry by-product.
pmc-13297824:
