Causal flow grew stronger within the salience network and from the attention network into it. The authors suggest stimulation shifts processing from outward attention toward internal sensing.
pmc-13392624:
Adonai James Chery and Atta Ur Rehman Ilham present a 55-year-old man whose worsening pain in both hips and groins was first treated as ordinary mechanical trouble. He grew weaker around the hips and steadily lost mobility, yet plain X-rays showed nothing that matched how bad he felt. The puzzle pushed the team toward blood tests for bone disease.

Testing found phosphate in blood far below normal alongside a sharply raised bone enzyme, while calcium sat only slightly low. Further checks showed his kidneys were leaking phosphate, and a hormone that drives that leak, FGF23, ran above its reference range. The picture fits softening of bone from phosphate loss. The authors urge clinicians to test phosphate early when hip pain, weakness, and fading mobility arrive together without injury.
pmc-13393524:
Amit Yadav and five colleagues isolated a black yeast fungus from cashew-oil-contaminated soil and characterised the soap-like molecule it secretes, a biosurfactant they name ES-414. Genetic barcoding placed the strain close to a reference Exophiala spinifera. The purified molecule is small, at four hundred fourteen daltons, and chemical tests describe it as glycolipid-like, part sugar and part fat. It also survives heat well beyond boiling-adjacent temperatures.

The molecule attacked fungal biofilms, the slimy fortresses that protect Candida infections, blocking formation by well over half against two Candida species at modest doses. It also killed or slowed five Candida species outright and jammed bacterial quorum sensing, the chemical chatter microbes use to coordinate, in a dose-dependent way. The authors present ES-414 as a multi-action candidate against stubborn fungal films.
pmc-13394624:
Camilla Tjønneland Mentzoni leads a 2026 audit of eclampsia care at two Norwegian university hospitals. Eclampsia brings seizures in pregnancy and can harm mother and baby. The team reviewed records from 2013 to 2022 and found 22 women with the diagnosis among more than ninety thousand births. A working group scored each case against guidelines to find lessons.

No woman had received magnesium sulfate, the standard guard, before her seizure. Brain scans were done in only half the cases. In 18 women the group found chances to improve care. For eight, better steps might have stopped the seizure. The audit urges wider guard treatment, firmer pressure control, and follow-up visits.
pmc-13396424:
Mitchell T. Wong and co-authors tested two staff-led programs for helping hospital patients sleep, in a 2026 study of medical-surgical wards. Poor sleep in hospital is tied to delirium, slower recovery, and heavier use of care, yet simple non-drug routines are rarely built into ward practice.

Three groups were enrolled in sequence: standard care, a nightly nurse-led sleep routine, and a combined routine shared by nurses and physicians. Outcomes covered how patients rated their sleep, their satisfaction, and how much hospital resource their stay consumed. The comparison shows whether adding physicians to a nurse program buys anything beyond the nurse program alone.
pmc-13396924:
Haruchika Yamamoto and co-authors report early results with a next-generation machine that keeps donor lungs alive outside the body before transplant. Their 2026 single-center study comes from a Toronto program that has run over 1,000 such perfusions since 2008.

Ex-vivo lung perfusion lets teams test and repair marginal donor lungs instead of discarding them. The newer TorEx system, introduced in December 2022, loads the organ chamber into one all-in-one device, simplifying setup for centers with less experience. Of 1,067 perfusions through September 2024, 193 used TorEx and 874 the first-generation system. Outcomes after transplant were compared between generations and against standard transplants.
pmc-13397324:
Takahiro Kumode and co-authors report an interim look at 500 Japanese patients receiving a modern first-line drug combination for an aggressive lymphoma, in 2026. POLASTAR is a prospective, real-world study of Pola-R-CHP, which swaps one drug of the classic regimen for the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin, in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

The analysis set held 485 patients with a median age of 71, including people over 80 whom the pivotal trial had excluded. Most carried mid-to-high risk scores. Doses of the two antibody drugs were delivered at over 93 percent of the planned intensity. Real-world safety and effect in older, frailer patients are the study's reason to exist.
pmc-13397524:
Qingfeng Fu and colleagues present a room-temperature route for breaking down Teflon waste, a plastic famed for resisting almost everything. Their 2026 paper uses a liquid sodium-potassium alloy that reacts with the material and keeps the reaction going on its own. The strong carbon-fluorine bonds in these plastics normally demand harsh heat to break.

Less than a tenth of plastic waste gets recycled, and Teflon-type waste mostly ends up burned or buried. Here the alloy strips fluorine away in a self-heating reaction sparked by contact charging, turning the waste into fluorine-doped carbon plus metal fluorides. The products could serve as useful materials, offering a fresh path for a waste stream that today has almost none.
pmc-13398524:
Yanjuan Hou and co-authors pin a kidney gene behind a genome-scan signal. Their 2026 study names ELF3 as the effector gene at a locus tied to kidney function, out of more than a thousand such loci still unexplained. In injured kidney tubules, ELF3 switches on and marks cells caught in a transitional, inflamed state ringed by immune cells.

Deleting the gene in mice after injury thinned those stuck cells, cut cytokine output and reduced immune cell gathering. ELF3 drives the effect by switching on parts of a noncanonical NF-κB pathway and escorting its key protein into the nucleus. The work frames ELF3 as an amplifier worth blocking in chronic kidney disease.
pmc-13398824:
Meng Zhang and co-authors uncover a two-factor module that arms millet and wheat against drought and salt while lifting yield. Their 2026 study works in foxtail millet, where the transcription factors TAF10 and ERF109 team up to switch on flavonoid-making genes. Flavonoids, plant pigments with protective chemistry, sit at the heart of the stress shield the pair builds.

Spraying the flavonoids themselves (apigenin, naringenin or hesperetin) rescued plants whose module was silenced. Field protocols for apigenin then raised wheat yields by 12.3 to 19.6 percent and millet yields by 15.8 to 23.9 percent under dry and salty field conditions in the trials reported. A spray-on shield beats breeding timelines where climates are already turning.
pmc-13399124:
Yuya Ueno, Shota Yamazaki, Hiromichi Hoshina, and Masahiko Harata report in 2026 that terahertz radiation can speed up repair of broken DNA in living cells. Double-strand breaks are the most dangerous kind of DNA damage. Slow or faulty repair can lead to cancer and other diseases. Terahertz waves sit between microwaves and infrared light and cannot ionize molecules, which makes them attractive as a gentle tool.

In their experiments, exposing cells to terahertz waves lowered the amount of chemically induced double-strand breaks. The effect size depended on the wave frequency used. Heating the samples instead raised the number of breaks, which told the team the benefit was not a simple warming effect. Earlier work showed terahertz exposure promotes actin polymerization, a process also involved in break repair inside the nucleus. The authors suggest such exposure might one day support treatments for diseases tied to genomic instability.
pmc-13399424:
Rafael Mathias Pitta and colleagues followed Brazilian men over time to see whether changing their own physical activity habits changed their risk of erectile dysfunction, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Earlier studies linked leisure exercise to lower risk, but they mostly froze people at one moment and came from wealthy countries. The effect of real-world habit change stayed untested.

The cohort drew on employer-sponsored health checkups at a São Paulo hospital between 2008 and 2022. The analysis included 925 men over 39 who had no erectile dysfunction at their first visit and who returned for a second assessment 300 to 800 days later. Each man was classed by how his activity pattern moved between visits: persistently inactive, becoming inactive, becoming active, or persistently active. Erectile function was scored with the standard international index questionnaire at both visits. The authors expected men who became or stayed active to fare better than those who stayed inactive.
pmc-13400224:
Nelson-Georges Dengo and colleagues report two years of a French national emergency committee that advises, within twenty-four hours, on pregnant and postpartum women with thrombotic microangiopathy, in a 2026 article. The committee, under the national TMA reference center since October 2023, convenes experts from eight specialties per case.

The first 76 reviewed women were most often in a preeclampsia context, 47 percent, or peripartum hemorrhage, 40 percent. Thirty-eight percent were first-time mothers. Acute kidney injury appeared in 62 percent, including nine women with renal cortical necrosis, the extreme phenotype the authors highlight. True TTP accounted for only thirteen cases, 17 percent, and none was judged atypical HUS. The committee changed management in 26 percent of cases, most often by de-escalating therapy, sparing women plasma exchange or costly drugs they did not need. The authors advocate real-time multidisciplinary conferences as standard support.
pmc-13400624:
Behnam Taherizadeh and colleagues apply, in 2026, an eagle-inspired search algorithm to place solar panels and batteries in local power networks. Adding solar generation and storage can cut losses and steady voltage, but only if units are sized and sited well. The team framed it as an optimization problem.

Their enhanced Bald Eagle Search was tested on two standard networks with 33 and 69 connection points, under solar-only and solar-plus-battery plans. It beat a genetic algorithm and a whale-inspired method on every run. On the larger network, daily energy losses fell by up to roughly half depending on setup, the weakest voltage improved, and operating costs were lowest. The authors claim the method scales across network layouts.
pmc-13400724:
Zakiur Rehman Ansari and colleagues present, in 2026, a man whose heart stent, placed years earlier, fractured and seeded a slowly draining chest fistula. Delayed inflammatory complications of stents are exceptionally rare, and a skin-draining tract years later can masquerade as a simple chest wall infection. Untangling it required several imaging methods.

The 53-year-old, who had diabetes and heart disease, had a right coronary stent placed in 2018 and later developed months of intermittent fever and a draining pit near the breastbone. Scans revealed the broken, blocked stent wrapped in inflamed tissue reaching through the diaphragm. Surgeons removed the stent, the inflamed tissue and the tract after antibiotic cover. The case shows how cross-sectional imaging guides such operations.
pmc-13401324:
Inês Martins Esteves wrote a 2026 cohort study of a programme-level revamp in specialist eye nursing training in the United Kingdom, asking whether structural reform of a whole curriculum lifts student grades. Post-registration programmes often stay fragmented across results, assessments, and workload even when theory favours joined-up design.

Nine cohorts of registered nurses, 106 students in all, were compared. Six cohorts, 73 students, finished the traditional structure between 2018 and 2021, while three cohorts of 33 students took the redesigned programme in 2022 and 2023. The revamp drew on constructive alignment, programmatic assessment, competency-based education, and cognitive load theory. Esteves also introduces the Integrated Programme Reform Model as a framework for programme-level reform. Tests whether the new structure was linked to measurable gains in achievement.
pmc-13401524:
Lidiane Araujo Cezário and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of long-term cancer survivors in Brazil moving from oncology follow-up back to primary health care. After five years at a major cancer centre, survivors are referred onward, and the study asks how that transition actually works.

At the National Cancer Institute, 91 survivors answered a structured phone questionnaire about demographics, lifestyle, nutrition, prevention, and surveillance. Their average age was about 69 years. The most reported late effects were cognitive difficulties, hormonal symptoms, sleep problems, and chronic pain. Fewer than half said they had been referred to a primary care unit after treatment ended. Only 11 members, about 12 percent, recalled receiving a discharge summary to hand to their primary care provider, exposing a weak handover.
pmc-13402424:
Amouzadeh and co-authors study, in 2026, what makes mobile banking hard for older adults. They test six widely used Iranian banking apps through expert review and hands-on trials with 1,200 users aged 60 and above. Five human-computer interaction experts applied smartphone usability rules, while the older users completed tasks, rating scales, and interviews in a mixed-methods design.

The experts logged 135 usability problems, with error blocking the most severe category at a mean severity of 2.27, followed closely by visibility of system status at 2.22 on their scale. Usability scores diverged widely between apps, from 27.50 for the worst to 59.02 for the best on the hundred-point System Usability Scale. Age mattered within the older group too: users aged 60 to 63 averaged 54.2, while those aged 72 to 75 averaged 45.3 in the comparisons. Talks blamed cultural mismatches and cognitive overload as key barriers to handling money alone.
pmc-13402924:
Qing Li and Mario Plebani argue that machine learning in laboratory medicine needs two kinds of traceability kept distinct. One is the metrological kind that anchors a measurement to reference standards. The other is an algorithmic kind that lets auditors rebuild how a model turned data into output. Labs now use learning models to interpret tests, predict outcomes, and run operations, and each use carries different proof burdens.

A model can eat perfectly traceable lab values yet transform them in ways that leak information, hide uncertainty, or drift after deployment as methods and populations shift. The authors propose a functional framework aligning calibration thinking with model documentation, plus traceability dossiers and tiered rules backed by international teamwork. Their aim is reproducibility and comparability strong enough for clinical trust, without pretending a training set is a reference material.
pmc-13403024:
Tierra L Mosher leads a team reporting a 26-month-old girl whose acute liver failure traced to HHH syndrome. It is a rare urea cycle disorder named for its three blood and urine markers: high ornithine, high ammonia, and homocitrullinuria. The condition can bring lethargy, unsteadiness, seizures, coma, and liver failure, and newborn screening does not catch it. She was diagnosed one week into her admission.

Liver tissue showed an acute hepatitis-like injury with many acidophil cells and glycogen-filled nuclei, a pairing the authors say is rarely discussed. Acute care used intravenous dextrose and intralipids; long-term care restricts protein, adds glycerol phenylbutyrate to mop up nitrogen, and supplements citrulline to support the cycle. A telling clue was the child own avoidance of protein. The authors urge early metabolic labs and biopsy in pediatric liver failure.
pmc-13404624:
Cia Sin Lee and co-authors examine, in 2026, how health workers in Singapore viewed the OPTIMUM remote monitoring system for diabetes. The system was rolled out in primary care across the country after a trial showed good health outcomes. Knowing what helped or hindered its use matters for keeping it running.

Staff involved in the trial gave individual semi-structured interviews, which were transcribed, coded and analysed for themes. Analysis followed the CFIR framework, which sorts influences into the tool itself, outside pressures, clinic setting, individual staff and process. Workers said remote monitoring helped patients change habits and that its treatment algorithm allowed steady monitoring with tailored advice. Other setting and workload factors also shaped how the system landed.
pmc-13405024:
Shahana Singh and colleagues describe a 2026 quality project to strengthen child health checks at a Delhi primary care centre. Young children often arrive with one complaint while other problems stay hidden. The IMCI approach, a standard method for assessing sick children, covers danger signs and common illness together.

Age-specific checklists were introduced for children from 2 months to 5 years, backed by a dedicated children's clinic room and better measuring equipment. Two six-week improvement cycles followed. Complete assessment rose from low levels to 50 percent by the second cycle in the reported figures. Checking for danger signs reached 97.2 percent, and screening for cough, fever and diarrhoea all climbed.
pmc-13406324:
Yunjiao Shen and co-authors test the plant Centella asiatica against diabetic liver and fat problems in mice, in 2026 work. Diabetic mice were created with a fatty diet plus streptozotocin, then treated with plant extract or its component asiatic acid. A standard diabetes drug served as comparison.

Fasting glucose fell by about half in both treatment groups, 51.01 and 53.01 percent in the reported figures, with better glucose tolerance and blood fats. Liver fat and insulin resistance eased as well. The mechanism traced to pyrimidine metabolism: liver uridine and related compounds rose, supporting glycogen storage. A protein called UPP1 sits at the centre of the proposed pathway.
pmc-13407324:
Barbora Mechúrová and co-authors review what builds trust when a patient meets a doctor for the first time. While trust in long-term relationships is well studied, the very first encounter is not. Their 2026 scoping review searches PubMed for studies where trust was measured around that first visit.

From 2,825 initial records, ten studies passed full screening for thematic analysis. Trust was shaped in three phases. Before the visit, reputation, care coordination, and past good experiences helped. During the consultation, warmth, visible technical skill, information sharing, participation, listening, and empathy built trust. Afterward, symptom relief reinforced it, and apologising for errors proved crucial. Barriers included little chance to ask questions, time pressure, unmet expectations, and stigmatising language. The authors conclude trust formation starts before the door opens.
pmc-13407724:
Keng Siang Lee and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, to build expert consensus on using artificial intelligence to measure vestibular schwannomas, benign tumours of the hearing nerve. Growth decides treatment for these tumours. Volume measurement beats simple diameters for sensitivity. Yet hand segmentation is slow and variable. AI tools can now outline tumours on MRI automatically.

The plan runs in three phases. First comes a systematic review of how tumours get measured. That drafts candidate indicators. A steering committee then refines them into questionnaire items. Last comes a two-round Delphi survey plus a consensus meeting. Experts come from British and European skull-base societies. The resulting core reporting set will be spread through journals, funders, and conferences, aiming to standardise how AI-assisted measurement enters routine care.
pmc-13408624:
Homayouni-Rad and co-authors review, in 2026, the psychobiotic potential of postbiotics, the metabolic leftovers of probiotic bacteria, for depression, psychosis, and mania, a little-studied corner of gut-brain research. Their search covered PubMed, Medline, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library for English-language studies from January 2015 to January 2025, covering mood control, brain inflammation, and neurotransmitter tuning.

The surveyed evidence shows postbiotics raising serotonin and GABA signals, damping neuroinflammation, and tuning the body's stress axis. One cited mix, a Lactobacillus brevis strain from Thai fermented sausage, carried a GABA content of 2.85 milligrams per milliliter in the reported assay, showing how potent these metabolites can be. The clinical need is large: depression was about 50 percent more common among women than men in 2023, one of the gaps the review cites. The authors conclude postbiotics are promising drug candidates but insist on proper trials to pin down how they work and dosing.
pmc-13408724:
Saud Alsaleh, Mariam Shikshok, Ahmed Abdel-Aal, and Ammar Almehmi review in 2026 how to perform a kidney biopsy through the skin safely and well. The procedure diagnoses kidney disease, tracks treatment response, and informs prognosis, and it has evolved from a blind stick into an image-guided technique. Major bleeding still occurs in roughly one to six percent of cases in modern series, so preparation matters.

The narrative review gathers current guidance on when to biopsy, when not to, how to plan and perform the sampling, and how to manage the hours around it. Difficult groups get their own discussion, including patients with severe obesity, pregnancy, advanced age, a single kidney, or abnormal anatomy. Alternatives for cases where the standard route is impossible close the survey, giving nephrology teams a single bedside reference.
pmc-13408924:
Michał Papaj, Lingyuan Kong, Stevan Nadj-Perge, and Patrick Lee propose in 2026 an explanation for a strange pattern seen in flakes of iron-based superconductors. In them, the superconducting gap itself rises and falls with the rhythm of the crystal lattice. Their model starts from materials whose unit cells already break internal symmetry, and lets the superconductivity break fourfold rotation symmetry as well, a nematic state.

That combination textures the electronic surface. The gap peaks on one iron sublattice and dips on the other. The pairs themselves carry no net momentum. The authors spell out how local probes could read the signs of the pairing components from the pattern and even watch a transition into a mixed two-component state. Their framework turns a microscopy curiosity into a diagnostic for the nature of unconventional pairing.
pmc-13409624:
Yu Zhang, Rui Zhu, and Yin Li propose in 2026 a way to search encrypted cloud documents by meaning without the server ever reading them. Searchable encryption usually forces a trade: coarse indexes make queries slow, while expanding a query with related terms drags in noise. Their scheme, SES-HI, attacks both ends of the problem at once.

A two-stage clustering pipeline builds a balanced, many-branched index whose groups are semantically tight, sharpening the bounds that prune dead branches early. Query expansion is guided by topic modelling and then filtered by word-embedding similarity to keep the noise out. A dual pruning rule, global threshold plus top-k competition, trims the ranking work further. Security is proven against adaptive keyword attacks under a stated leakage profile, and experiments on a standard text collection improved the accuracy-latency balance over leading rivals.
pmc-13412324:
Lanlan Ji and co-authors present CellCover in 2026, a method that picks small gene panels defining a cell type when genes are judged together rather than one by one. Single-cell RNA atlases keep growing, and naming cell classes inside them depends on marker genes. Standard differential expression tests miss redundancy between genes, so panels picked that way carry wasted overlap.

CellCover treats panel selection as a set-covering puzzle over on-off expression data, which scales to the huge cell counts in modern atlases. Trials on blood and brain data showed leaner panels with signals distinct from standard picks. Applied across mouse, primate, and human data, the method tracked brain development stages and dated parts of a key stem cell program to rodent ancestors.
pmc-13413524:
Tenzin Choden Gyeltshen, Dimple Sajin, and Hang Thu Ta sift in 2026 through published liver-on-a-chip systems to find the settings that recur most often. These microfluidic devices aim to replace flat cell cultures and animal tests for drug screening, yet every lab builds them differently, which hampers comparison. The analysis catalogued cell sources, seeding densities, scaffold materials, and the assays used to prove the mini-livers work.

Immortalized HepG2 cells dominate current platforms by a wide margin in the literature surveyed. Typical seeding runs near three million cells per millilitre for flat systems, with lower ranges in three-dimensional builds. Collagen I, alone or blended with Matrigel, is the commonest scaffold, and albumin plus urea serve as the trusted function checks. Benchmarks for builders close the paper.
pmc-13413624:
Edwin Chrabieh and colleagues review in 2026 whether low-level light therapy can speed burn wound healing. Photobiomodulation uses red or near-infrared light at gentle intensities to nudge tissue repair and calm inflammation, a trick borrowed from cosmetic and rehabilitation practice. Their systematic search across three databases through 2024 gathered every study of the therapy in human burn patients that reported a clinical outcome.

Seven studies covering 190 patients qualified for the synthesis. Healing time and pain scores were the outcomes most often reported, with scar quality and wound area close behind. Results leaned promising, suggesting faster closure and less pain, yet dosing varied wildly and reporting was inconsistent, blocking any pooled analysis. The authors demand standardized, high-quality trials before burn units adopt the light.
pmc-13415824:
Amira A. E. Satti and co-authors reuse old vancomycin, a drug waste set for burning, to guard steel pipe from acid rust, in 2026. Tests used X60 carbon steel in strong hydrochloric acid. Weight loss, cell based power tests, surface scans, and math models all weighed the drug's guard film.

Protection rose with dose, reaching about 94 to 95 percent efficiency at room temperature by the best measures. Rust flow fell from 244 to 54 in the units used as dose rose. Scans showed a drug coat on the steel face. The coat forms one layer thick and sits by weak force, not strong bonds, the fits say.
pmc-13416124:
Reham A. Mohamed, Ali S. Shanour, and Taha A. El-Sayed bend test concrete floor slabs reinforced with carbon fiber polymer bars instead of steel, in 2026. Seven square high strength slabs were built: one steel reference and six with carbon bars at two thicknesses and three reinforcement levels. Carbon bars resist corrosion yet snap without yielding, unlike steel.

More carbon raised ultimate load by up to about 48 percent within a thickness group. Thickening slabs from one hundred to one hundred twenty millimeters added similar gains. Carbon slabs cracked in a more localized pattern and deformed less before failure. Computer models matched test loads within about seven percent.
pmc-13417224:
Yongze Wang and co-authors link microbes and enzymes with electricity to make decanoic acid from carbon dioxide, in a 2026 proof of concept study. Decanoic acid is a ten carbon fatty acid used in industry. The first stage uses a bacterium to turn the gas into acetate, fed by hydrogen from splitting water.

The second stage, run in glassware with enzymes, lengthens acetate into the final acid using recycled helper molecules. Labelled carbon tracing proved gas derived carbon reached the product. The system made a modest amount with about 81 percent specificity under tuned conditions. The hybrid design points toward making longer chemicals from waste gas and green power.
pmc-13417724:
Naser Aghamohammadzadeh and colleagues run an eight week trial of vitamin D3 plus flaxseed oil in older patients with type 2 diabetes in Iran, published in 2026. The trial was triple blind and placebo controlled, enrolling 104 patients, of whom 102 finished. The active group took flaxseed oil daily and high dose vitamin D every two weeks.

The main inflammation marker fell more in the active group than in controls. Exploratory outcomes also favoured the pairing, including weight, fasting glucose, insulin resistance, triglycerides, and physical quality of life. Side effects were few. Larger trials must confirm the secondary gains before clinical adoption, the authors note.
pmc-13418124:
João Vitor dos Santos Canellas and Fernando César Paraizo Borges argue for a fairer way to judge late registered review protocols, in a 2026 commentary. Registering a systematic review plan in advance is the gold standard because it locks methods before results are known. Late registration cannot prove that lock, and the authors do not claim it can.

They propose judging late registrations by transparency instead of timing alone. Reviewers should check whether lateness is admitted, reasons are given, and plan changes are documented and justified. Rigour and completeness of reporting also count. Such appraisal could guide editors without pretending late registration equals early registration.
pmc-13421224:
Choi and colleagues reported in 2026 a fatal multi-germ infection in an eight-year-old spayed female cat. The cat had mouth nodules and breathing distress for nine months despite treatment. Long-term immune-suppressing drugs for skin allergy and mouth swelling, including cyclosporine and prednisolone, had weakened its defences.

After death, gene tests and full genome reading named the culprits. The cat carried Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and M. kansasii, plus Klebsiella pneumoniae and a drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Culture had failed partly because Klebsiella overgrew the slow mycobacteria in the lab dishes. The authors argue that immune suppression blurred the classic signs of disease from these germs and let extra germs join in. They urge gene testing when standard cultures fail in immune-suppressed pets.
pmc-13421524:
Sunami and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study of a four-nickel cluster that can break and remake carbon-hydrogen bonds, among the most stubborn bonds in chemistry. Metal clusters holding hydrogen can attack such bonds, but nickel versions are scarce. The team made it from a nickel starting material and a boron reagent, with bulky phosphorus ligands.

The cluster has a pyramid-like four-nickel core with hydrogen atoms capping its faces. At mild heat it swapped light and heavy hydrogen with benzene, toluene, and even octane, and with its own ligands, showing the breaking runs both ways. It also drove a catalytic exchange between two solvents. Computer work points to one ligand slipping off as the trigger step. Such reversible breaking is a prized first step toward turning cheap hydrocarbons into products.
pmc-13421824:
Guiming Li leads a twenty-one-author team explaining, in a 2026 study, how arsenic trioxide destroys the fusion protein that drives a form of lymphoma. The NPM-ALK protein keeps its kinase permanently on in anaplastic large cell lymphoma, and arsenic — an old drug with promise here — had no clear mechanism.

Screening and chemical proteomics converged on STUB1, a cellular disposal tagger. Arsenic acts like glue, stabilising a three-way complex that lets STUB1 mark NPM-ALK for shredding; patients whose tumours carry more STUB1 survive better. Structural modelling implicates specific sulfur-bearing residues in the grip. Forcing STUB1 upward, or activating it with an approved heart drug, deslanoside, made arsenic far more potent against tumours in dishes and in animals.
pmc-13422124:
O'Sullivan, Omond, and Sedaghat build a roadmap for keeping internationally trained doctors in rural Australian general practice, where such doctors supply two thirds of the workforce in small towns. Their 2026 realist evaluation runs interviews and workgroups from late 2024 to mid 2025. A ten person advisory group and thirty one external voices, from regulators to trainees, take part. The question: what support works, for whom, and at which career stage.

The roadmap runs in three seasons. On arrival, central clear information about training and rural life builds comfort. In a new workplace and town, supervised early practice, skill bridging, and links to peers and community build confidence and belonging. During specialist training, family aware, fairly matched placements that build on prior skills deepen professional bonding. Early, continuous, layered support is the thread: one off help fades, while joined up support across agencies helps doctors qualify, feel valued, and stay.
pmc-13424024:
Chengjie Feng and six colleagues test two yardsticks for spotting fast progressors in primary open-angle glaucoma, the commonest form of the sight-stealing disease. Using five years of real-world records for 162 patients and 315 eyes, they compared decline rates on the visual field index against the older mean deviation measure, then hunted for risk factors.

The index flagged 0.92% of eyes as fast progressors, while mean deviation flagged 2.75%; moderate-speed decline appeared in roughly a fifth to a quarter of eyes by either measure. Moderate decline grew commoner as baseline damage advanced. Worse starting vision scores, thinner corneas, stronger short-sight, and older age independently predicted faster index decline, guiding who needs the closest watching.
pmc-13424824:
Dominique Enyama and seven colleagues investigate what helps or hinders breastfeeding in Bafia Health District, Cameroon, where national rates trail World Health Organization targets. Their cross-sectional study ran at six facilities. It examined 422 newborns for starting breastfeeding within the first hour and 544 older infants for exclusive breastfeeding to six months. Structured questionnaires and adjusted statistical models supplied the data.

Local rates beat the national picture: 73.7% of newborns started within the hour and 53.9% were exclusively breastfed. Vaginal delivery, knowing one is pregnant early, and carrying a single baby favoured a fast start. Continued exclusivity rose with pregnancy awareness, a mother not in paid work, more schooling, and Muslim faith. The authors back stronger education during pregnancy.
pmc-13425524:
Mäkinen and colleagues profile the fungi living in saliva in this 2026 cohort study of oral cancer patients, an angle most microbiome research ignores in favor of bacteria. They sequenced fungal DNA from saliva of 75 patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma before treatment, 27 of them again after about four years, and 81 cancer-free controls.

Before treatment, patients' fungal communities were less diverse than controls' by the Shannon index, with a significant gap at p equals 0.001 in the analysis, and Candida albicans, a common yeast, was more abundant. Patients also more often carried the Candida-driven community type, called a mycotype, rather than the Malassezia-driven alternative. After successful treatment the balance shifted toward the Malassezia type, resembling control profiles more closely. The authors link the Candida-dominated state to the cancer itself rather than to its therapy.
pmc-13425924:
Shangwen Qi and colleagues appraised cheaper ways to detect lung disease linked with rheumatoid arthritis in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease often begins silently, and high-resolution CT, the reference standard, is costly and uses radiation, limiting routine screening. Candidate alternatives include blood biomarkers, machine learning models, and lung ultrasound.

Searches of PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Web of Science gathered accuracy studies for these tools, most prediction models being logistic regression based. The authors judge whether such tests can serve as add-on screening beside CT rather than replacements for it. A cheap first test that flags who needs the full scan could spare cost and rays while still catching sick lungs at an early stage.
pmc-13426124:
Younan and colleagues published a 2026 design study on opioid safety for young bowel-disease patients. Teens and young adults with inflammatory bowel disease often live with chronic pain. Long opioid use in this group raises the risk of overdose harm. The team interviewed seven young patients and thirteen clinicians to shape a digital tool.

A joint workshop then brought patients and clinicians together to compare notes. Both sides ranked learning, open talk, and joined-up care above pain scores alone. Young patients stressed trust as they shift from child to adult services. Clinicians wanted better ways to watch risk across scattered care teams. The findings lay groundwork for a tool built with its users. Pain care, not opioid control alone, sits at the tool's heart.
pmc-13426224:
Zichen Rao and colleagues propose annexin A1 as a blood marker for cyclic Cushing disease in a 2026 diagnostic study. Cyclic disease, with cortisol swinging between high and low phases, is notoriously hard to catch because testing during a quiet phase looks normal. The team compared four patients with pituitary cyclic Cushing syndrome against fifty-six with conventional Cushing disease using protein profiling and single-cell sequencing.

Annexin A1 was markedly higher in tumors and blood of cyclic cases, confirmed by tissue staining and immunoassay. Measuring serum annexin A1 even during remission showed promising diagnostic ability, offering a route to earlier recognition.
pmc-13426424:
David Gilad and colleagues tested an artificial intelligence scheduler for night-call rosters in a children's hospital residency program. The study compared one year of the old rule-based scheduler with one year of the new constraint-based system.

Across 6,519 shifts, average calls per resident each month did not fall, but the spread between residents shrank by about half. Months breaching the cap of six calls dropped from about 17 percent to about 4 percent under the new system. Bad patterns such as back-to-back weekend calls and call-rest-call chains also fell sharply. Schedules reached staff about twice as early, and fairness improved for junior and senior residents alike, Gilad reports.
pmc-13427424:
Jia Liu and coauthors present a 2026 protocol for programming DNA crystal shape inside microscopic emulsion droplets. Their method builds a dual-inner-phase glass capillary device making water-in-oil-in-water double emulsions that co-encapsulate DNA crystal building blocks and modifiers at controlled flow rates. Osmotic shrinkage then concentrates contents to trigger confined crystal growth.

Methylene blue tests validated predictable encapsulation, and the setup controlled aspect ratio in one crystal system while steering shapes directionally in a 13-mer system. Materials scientists gain a recipe for growing designer DNA crystals with tuned morphology for nanotechnology use.
pmc-13427524:
Bruno Holanda Ferreira and coauthors studied neighborhood supports for activity in older adults in São Paulo, Brazil, in a 2026 population-based study. Overall activity levels were low in this older population despite activity's role in preventing heart and metabolic disease and preserving function. Awareness of public exercise programs was associated with higher activity, and activity ran higher in the Southeast and East zones than in the North of the city.

Proximity to public spaces and feeling safe showed no independent link after adjustment for personal and regional factors, yet a greater total count of facilitators tracked with more activity. Municipal programs may gain most by stacking several supports and advertising them widely.
pmc-13428024:
Attieh and colleagues report a 2026 case of blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome in an 83-year-old man, a rare vessel disorder usually diagnosed in childhood. He arrived with worsening fatigue and severe anemia needing repeated blood transfusions, and he had a history of gut bleeding and recurrent anemia that earlier checks had not explained.

A camera exam of the upper gut found nothing, but colonoscopy revealed many bluish, compressible vein malformations scattered through the first parts of his large intestine. A swallowed capsule camera ruled out small bowel involvement. Because the lesions were too many and too widespread to remove or treat through a scope, he was managed with transfusions and close outpatient follow-up. The authors urge considering vessel malformations when elderly patients have obscure, recurring gut blood loss.
pmc-13428224:
Andrea Calvo and colleagues examine thinking and behaviour changes at diagnosis in primary lateral sclerosis, a rare disease that damages upper motor neurons. Their 2026 population-based study draws on a regional register covering diagnoses made in Piedmont and Valle d'Aosta between 2007 and 2021.

Thirty-two patients received full neuropsychological and behavioural testing within three months of their first specialist visit. Cognitive or behavioural impairment appeared in 29.3 percent of patients, most often in executive function, memory, and social cognition, and was already present in early disease. Compared with healthy controls, patients scored worse across several domains and reported more anxiety and depression. Impairment frequency matched a comparison group with upper-motor-neuron ALS, though apathy was more common in that group. No patient met criteria for frontotemporal dementia.
pmc-13429124:
Chen and colleagues searched in 2026 for an immune link between heart failure and ischaemic stroke, meaning stroke caused by a blocked vessel. The team combined human genetic data with single-cell data from mouse models of both diseases.

Genetic analysis supported a two-way link, with each disease raising risk of the other. Both mouse models showed growth of inflammatory monocytes, a type of white blood cell, marked by a surface protein called Ly6C. Among candidate genes, NRIP1 stood out as protective and tied to these monocytes in both diseases. In cell tests, the drug tretinoin, related to vitamin A, eased injury and inflammation by acting through NRIP1. The authors propose the NRIP1-monocyte pathway as a target for treating both diseases together.
pmc-13429524:
Magda Rosa Ramos da Cruz and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, twenty years of one diet plan wrapped around weight-loss surgery. Their Brazilian center used the same routine for 622 adults operated between 2004 and 2024. Patients ate a ten-day anti-inflammatory diet before surgery, then followed a two-stage liquid plan. After surgery, food textures advanced in a fixed order from liquids to purees to solids over thirty days.

Five operation types were covered, led by gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy. Early gut symptoms stayed low: constipation led at about 9 percent, with vomiting close behind. Leaks at the surgical joins, the feared complication, appeared in only about half a percent of patients. Four in five patients had no symptoms at all in the first month. One intestinal technique produced symptoms most often yet still under a third. The authors credit the shared pathway, while asking for larger prospective tests.
pmc-13430024:
Reuben Kapur and co-authors show, in a 2026 study, that obesity can feed a mutation-driven blood cancer, and that two existing drug types can starve it back. Data from over 440,000 UK Biobank participants linked obesity traits with higher levels of an inflammatory signal, IL-17A, and greater myeloid cancer risk. Mutant blood stem cells carrying a fault in the PTPN11 gene were transplanted into lean and obese mice to test the connection directly.

In obese mice the mutant cells expanded faster, rewired fat metabolism, and surrounded themselves with suppressive macrophages while T cells tired. A drug pair, an antibody blocking IL-17A plus a GLP-1 drug of the type used for diabetes and weight loss, reversed much of that picture. Immune presentation recovered, T cells reawakened, and leukemia burden fell. Metabolic treatment as cancer support is the provocative suggestion.
pmc-13430524:
Enjuro Harunari, Sara Fushimi, and Yasuhiro Igarashi reported a new natural compound in 2026, drawn from the broth of a Rhodococcus strain grown in culture. They named the compound rhodopyran. Its flat shape was mapped with nuclear magnetic tools and mass reading, and the way its parts sit in space was judged from signal patterns and close-contact clues.

The compound joins two ring systems and carries an acid group, a mix the authors call rare for this group of bacteria. One part of its exact shape in space stays unknown. Rhodococcus is better known for breaking down other chemicals than for making new ones, yet gene studies hint at large untapped skill. The authors present the find as proof that this genus can yield fresh building blocks for study.
pmc-13431024:
Van Duinkerken and colleagues reported in 2026 on Dutch youth and adults followed from 2022 to 2024 after pandemic trauma. They asked what shaped mental health after traumatic events lived through during the COVID-19 pandemic, such as severe illness or losing a loved one. Stress symptoms and wellbeing were tracked in repeated surveys. The team weighed event features against personal traits such as prior vulnerability.

Across about fifty-eight hundred survey rounds, stress symptoms eased only slightly over time. Personal vulnerability factors linked to symptom levels far more strongly than anything about the event itself, and only personal factors mattered for general wellbeing. Open answers told why: lockdowns cut social contact, mourning rituals were blocked, and infection fear lingered. The authors urge future crisis policy to protect social connection as part of recovery.
pmc-13432524:
Giorli and colleagues ran the AMULET study on 40 adults with severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. All were treated with dupilumab, an antibody blocking interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signals. The team asked whether the drug restores mucociliary transport. That is the nose's self-cleaning conveyor of beating cilia. Transport time in these patients is markedly prolonged, leaving mucus thick and stagnant.

At baseline the mean transport time was 28.53 minutes, far slower than healthy clearance. Within the first treatment interval it fell to 16.60 minutes in this patient group. By the second recorded visit it had normalized at 13.35 minutes on average. Values kept easing to 11.05 minutes by the final visit. Every patient had normalized by twelve months of therapy. Nearly all participants, 95 percent, were excellent or good responders. The authors propose transport time as a marker of mucosal recovery.
pmc-13432824:
Murtaza and co-authors argue that plant hormones should not be drawn as one-way pipelines, in this 2026 review. They are better seen as a two-way conversation with metabolism. Hormones steer growth and stress responses, yet the review shows sugars, amino acids, and metabolites talk back, adjusting how much hormone a plant makes, moves, senses, and destroys.

The synthesis covers ten signaling systems, from auxin and gibberellins to melatonin. It identifies shared metabolic nodes that coordinate several pathways at once. These include sucrose and its signal trehalose-6-phosphate. They also include the acid-cycle intermediates citrate and malate. Redox guardians such as glutathione and ascorbate round out the list. New tools including live hormone biosensors, single-cell omics, and isotope tracing are moving the field from static maps to predictive models. The authors frame the view as a guide to engineering crops that balance growth against stress tolerance.
pmc-13433324:
Clément and a large team scan the genomes of wild beech trees where they grow in this 2026 study. Budbreak timing in European beech depends on both weather and genes, and previous garden experiments found only a few weak regions. Working in situ, in two range-edge populations surveyed over two years, avoids moving trees but exposes the full natural variation. The team ran genome-wide association tests linking DNA variants to budbreak in the field.

The significant DNA regions differed between the two populations and between years, evidence that local adaptation has occurred and that genes interact with the year's environment. Individual regions explained anywhere from almost nothing to over half the variation in some analyses. The architecture is mixed. Many effects are small, and a few are large. The diversity, the authors say, could feed assisted migration to prepare beech forests for climate change.
pmc-13434124:
Jian-Xun Zhao and co-authors rubbed a film in 2026 into being that pairs liquid metal bridges with ceramic grains to cut touch drag at power joints while standing hard wear. Touch drag caps batteries, switches, and spin joints, since true touch spans a scrap of the face and wear shaves it more. Liquid metal wets faces well yet bends too soft alone.

Rub fire built the mix on the spot: two thirds of its bulk is tiny charge-fit ceramic grains, laced by fluid metal through true metal bonds. The film posts top marks on both fronts at once, with huge current room and rock-grade hardness. The authors pitch rub-born builds as a road to joint goods that need not trade strength for flow.
pmc-13434324:
Jiacheng Zhang and coauthors build a hollow frame material in 2026 to pull uranium from seawater. Sunlight driven capture must gather two rare inputs in one spot before solid uranium can form. Their frame splits the jobs across an inner and an outer layer.

The inner layer makes and stores peroxide, the helper that sets uranium solid. The outer layer grabs uranium ions from the flow. Flows moving in two directions meet at a rich boundary where solid keeps forming. Uptake reached 25.1 milligrams per gram in real seawater. That rate is 3.9 times the rate of a solid twin material.
pmc-13435824:
Bülbül and colleagues standardize ultrasound measurement of ram testes in this 2026 veterinary study. Testicular ultrasound supports breeding soundness checks, but grayscale brightness values depend on how the measurement window is placed, and no standard existed. The team scanned 29 healthy, fertility-proven Güney Karaman rams in breeding and non-breeding seasons, taking ten standardized regions per testis and producing 1,160 spot measurements for analysis.

Brightness rose with age. It was much higher in August than in March. The reported values averaged about 71.65 in August, against about 60.89 in March for the two sampling points. Position mattered even more: spots below the central band of the testis averaged roughly double the brightness of spots above it. Transverse images also read brighter than lengthwise ones, leading the authors to demand standardized multi-site sampling in future work.
pmc-13436424:
Sandra Jablonska, Niru Shanbhag, and Alex Kula track Staphylococcus epidermidis strains across body sites in seventy six healthy women in 2026. The skin germ also lives in nose, mouth, gut, and urine paths. Genome reads cover 114 isolates from skin, nose, mouth, and urine.

Identical strains turned up at several sites in one woman, and sometimes across women. Gene sets did not sort by body site, which points to a shared pool. Virus inserts inside the germs also moved freely between isolates. A prediction model failed to guess source site from genes. The germ looks like a generalist, not a niche specialist.
pmc-13436824:
Gamain and colleagues report a 2026 study of malaria parasites and a protein that helps them stick inside the placenta during pregnancy. The parasite Plasmodium falciparum remodels the red blood cells it infects, placing sticky proteins on their surface. One, VAR2CSA, binds a placental receptor called CSA and carries phosphate tags. The team tested whether a parasite enzyme, the kinase FIKK1, adds those tags.

In lab tests, FIKK1 did phosphorylate VAR2CSA, meaning it attached phosphate groups to the protein. That tagging increased how strongly the protein bound the placental receptor. In engineered parasites, the enzyme sat in the same small structures, called Maurer's clefts, where VAR2CSA passes on its way to the cell surface. That enzyme is a possible drug target, since blocking it could protect pregnant women.
pmc-13437224:
Mohamad Mohty led a pooled look at two European registries tracking defibrotide, a drug used for a dangerous liver complication after stem cell transplant. The condition, called veno-occlusive disease, blocks small liver veins and can kill if untreated. Their 2026 report covers 275 adults, of whom 215 had severe disease and sixty had milder forms.

Median time to clearing was about eighteen and a half days for severe cases and about sixteen and a half days for milder ones. Among patients whose disease cleared, nearly a third in each group needed more than twenty-one days of treatment. Survival at day one hundred after transplant reached 82 percent overall among those who cleared, higher in milder cases. Serious side effects appeared in 31 percent of the cleared group. The authors read the record as support for the drug, noting that stopping at three weeks would cut many courses short.
pmc-13437524:
Muxin Zhang and colleagues report a rare mishap during hip replacement: a trial head, the test ball for sizing the new joint, slipped into the patient's pelvis. Their 2026 case report walks through the team's on-the-spot choices and reviews earlier reports. Rather than opening the abdomen, the surgeons partly divided a thigh muscle to reach in and pull the piece out.

The retrieval took about thirty minutes. No nerve, vessel, or organ injury was found. Four weeks after discharge the patient's hip score sat at seventy-seven points, rising to eighty-three by seven months. Standard rescues for a lost trial head, opening the belly or using a camera, carry real risk of their own. The authors offer their route as a gentler option worth having in the playbook. They grant one case cannot set a rule, and call for wider reports to build a shared plan.
pmc-13439124:
Goncalves and Côté map every gene that shifts antibiotic susceptibility in a notorious pathogen in this 2026 study. Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes hard-to-treat infections and survives antibiotics through many strategies. The team used an ordered library of mutants, each missing one gene. They grew every strain in low doses of antibiotics from several classes. They scored how each missing gene changed growth. That built a susceptibility network for the whole genome.

The network proved dense: a large share of the genome's genes influenced susceptibility to at least one antibiotic class in their screen. As expected, genes controlling efflux pumps, which expel drugs, and outer membrane permeability were central players. Less predictably, many genes with no known resistance role also shifted susceptibility, giving the authors new leads for strategies against multidrug-resistant strains of this bacterium.
pmc-13439324:
Abhilash Mishra and colleagues chase a physics effect in an ordinary magnetic crystal, reporting axion-like behaviour in chromia in 2026. Axion electrodynamics began as high-energy theory, where a field links electricity and magnetism in a simple even-handed way. In solids, the same maths would show as a magnetoelectric response equal in every direction, a pattern never cleanly seen. The team worked with chromia, an antiferromagnet with no exotic topology, using low-frequency alternating measurements backed by computer simulation.

Signals showed the even, single-value response expected from an axion term once rival contributions were suppressed. The response crossed zero at 168 kelvin, a fingerprint tying it to the axion part rather than background effects. The authors present chromia as a workable platform for axion physics in a bench-top material, with paths toward new magnetoelectric devices.
pmc-13440024: Paloma Navarro Negredo and co-authors publish a correction to their study of an engineered IL-10 cytokine in the aged brain. The notice is a correction only, with no new experiments or findings. Two figure faults are fixed: swapped legend colours for CD8 and PD1 in one panel, plus a duplicated image replaced by the correct panel from the original dataset. The authors state that the analysis was right and that results and conclusions stand unchanged.
pmc-13440124:
Yajing Li and colleagues profile microbes washed from the lungs of lung cancer patients at different stages, reporting a 2026 pilot study. Whether the lung microbiome shifts as non-small cell lung cancer advances was largely unmapped. Fluid from airway washing came from 26 patients with early-stage disease and 31 with advanced disease. Quantitative gene sequencing catalogued microbes and their genes, while flow cytometry sorted T cell types in the same fluid.

Distinct microbes marked each group, with two genera enriched early and three enriched late. Advanced disease also carried higher activity in four microbial genes and a T cell balance tilted toward CD8 cells over CD4 cells. One friendly genus, Bifidobacterium, tracked against that T cell ratio. The authors present the signatures as early clues linking airway microbes, immunity, and cancer stage, pending larger confirmation work.
pmc-13441724:
Lulua Alasousi and colleagues measure satisfaction at a Kuwaiti family medicine appointment clinic, reporting a 2026 survey from Nassem Health Centre. Kuwaiti primary care still runs mainly on walk-in visits, despite world evidence favouring booked family medicine. Consecutive patients at the appointment clinic answered a seven-item questionnaire grading the doctor-patient relationship on a five-point scale. After incomplete forms were dropped, 253 responses were analysed across a full year of recruitment.

Satisfaction ran strikingly high, with item averages near the top of the scale and most respondents picking the highest category each time. Scores bunched against the ceiling, a pattern the authors note openly. Age groups differed in satisfaction, while other groupings did not. The scale itself proved consistent and single-dimensioned. The authors present the appointment model as well received, while the ceiling pattern cautions against reading small score gaps as real quality gaps.
pmc-13441824:
Wenbo Mi and colleagues run a long-term field trial asking whether blending organic matter with chemical fertiliser beats either alone for soil and maize, reporting in 2026. Six regimes were compared: nothing, nitrogen alone, nitrogen plus phosphorus, manure alone, manure with mineral fertiliser, and straw with mineral fertiliser. Soil quality was scored with an index, and bacterial communities were sequenced to see how soil life responded.

Both blended regimes lifted the soil quality index and maize yield, with manure plus minerals ahead of straw plus minerals. Soil carbon, total nitrogen, and microbial biomass carbon did most of the work behind the gains. Manure blending also widened bacterial diversity, while key groups such as Lysobacter tracked soil properties closely. Diversity itself fed back positively on soil quality. The authors back combined organic and mineral feeding as the practical route to healthier soil.
pmc-13441924:
Long Tang and colleagues build a risk calculator for patients carrying three heart conditions at once, a stacked group prone to serious events, in a 2026 multicentre study. The patients combined high blood pressure, heart failure with preserved pumping, and unstable angina. Six Chinese centres contributed 1,669 such patients, split by hospital into building, validation, and test groups. Candidate predictors were winnowed by three selection methods before entering a survival model drawn as a nomogram, a points-based bedside chart.

During a median four years of follow-up, 254 patients suffered major events, defined as cardiac death, unplanned artery reopening, or heart failure readmission. Five predictors survived every filter: diabetes, past heart attack, an inflammation index, triglycerides, and a heart strain hormone. The finished chart estimates event risk at two, three, and four years for each patient. Accuracy, calibration, and usefulness checks are reported across the hospital groups.
pmc-13442524:
Vincent Billock and colleagues ask what brain cells that damp mixed senses are good for in a 2026 paper. Some cortex cells take in two senses at once, such as sight with sound, yet fire less than the sum of parts. The team tests two math rules for how such cells might blend cues into one weighted mean.

One rule weights each cue by how much it can be trusted, a best-guess method tied to Bayes logic. The twin rule weights cues by their raw size in a curved way that Schrödinger first sketched for two-eye blending. Real firing from sight-sound, sight-touch, and sound-touch cells fit the curved rule more closely. Yet curved-rule output tracked best-guess output well, so the authors argue that nerve cells may reach a Bayes-like result through a simpler curved trick.
pmc-13444124:
Lingjie Yuan and colleagues report one catalyst that runs three oxygen and hydrogen reactions for green energy gear in a 2026 paper. Cheap triple-duty catalysts are rare, since each reaction asks its own surface tricks. Their crystal, Sr2CoRuO6-delta, holds a tidy double perovskite frame with super-exchange links.

As a zinc-air battery air plate, it gave a peak power mark of 216 mW per square centimeter and a life span up to 1,000 hours in liquid cells. Flex cells kept working across heat swings and bends. In a membrane water splitter it served both poles at a cell mark of 1.90 V for a stiff current load. Live surface probes caught the true active skin in each reaction.
pmc-13444224:
Xiaomei Liao and colleagues redescribe a deep-sea cucumber, Deima oloughlini, with its full gene ring in a 2026 paper. Two specimens came from the Indian Ocean's Ninety East Ridge in 2022, hauled from depths of 2,447 to 2,557 m. Gene checks on COI and 16S marks confirmed the name.

The find is the first record of the species in the northern Indian Ocean. Bone-like ossicle maps from five body zones aid future name checks in the genus. Its mitochondrial ring spans 16,263 letters with 13 protein genes, 22 transfer RNAs, and two ribosomal RNAs. A+T content hit 72.2 percent of the ring in their count. The authors add rare gene data for a poorly known deep-sea family.
pmc-13444524:
Jieyu Song and colleagues run a first-in-human pilot of a lentiviral vaccine, J-51, for chronic hepatitis B in a 2026 trial. Seven patients with low virus marks took varied doses in step-up cohorts, from 50 million to 2 billion units. The open-label study weighed safety first, with surface antigen drops as the early gain mark.

No serious harms showed at any dose, and all side effects stayed mild and self-limited in the run. In the six-person clean set, three patients cut their HBsAg by more than 0.5 log units from the start marks. One patient in the top-mid cohort cleared the antigen fully by week 52. Responders shared low start marks, under 120 IU per milliliter in the report. The team backs a larger, blinded trial next.
pmc-13445524:
Yanlong Li and colleagues chart the burden of mental disorders across China and its provinces from 1990 through 2023, in a 2026 analysis of world burden data. Past studies used older data rounds or covered only slices of the population. Their work uses the newest round to give a full national and provincial picture.

Rates of mental illness, adjusted for age, rose by about a seventh over the three decades, and disability rates rose by a like share. Depression and anxiety carried the largest share of lost healthy years, while eating disorders grew fastest. Burden varied widely by province, with Hong Kong, Gansu, Macao, and Shandong at the high end. Women bore more depression, men more autism and attention disorders, a split that shapes where services should grow.
pmc-13446324:
Muhammad Z. Chauhan and colleagues map how research output and clinical load trade off among United States eye doctors, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The team linked journal records from 2021 to 2023 with Medicare claims and a national provider file. Only doctors with at least one journal paper in that span counted, which set the lens on publishing clinicians.

The group held 2,914 doctors, about two thirds of them men, with a median of nineteen years in practice. Publication score and clinical volume linked weakly in reverse: more of one went with a bit less of the other. Women matched men on publication score yet logged far fewer clinical units. Five flagship eye centers held near a quarter of all publication credit, a sharp pile-up the authors flag.
pmc-13446924:
Paulo Ney Solari and colleagues run a case-control study on what drives HIV passing from mother to child in Angola, in a 2026 paper from a referral maternity hospital in Luanda. Records from 2019 to 2024 covered two hundred four mother-infant pairs. Sixty-eight babies had HIV, matched against twice as many exposed babies without it, by birth year and mother's age.

Suppressed virus levels in the mother cut the odds of transmission to a small fraction, as did steady clinic follow-up for the child. Caesarean birth, age over twenty-five, schooling, early start of treatment in pregnancy, and four or more prenatal visits each cut odds too. The authors read the pattern as gaps in the prevention chain, not drug failure. They urge stronger tracking of pairs in care.
pmc-13447424:
Dan Chen and colleagues ask how personal experiences of unfair treatment colour views of government performance in China in a 2026 analysis. Public judgements of government matter for reform and planning, yet their roots in daily fairness experiences are less studied. Social trust and life satisfaction may carry the effect in a chain, each step weakening the next.

A national family panel dataset from 2016 supplied more than thirteen thousand residents for correlation and mediation modelling. People who reported more unfair treatment rated government performance lower. Trust in others and satisfaction with life both sat in the pathway, passing part of the effect along in sequence. Eroded trust left people less satisfied, which further dimmed their view of government. Fairness in daily dealings thus emerges as quiet infrastructure for public confidence.
pmc-13447824:
Eleanor Spens and Neil Burgess model the exchange between episodic and semantic memory as packed retrieval-augmented generation in 2026 work. Episodic memory in the hippocampus holds single events, while semantic memory in the neocortex holds general knowledge, and their cooperation underpins recall and problem solving. How the two systems trade information over time has lacked a concrete account.

Their model stores experiences in the hippocampus in compressed form, then replays them to train a neocortical network. The network learns the gist of episodes and patterns that carry over to new problems. During recall, hippocampal retrieval feeds fitting episodes into working memory, where neocortical knowledge shapes the rebuild. Model runs reproduce known effects such as schema-driven warping of recall, showing how detail slowly gives way to gist.
pmc-13447924:
T Sakthivel and K Balasubramanian propose a cross-domain cyber defence framework spanning homes, office networks and industrial control systems in 2026 work. Smart home devices, company systems and factory controls now link up, growing the attack surface for ransomware, insider threats and protocol exploits. Defences built for one domain rarely share warnings with the others, leaving multi-stage attacks hard to spot.

Their system fuses telemetry from all three domains, watches behaviour for anomalies without relying on known attack patterns, scores risk with weighted chances and steers adaptive responses. Tests across mixed data covering break-ins, botnets and factory feeds showed it caught most attacks with few false alarms. Response ran about twice as fast as older methods in their experiments. Head-to-head tests favoured the system over three rival approaches.
pmc-13448524:
Martin Hendrick and Gabriele Manoli model the roughening of city surfaces through multiplicative noise in a 2026 study. Their starting model treats building height growth as geometric Brownian motion, where random shocks scale with current size and drift follows economic growth.

Adding spatial coupling, where neighbours influence each other, tamed noise-driven fluctuations and shaped realistic urban texture. In the continuous limit the coupled model becomes a classic surface growth equation long used in physics. Roughness exponents measured from global city data fell inside that equation's expected range for most cities. City growth thus joins a well-established statistical physics family, with local interaction moderating pure multiplicative randomness.
pmc-13448824:
Jiahui Shi and co-authors engineer in 2026 a zinc alloy meant to fix load-bearing bones and then dissolve once healing is done. Adding trace rare-earth elements to a zinc-lithium-manganese base created internal phases with a mixed grain structure. The resulting material reached a tensile strength of 772 megapascals and bending strength of 1,207 megapascals, close to medical titanium.

Those same phases even out the alloy's breakdown, releasing zinc ions at a controlled rate rather than in bursts. The tuned ion levels switched on the Rap1 signaling pathway in bone-forming cells. Implants of the alloy produced about twice as much new bone as titanium implants in the team's tests. The authors present the zinc-lithium-manganese-yttrium alloy as a degradable alternative to permanent metal fixation for demanding orthopedic repairs.
pmc-13450024:
Shijie Ma and colleagues engineer in 2026 an oral nanomedicine against Helicobacter pylori. The borrowed coat survives stomach acid, slips through mucus, and homes to stomach lining cells. Inside the infection's peroxide-rich pockets the core breaks open on cue. In mice, a seven-day course beat shortened triple therapy on both bacterial burden and metaplasia gains.
pmc-13450524:
Yasmine Gillespie and co-authors present a 2026 case of Goltz syndrome, a rare gene disorder, in a baby boy. The condition is tied to the X chromosome and is most often seen in girls, since it is usually fatal for boys before birth. Boys who survive tend to carry the faulty gene in only some of their cells.

The baby was born at full term with many birth defects, among them a hernia of the chest, a small belly wall opening, and fused, extra fingers with a claw-like shape. Pale streaks ran along his arms, sides, and thighs in a pattern that follows early skin lines. The team says the case widens what doctors know of the syndrome in boys and shows why gene tests must hunt for patchy forms.
pmc-13451424:
Kong, Fei, and Li sorted the cultural landscapes of 520 traditional villages in China's Min River Basin. The aim was to guide heritage protection and tourism planning.
