A K-modes grouping method sorted the villages into distinct cultural landscape types from those scores. Layering the clusters over district lines, main local cultures, and river systems gave eight named cultural landscape zones for the basin. They range from the Northern Fujian zone on the Jian River to the Min-Hakka zone along the Jiulong River in the zoning map. The authors intend the zones as a reference for naming each village cluster's tourism flavor. The zones also support keeping cultural context alive and planning joined-up protection of the old villages.
pmc-13451524:
Shi, Wei, and Zhang hunt for genes tied to interferon gamma, an immune signal that runs awry in primary Sjögren's syndrome. In this long term disease the immune system attacks the glands that make tears and saliva. Their 2026 study mines public gene data from patient blood. It adds single cell sequencing, which reads genes cell by cell, and checks the results with a lab test on patient samples.

Four genes stood out: HERC6, IL15, CD58, and PTGS2, and a model built on them sorted patients from healthy people with high accuracy. Immune profiling showed a broadly disturbed cell mix in patients. Single cell maps pointed to macrophages, large immune cells that engulf debris, as central actors with altered development paths and stronger signaling to other cells. Lab checks confirmed that three of the four genes run higher in patients, backing them as candidate markers and drug targets.
pmc-13452224:
Velampatti Selvaraj and Chandrasekaran make a coveted nanomaterial inside a shock tube in milliseconds. Their 2026 paper targets turbostratic boron carbon nitride. This layered material's rotationally disordered stacking and wide layer spacing suit energy storage and catalysis. It resists direct synthesis with good crystal quality, though. Their reactor fires melamine and boric acid through reflected-shock temperatures above six thousand kelvin for two to three milliseconds.

The ultrafast quench, around a million degrees per second, froze the disordered stacking in place before it could settle into an ordered phase. The resulting few-layer nanosheets showed the expanded spacing, interference patterns, and high in-plane crystallinity the team wanted under electron microscopy. Electrochemically, the material delivered a double-layer capacitance of 878 millifarads per square centimetre, far above conventional boron carbon nitride electrodes. The authors credit the enlarged spacing and abundant defects, and pitch the solvent-free, single-step route as scalable.
pmc-13452324:
Lukas Pasold, Luca Eisentraut, and Ricardo Buettner release in 2026 a satellite photo set for teaching machines to spot railways across France. The set holds 10,000 true-color chips, split evenly between scenes with and without rails. Each chip is a small square that covers about five hundred meters of ground.

Rail spots came from open map lines, spread evenly and spaced apart, while no-rail chips were drawn nearby yet checked to cross no rail line. Photos come from the Sentinel-2 craft, merged from the least cloudy passes in a one-year window. A table lists each file, its class, and a steady ID, a base for tests of vision models and map learning.
pmc-13453024:
Xiaoxing Hang, Taiwei Jin, Jun Hua, Xuenong Zhang, and Wenlin Song build a gel that carries timolol through the skin to treat a common infant birthmark tumor. These superficial infantile hemangiomas are soft red growths, and timolol eye drops used on skin soak in poorly and fade fast. Their 2026 design packs the drug into liposomes, tiny fat bubbles, set inside a carbomer gel.

The bubbles measured about 139 nanometres wide and held about 65 percent of the drug load. Through lab skin tests, the gel delivered 1.9 times more drug than a plain gel and four times more than the drug solution. It reached 400 micrometres deep, far past the rival forms, and in mice it shrank tumors by about 81 percent. The gel caused no skin irritation and no body wide harm in the tests.
pmc-13454024:
Ping Wang and Xu Li study how mindset and food habits track with how athletes rate their own performance inside one sports organization in Rizhao, China. Their 2026 survey covers 100 competing athletes who rated motivation, anxiety, resilience, and confidence, plus their eating and drinking routines. Performance here means each athlete's own rating on a ten point scale.

Inner drive showed the strongest link to self rated performance, with a correlation of 0.68. Pre competition eating and mental resilience followed, while worry based anxiety pulled the other way. Together the factors explained 61 percent of the spread in ratings, and supplement use added nothing solid. Good eating habits also softened the drag of stress: athletes who ate by plan lost less performance as stress rose. The authors urge joint mind and menu coaching.
pmc-13454124:
Yunting Zhang, Fan Zhang, and Zili Zhang test whether a large language model can lift undergraduates' art history exam scores. Proof for AI help in art education is scarce, so their 2026 pilot builds a 104 question set with skill level tags. Three models first sat the set alone, and DeepSeek-V3 scored highest at 96.2 percent, so it became the helper.

Six students then answered with and without the model in a crossover design, each serving as their own control. Median accuracy leapt from 43.3 percent solo to 93.3 percent with help, a gain seen in five of the six students. Gains held across all four topic areas, and common errors shrank sharply. Teachers and students rated the model's explanations clear and coherent, with teachers the more cautious. The authors urge larger tests, including delayed recall checks.
pmc-13454224:
Guohai Wei and five co-authors hunt for risk factors behind bad outcomes when HIV patients with kidney failure catch infections on dialysis. Their 2026 study follows 70 such patients at a Guangxi hospital from 2019 to 2024, tracking nine months of treatment. A bad outcome means death or severe complications that stretch the hospital stay.

Bad outcomes hit 48 patients, or 68.57 percent, while 22 came through without severe events. Ages in the group spanned 11 to 86 years. Two blood measures stood out in the final model: low hemoglobin and low platelet counts each raised the risk of a bad outcome. The authors argue that spotting and treating these blood shortfalls early could improve the odds for a group whose infection risk already runs high.
pmc-13454724:
Keith M. Bellizzi and Rebecca M. Saracino open, in a 2026 editorial, a research collection on loneliness and social isolation among older adults living with cancer. The two states differ: loneliness is felt disconnection, while isolation counts actual contact and support. Both predict worse mental and physical health, faster decline, and earlier death in older people.

Cancer can deepen the split through symptoms, treatment strain, caregiving demands, and shaken identity. Contributions in the collection move past counting cases toward mechanisms, better measurement, and workable remedies. One study using a long-running women's health cohort tied loneliness and isolation to poorer mental quality of life and more depressive symptoms, with or without a cancer history. The editors argue that social connection deserves a place beside drugs and surgery in survivorship care.
pmc-13455624:
Jinxuan Ma and Wanlin Guo present, in a 2026 theory study, a model of how the brain handles information with striking thrift. Artificial intelligence beats humans at set tasks yet burns enormous energy, while the brain runs on about twenty watts. The authors propose that neurons gather into sphere-like assemblies whose combined electrical rhythms form orderly attractor patterns.

Using chaos mathematics and fractal theory, the model treats memory and processing as the shaping of those long-lived rhythms. Its numbers are bold: storage near 7.5 quintillion bytes, far above older estimates, and computing power likened to tens of thousands of top graphics chips. Efficiency reaches a claimed 79 percent against a physical limit, orders beyond current chips. The authors offer the sphere model as a design cue for leaner artificial systems, while the claims await experimental tests.
pmc-13456724:
Samin Rostamzadeh, Fatemeh Shahrahmani, Seyedehsahel Rasoulighasemlouei, and Rahim Mahmodlou describe, in a 2026 case report, an elderly woman whose two breasts harbored two different cancers at once. Cancer in both breasts at the same time is rare, and differing tissue types make it rarer still. The patient, aged 80, had never been screened and arrived with a lump she could feel in the right breast.

Imaging found lesions on both sides. A needle biopsy proved ductal cancer on the right, already in the armpit nodes. The left needle sample looked harmless, yet it clashed with the images, so surgeons removed the area and found lobular cancer hiding there. Both tumors fed on hormones and lacked the HER2 marker. Given her age and other illnesses, she had both breasts removed without chemotherapy. The authors stress matching images against tissue results, and cutting again when they disagree.
pmc-13456824:
Sophia Mathew Masha and three colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a twisted small intestine in a man who had never had abdominal surgery. A volvulus, where bowel loops spin on their stalk, can strangle its own blood supply within hours. Causes are usually scars or malformations, and neither was present here.

The patient, a 30-year-old man, arrived after three days of blockage symptoms, feverish, restless, and severely dried out. Scans showed stacked air and fluid levels with a suggestive swirl. Emergency surgery found a forty-centimeter loop of starved bowel spun a full turn clockwise, about ninety centimeters from the colon junction. The authors link such primary twists to habits like huge meals after fasting. Their message is vigilance: with a virgin abdomen and vague signs, surgeons should operate on suspicion rather than wait for perfect proof.
pmc-13457024:
Nebojša Prijović and seven colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether a simple blood ratio foretells how bladder cancer patients fare after bladder removal. The ratio divides an inflammation marker by albumin, a nutrition-linked protein. The team reviewed 491 patients who had radical cystectomy between 2017 and 2021, with survival tracked into 2022.

The ratio ran higher in patients whose tumors were not the standard lining type. It also climbed alongside vessel invasion, positive lymph nodes, and advancing tumor stage. In adjusted models, the ratio joined age and tumor features as an independent predictor of survival after surgery. The authors argue that a cheap preoperative blood test can sharpen prognosis talks and follow-up planning. They note the single-cohort design and call for confirmation in other hospitals before the ratio guides real decisions.
pmc-13457524:
Gashaw Arega and colleagues measured how long it takes children with solid cancers in Ethiopia to reach a confirmed diagnosis. Their 2026 prospective study followed 250 newly diagnosed children under fifteen at Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital in Addis Ababa over one year, recording each step from first symptoms to treatment start. Brain and spinal tumors were the most common type, at 24 percent of cases, followed by kidney tumors at 17.2 percent of the group studied.

The median time from symptoms to diagnosis was 99 days, and the median total delay reached 112 days for these children. Parents took a median of 38 days before seeking care, while misdiagnosis and treatment for non-cancer conditions drove referral delays in 63.6 percent of cases beyond two weeks. Parental education, community health insurance, tumor type, and tumor site each significantly affected how quickly diagnosis happened.
pmc-13459024:
Lindsey M Filiatreau and co-authors studied people entering HIV care in Cameroon who reported thoughts of death or self-injury, and what those thoughts meant for their treatment path. Their 2026 paper followed 426 adults who enrolled at three public treatment centers between 2019 and 2020, interviewing them at entry and tracking clinic records for two years. The team measured delayed start of antiretroviral therapy, the standard HIV drug treatment, and later disengagement from care entirely.

Seventy-one participants, 16.7 percent of the cohort, reported self-injurious thoughts at entry, and 24 of them described active thoughts of hurting themselves. Those thoughts were strongly linked with starting treatment late rather than the same day, with an adjusted effect size of 1.8 in the reported analysis. They also pointed toward more dropout from clinic over two years, though that difference was not statistically significant. The authors call for urgent mental health support inside HIV services.
pmc-13459324:
Ramya Ramaswami and co-authors report nine-year cancer outcomes from the landmark START trial, which randomized people with HIV to start antiretroviral therapy immediately or defer it until immune counts fell. The trial enrolled 4,684 adults whose CD4 counts were still above 500, and its 2015 unblinding, showing early treatment cut serious illness, prompted worldwide guideline changes. Their 2026 analysis tracked cancer diagnoses through 2021, splitting results into periods before and after the deferred group was advised to start treatment.

Over a median of nine years, 120 participants developed cancer. Starting treatment immediately halved overall cancer risk across the whole period, with a hazard ratio of 0.50 for the immediate group. The protection concentrated in infection-related cancers and was strongest before 2016, when the contrast between arms was widest, then persisted more weakly afterward. For cancers unrelated to infection, timing of treatment made no significant difference.
pmc-13459424:
Mahdieh Khorashadizadeh and co-authors present a 15 year old Iranian boy with two rare congenital defects appearing together. One is scimitar syndrome, where a lung vein drains to the wrong place. The other is horseshoe lung, where the lungs fuse behind the heart. He arrived after fainting and coughing blood following physical exertion, an unusual presentation for late childhood. In their 2026 case report, imaging also showed partial anomalous pulmonary venous return and an underdeveloped right lung. The team first tried blocking the abnormal vessels through a catheter.

The embolization initially succeeded, but bleeding returned after three weeks, marking the minimally invasive approach as failed in this case. Surgeons then removed the affected lower lobe segment of the right lung. His breathing improved, no further bleeding occurred, and he went home on the seventh day after surgery. At the two month follow up, nothing suggested the problem had returned.
pmc-13460224:
Junyi Chen and colleagues describe in 2026 a fully camera-guided way to redo mitral valve surgery on a beating heart, using high potassium to slow the heart rather than stop it. Repeat valve surgery usually means reopening the breastbone, a hazardous route through scar tissue. Their retrospective review compared 43 patients treated through a small right chest incision with 68 treated by conventional reopening, in cases from 2020 into 2026.

The camera group finished bypass and surgery faster, lost far less blood, and needed much less transfused blood and plasma. Drainage, ventilation time, intensive care stay, hospital stay, and total cost all fell, and pneumonia occurred less often. No deaths, strokes, or reoperations for bleeding occurred in the camera group, supporting the technique as safe in experienced hands.
pmc-13461324:
Liu and co-authors ran a 2026 training study combining blood flow restriction with eccentric exercise, which lengthens muscles under load, in college sprinters. Cuffs on the upper thigh partly restrict blood flow during training to amplify gains. Sixteen male sprinters were split randomly into cuff and non-cuff groups of eight.

Both groups trained eccentrically three times weekly for six weeks, with the cuff group held at a set pressure during sessions. Liu measured hip strength, thirty metre sprint, vertical jump, anaerobic capacity, and leg circumference before and after. Both groups improved across the board, but the cuff group gained more hip extensor strength and jumping power. Cuff training also strengthened the weaker side, reducing imbalance between legs.
pmc-13461624:
Jiahao Dong, Zhongyu Peng, and Tao Chen offer a 2026 reinterpretation of an old idea in Chinese medicine: that the kidney governs the bone. Older readings stressed hormones alone, which cannot explain effects under stress, inflammation, or nerve injury. They recast the idea around a brain-bone axis: brain, hormone, and immune systems as one network. Herbal and hands-on treatments are then read as working at several network levels.

Their model has three tiers, from brain control through body-wide signals to the local bone setting. Kidney-tonifying herbs steady a key hormone control loop. Blood-activating methods and acupuncture link to nerve tone and blood flow near bone. Acupuncture and moxibustion tie to calmer immune activity inside bone. Hard problems remain, including timing differences and lab-to-clinic gaps. They suggest tools such as light-based nerve control and multi-layer gene studies for testing.
pmc-13462224:
Xin Wei, Siqin Hu, and Chen Lin present a 2026 model predicting spots where a chemical tag, crotonylation, lands on proteins. The tag, attached to lysine, helps control cell signaling and metabolism, and appears widely beyond the histones that package DNA. Finding spots in the lab is slow and costly, and few prediction tools exist for non-histone proteins. Their model, DFN-Kcr, reads sequences two ways at once.

One branch uses embeddings from a protein language model, the other reads the raw amino acid code. Filters in one branch catch short local patterns, and an attention design in the other tracks long-range links. A gating step blends both branches. In tests the model beat leading methods on sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and a quality score. The team offers a web server so researchers can run predictions at scale and guide lab checks toward likely tag sites.
pmc-13463924:
Akihisa Matsuda and colleagues report a multicentre retrospective study from Japan, published in 2026, on chemotherapy after stent placement in patients whose bowel cancer blocks the colon and cannot be removed. A self-expanding metal stent can reopen the bowel, but how safely chemotherapy can follow was unclear, so the group tracked 289 patients nationwide.

Chemotherapy began a median of eleven days after stenting. Stent-related complications affected about thirty percent of patients, most often migration of the stent, re-blockage, or perforation of the bowel wall. Median survival was just over seventeen months, and patients who also had the primary tumour removed lived longer, though the authors caution that this comparison is prone to selection bias.
pmc-13464424:
Hiroyuki Kato and five co-authors review care for liver cancer that has invaded the portal vein, the liver's main inflow vessel. Such invasion marks advanced disease with fast spread and poor survival. Drugs remain the default, yet the review asks which patients might still gain from surgery or mixed approaches.

Treatment paths now blend surgery, radiation, vessel-directed therapy, and modern immune drugs in planned sequences. Care before surgery can shrink disease enough to allow a full removal, a route called conversion surgery. Practice differs between Asian and Western centers on how boldly to operate. The authors close with a team-based frame that weighs tumor extent, liver strength, drug response, and patient fitness together.
pmc-13464924:
Farzan and co-authors tested in 2026 how well medical interns at an Iranian university diagnose mouth diseases. Doctors, not dentists, often see oral lesions first, so the skill matters. Sixty-six interns worked through 19 written clinical scenarios built around key diagnostic features. Most scenarios included photographs. The instrument had been validated by expert rounds before use.

Performance fell short. The average score was about seven points on a scale stretching to roughly 14. The best intern reached under 14, and the weakest scored under two. Male interns scored higher than female interns. Stronger students by grade point average scored clearly higher, while age made no difference. Interns recognized distinctive conditions like oral thrush and denture-related inflammation readily. They stumbled on vague presentations such as reflux damage, burning mouth syndrome, and dry mouth. The authors call for case-based, cross-disciplinary teaching inside medical school.
pmc-13465024:
Ceyhan and Gürel built in 2026 a lung cancer sorting net that reads CT scans slice by slice. A map shows which slices drove each call. The pair turned each scan's marks into a wave map, a chart of how the marks rise and fall down the stack. A net with two focus heads read the maps to sort tumor types.

The net matched known nets on truth, catch rate, and blend scores. The slice map did the new work: it ranked slice groups by pull on the call. High pull zones lined up in runs down the stack, not lone spikes, which fits how tumors span slices. The authors pitch the map as an aid for scan doctors.
pmc-13465224:
Wang and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a large series of personalized eye socket operations for thyroid-associated orbitopathy. The autoimmune condition pushes the eyes forward and can crush the optic nerve. The single-surgeon series covered 199 patients and 263 eyes treated between 2021 and 2025. Four strategies were compared. They ranged from fat removal alone to combined inner-and-outer wall bone decompression through the nose.

Every strategy worked. Average eye protrusion fell from about 21 millimeters to about 15 millimeters. Vision scores improved markedly, most dramatically in the nearly half of eyes where the optic nerve was threatened. Combined two-wall operations pulled the eye back furthest, by more than seven millimeters. The endoscopic inner-wall approach carried the lowest complication rate, about four percent against nine percent overall. New or worsened double vision was the commonest problem. It often settled or yielded to later muscle surgery.
pmc-13465424:
Shulin Yu and six co-authors fingerprint Astragali Radix, a prized food-medicine root, by its scent chemistry to tell how it was grown. Wild, near-wild, and farmed roots fetch different prices, yet looks alone cannot sort them. One hundred seventeen roots from the three patterns faced two complementary scent-reading machines.

The two machines caught overlapping but distinct scent sets, with farmed roots showing the richest list on one platform. Pattern models separated the three growth styles, more cleanly on the second platform. Explanation tools nominated ten candidate marker compounds across both machines, from gamma-hexalactone to 1-octen-3-one. The markers trace back to fat, scent, and terpene pathways in the plant, which gives graders a chemical footing beyond appearance.
pmc-13466324:
Chiara Olla, Luigi Stagi, Daniele Chiriu, and Carlo Maria Carbonaro cook a simple plant-derived compound into glowing carbon materials at low temperature, comparing air with vacuum, in a 2026 study. The starting material, phloroglucinol, is rich in oxygen and known to form light-emitting carbons. Samples baked at modest heat for five or ten hours under each condition.

Air-treated batches formed loose, filament-like networks, while vacuum batches packed into rounder clumps with fibrous insides. Vibration spectra showed the tidy starting crystals giving way to disordered carbon with small graphitic patches. Light measurements found several emission centers whose brightness and timing shifted with treatment, and computer modeling helped explain the glow.
pmc-13466524:
Silvana Alfei and colleagues test lab-made variants of three tree bark compounds against a stubborn childhood nerve tumor, in a 2026 study. High-risk neuroblastoma often learns to resist standard drugs, so new chemistry is needed. Seven modified compounds built from betulin, betulinic acid, and ursolic acid were compared with their natural parents and with a standard chemotherapy drug.

Several variants formed tiny bubbles in water and carried strong positive charge, traits that favor entering cells. Most derivatives killed tumor cells better than their natural sources and better than the standard drug, especially in a drug-resistant cell line. One ursolic acid derivative stood out as the most active, weakening survival pathways and stopping colony growth.
pmc-13467024:
Chiara Losi and colleagues watch how a large apple snail rebuilds its immune cell supply after blood-like fluid is drawn off, in a 2026 study. Snails let researchers sample repeatedly, and cell clusters in the snail's kidney act as immune depots. Cell counts in circulation shifted noticeably over the two days after withdrawal.

Kidney depot area shrank for a while, suggesting resident cells mobilized into circulation. Public gene data showed two blood-cell-making genes expressed strongly, and unevenly, in both circulating cells and kidney tissue. Direct staining located their activity. In animals without tidy immune markers, this combined approach sketches how a mollusk balances stored and patrolling defenders.
pmc-13467624:
Laura V. Morales, Sonia Sentellas, and Javier Saurina present a 2026 method for telling commercial dark chocolates apart by their chemistry. Chocolate makeup shifts with cocoa type, fermentation, roasting, and recipe, so reliable chemical fingerprints are hard to find. The team profiled amino acids and biogenic amines in 91 dark chocolates ranging from 56 to 100 percent cocoa, using sensitive mass spectrometry.

Because the instrument runs stretched over days, signals drifted downward by as much as 91 percent. Correction steps based on internal standards and quality-control samples improved precision up to 18-fold. In the cleaned data, 19 amino acids and 8 amines were measured, and the strongest pattern tracked cocoa content. The cleaned profiles also carried information about variety and origin, supporting chemistry-based checks of what chocolate labels claim.
pmc-13467724:
Yuan Tian, Xinmiao Wang, Jinhui Wu, and Jiancheng Qi report a materials study, published in 2026, building an air filter membrane inspired by honeycomb and dragonfly wings. The finest airborne particles, called PM0.3, damage lungs, and ordinary filters force a trade-off between catching them and letting air through, so the team electrospun nanofibres onto a honeycomb-patterned collector.

The resulting membrane caught over ninety-eight percent of the finest test particles while keeping the pressure drop very low, staying about eighty-five percent transparent, and letting air pass freely. The authors point to uses in protective masks, window screens, and air purification where visibility and breathability matter.
pmc-13467824:
Suchshikh and colleagues sequence the full genome of a Staphylococcus aureus strain taken from a cow with severe udder infection in Kazakhstan, in 2026 veterinary genomics research. The six-year-old cow's mastitis had resisted treatment. The team confirmed the isolate by culture, staining, and a species-specific gene test. They then sequenced it with a portable nanopore device and compared its gene profile against typing databases to place it among known lineages.

The assembled genome measured 2,771,674 base pairs with a GC content of 32.83 percent, sequenced at 77-fold average coverage across its length. Typing assigned the strain to sequence type ST151, and a finer comparison matched 1,654 of 1,716 tracked gene loci to its closest known profile. In mouse tests the isolate killed in a dose-dependent way, with a lethal dose near 6.3 million colony-forming units. Suchshikh presents the genome as a reference for tracking mastitis strains in Central Asian dairy herds.
pmc-13467924:
Luca Canovi and ten colleagues published this 2026 systematic review on fast heart rhythms arising above the ventricles in two inherited heart conditions, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and Brugada syndrome. Both are famous for dangerous ventricular rhythms and sudden death, but the upper chambers suffer too. Following PRISMA guidance, the authors searched to December 2025 and kept 30 studies reporting atrial fibrillation, flutter and related upper-chamber rhythms in these patients.

These rhythms proved consistently more common in both conditions than in the general population. Atrial fibrillation dominated, often striking young patients whose atria looked structurally normal. The review ties the rhythms to harm: inappropriate shocks from defibrillators, worsening heart failure, recurrence of ventricular arrhythmias, and a clotting risk that standard risk scores often miss. In cardiomyopathy the rhythms tracked right-ventricle dysfunction and atrial enlargement, while in Brugada syndrome they reflected electrical instability. The authors call for future work to build tailored risk tools.
pmc-13468224:
Zhengnan Zhao and co-authors try in 2026 to sex ginkgo trees from leaf light spectra, and discover the answer changes with the season. Ginkgo is prized for landscaping and medicine, but males and females are hard to tell apart outside flowering and fruiting. The team collected hyperspectral images of leaves from mature trees at flowering, green-leaf, and yellow-leaf stages and trained machine learning classifiers on each.

Single-stage models performed very well, with test accuracies between 95.77 and 97.12 percent depending on the stage. The informative wavelengths, however, migrated from visible light in summer toward near-infrared in autumn, with almost no bands shared across all stages. A single year-round model collapsed to near chance when carried across stages. The result is a caution and a guide: spectral sexing works, but the calendar must be built into the model.
pmc-13468324:
Tao Lyu, Yuchen Cheng, and Woonjung Kim bake an herbal powder into cookies in 2026 to see whether its prized phenolic compounds survive the oven. The powder comes from Cynanchum thesioides, a traditional plant, and was added to a model cookie matrix at zero, one, three, and five percent by weight. After baking, the team measured phenolic totals, antioxidant activity in three standard assays, and physical traits of the cookies.

Antioxidant power climbed steadily with dose. The two radical-scavenging scores rose from 8.04 to 46.33 percent and from 17.02 to 36.43 percent across the dose range, and total polyphenols roughly doubled. The powder also shifted moisture, spread, hardness, color, and acidity of the cookies, while density stayed put. The results show a functional cookie can carry measurably more antioxidants, at the cost of changes bakers would need to manage.
pmc-13468524:
Moțiu and colleagues report a 2026 study profiling Romanian pălincă-based drinks, enriched versions of the protected traditional fruit spirit. Artisan makers add honey, wild fruits such as blackthorn and rosehip, or wood materials to grape and plum distillates. The team measured physical traits, color, antioxidants, and trace elements with a sensitive mass method, and screened elemental safety with standard hazard formulas.

Honey enrichment changed the drinks most: more dissolved solids, conductivity, cloudiness, color depth, and minerals, with lower final alcohol. Statistical pattern tools separated the drinks by ingredient and process, showing recipes leave readable chemical fingerprints. For a protected tradition moving into flavored products, such profiling protects authenticity and consumer safety at once: it can prove what is in the bottle and flag elemental risks before sale.
pmc-13468724:
Aiguang Zhang and colleagues set a harder test in 2026 for forecasting greenhouse air temperature. The model must predict hour after hour without ever peeking at real future readings, because a working greenhouse controller never sees them either. Weather inputs were also forecast and fed back recursively, so errors could compound exactly as they would in deployment. A liquid neural network, a continuous-time model, faced three established rivals under identical data conditions.

Across ten repeated runs, the liquid network posted the lowest one-step error, with mean absolute error of 0.4771 degrees Celsius. The study then analyzed how errors from the generated weather variables propagate through the closed loop. Honest evaluation protocols matter in agricultural control. A model that shines with leaked future data can fail silently in a real greenhouse full of crops. That is the trap this protocol was built to expose.
pmc-13468924:
He and co-authors review a risk for college students: leaning too hard on AI tools for study. Their 2026 review pulls together ten years of work on this habit. The team is clear that AI dependency, as they use the term, is not a formal health diagnosis. It means a pattern where students ask AI first, hand over their thinking, and feel stress when no tool is at hand. Rates vary a lot by place, age, and course.

The review finds that the tests used to gauge this habit vary a lot. Some new scales show promise, but the field lacks one shared yardstick. Causes span weak self-control, high work load, peer norms, and tools built to be hard to leave. The team backs skills that teach students to check AI output, not just take it. It also calls for tests and tasks that keep students thinking for themselves.
pmc-13469424:
Shuyu Ding, Zihan Guo, Hengyu Ji, and Jinting He present a review, published in 2026. It covers three metal-linked forms of cell death. All three are now tied to Alzheimer's disease. Ferroptosis is driven by iron. Cuproptosis is driven by copper. Disulfidptosis is a newer death route. It ties to sugar and sulphur chemistry in stressed cells.

The authors summarise how each process works. They review the evidence placing each in Alzheimer's brain damage. Feedback loops with amyloid and tau proteins are included. These proteins define the disease. The three pathways form connected networks, the authors argue. They share control points. This could offer several new angles for drugs. The goal is slowing neuron loss.
pmc-13470524:
Zhang and co-authors tracked how microbes change as salt lakes dry out and brines grow more salty. Their 2026 study used salt ponds where water loss drives salt levels up step by step. The team took samples along this salt gradient and read the genes of the microbes in each. It also tested which carbon foods the microbes could use. The aim was to see if change comes in a smooth line or in sharp jumps.

As salt rose, the lead group of microbes switched and the range of types grew. Carbon use first fell, then rose again at the high salt end. Potassium, a salt that builds up late, was a key force in this shift. It held back most carbon use but boosted the use of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. The team says these shifts shape how salt lakes store and release carbon.
pmc-13470724:
Zhengtian Shi and co-authors compare in 2026 four ways of growing thin films of palladium diselenide, a layered material prized for light sensing. Vapor deposition routes differed in how selenium was delivered to the growing film. Microscope images checked the film shapes, and element analysis confirmed the palladium to selenium ratio matched the target compound.

Vibrational spectra showed the two signature peaks that identify this material. Films used as light driven electrodes produced current under visible light across the tested range. The current rose in a curved, nonlinear way as light intensity climbed, topping out at the best growth conditions. Output also held steady over time, which matters for devices. The authors present the comparison as guidance for making usable photoelectrode films rather than continuous sheets.
pmc-13471224:
Ysaac Zegeye and colleagues report in 2026 two patients whose skin Crohn disease surfaced during treatment for a different chronic skin condition. Both patients had hidradenitis suppurativa. That is a painful, recurring disease of abscesses and tunnels in skin fold areas. Both were receiving a biologic drug that blocks interleukin 17. Such drugs are a standard escalation for stubborn cases.

During that treatment, lesions appeared. The lesions proved to be cutaneous Crohn disease, an uncommon skin expression of the inflammatory bowel condition. The timing raised the question the case series is built around. Can blocking interleukin 17 unmask Crohn disease that was quietly present? That worry already exists for gut inflammation with this drug class. The authors present the pair of cases so clinicians weigh bowel symptoms and skin changes in patients on this therapy.
pmc-13471624:
Xu and co-authors describe three young infants whose common-cold coronavirus caused necrotizing damage to the windpipe, a rare and dangerous turn. Their 2026 case series from a tertiary pediatric intensive care unit covers infants seen in August and September 2025 with confirmed hCoV-NL63 infection and progressive hoarseness, breathlessness, and stridor.

Flexible bronchoscopy, a camera passed into the airway, showed the same pattern in all three: dead subglottic tissue, ulceration, and narrowing of the airway. The scope also guided urgent breathing-tube placement to secure each airway, and lavage fluid confirmed the virus. Follow-up scopes every 3 to 7 days tracked healing of the necrosis. The authors credit the scope with both the diagnosis and the rescue.
pmc-13473524:
Yan and co-authors found that leucyl-tRNA synthetase, an enzyme that loads the amino acid leucine onto its carrier RNA, surges in cholestatic livers and drives the injury that follows blocked bile flow. Their 2026 mouse study combined liver-specific gene knockdown and overexpression with bile duct surgery and bile-acid-treated liver cells.

Extra LARS made everything worse. The mechanism runs through hunger sensing. Cholestasis drains free leucine, unloaded carrier RNAs pile up and trip the GCN2 stress alarm, and LARS sits at the junction; its absence muted that integrated stress response in treated cells.
pmc-13474724:
Royi Barnea, Aviad Tur-Sinai, and Orna Tal study how senior hospital managers weigh fairness against cost in 2026. Eighty-two managers judged set scenarios where medical need was held equal while social and money traits varied. The study split two ideas: whether a trait feels usable in practice, and whether it feels right in principle. Managers run the middle layer where daily access choices are quietly made.

Most managers rejected open ranking under scarcity and backed equal care even when beds ran short. When ranking did occur, younger patients were favored, mostly on medical grounds. Money traits such as insurance or billing status were rarely backed as open criteria. A clear tension sits between fairness ideals and budget duty.
pmc-13474824:
Heydarikhayat and colleagues present a 2026 qualitative study of preventing medical errors in nursing, based on interviews in southeastern Iran. Twelve participants, nurses, managers, and faculty from three hospitals and a university center, gave in-depth interviews analyzed by a standard phenomenological method. 

One main theme emerged, named by the authors as the unfinished architecture of safe care, with six subthemes beneath it. The image is structural: prevention strategies exist as fragments, training here, reporting there, but they do not join into a building. Staff described reflection on prevention itself as the missing habit. For hospital leaders, the study reframes error prevention from blaming individuals to finishing a system whose parts already exist but were never connected.
pmc-13475124:
Damini and colleagues watch free-ranging ravens at a wildlife park to learn how scavenging birds judge risky new food sources, in 2026 animal behavior research. Ravens forage alongside wild boars there. In one experiment the birds chose between a familiar feeding site and an unfamiliar one; in a second, an unknown object appeared beside one site. The question was whether ravens use other animals, of their own species or different ones, as information about safety.

In both experiments, ravens delayed approaching food until the boars reached it first. At the new site they waited longer, stole more food from fellow ravens, yet visited in larger numbers than at the old site. The strange object deterred them more strongly at the familiar site, suggesting surprise hits harder where expectations are set. Damini concludes ravens flexibly read both companions and competitors before committing to a risky meal.
pmc-13475524:
Rose and colleagues studied in 2026 anti-mattering, the feeling of being insignificant and invisible to others, among students in the COVID-19 lockdown period. They surveyed 282 students early in the pandemic. Measures covered anti-mattering, loneliness, pandemic anxiety and worry, and social self-compassion and hopelessness.

Anti-mattering came with lower social self-compassion and hope, and higher hopelessness, both general and social. Anti-mattering, social hopelessness, and reduced hope together predicted loneliness. The authors describe a double risk: young people who feel lonely and insignificant at once struggle to picture a better tomorrow. Feeling unheard also seemed to harden people against kindness toward themselves. The authors discuss clinical and community lessons for easing isolation. The work links this newer construct into current loneliness research.
pmc-13476624:
Pauline M Berens and co-authors measure hip-to-groin vein length in 2026 from body scans using automated tools. Vein path length guides stent choice in blocked hip veins, yet population norms were scarce. A learning pipeline cut out vessels and traced center lines in scans. After quality checks, both-side vein paths were ready for 711 adults.

Left vein paths ran longer than right ones by about fifteen millimeters on average. Artery paths were measured beside veins for contrast. Age, height, and sex each shifted length in the pooled model. Norms like these help size devices before the procedure starts.
pmc-13477024:
Wang and Sánchez-Rivera wrote in 2026 on a fix for a weak link in prime editing, a gene tool that rewrites small code spots. The editor rig is big, and the usual ferry, a tame virus, loads it poorly and fades. The pair present work by Langley, Baudrier, and co-workers on a new ferry: shell balls that carry the rig ready built.

Four small doses, spaced three days apart, did the work. Edits landed at up to near three times the old rate, across many code spots and cell types. Nine in ten edits were in place by day three. The pair argue that dose timing, not the editor, capped past screens.
pmc-13477124:
Xiaofeng Wang and co-authors survey in 2026 how heart intervention doctors and surgeons in China view congenital heart care. Invitations went to senior specialists at 118 hospitals, and 162 valid replies came back: ninety surgeons and seventy-two intervention doctors. Both groups backed combined, stepwise care and long-term team follow-up alike. Demographic traits did not differ between groups.

Choices split where trades meet: each side favored its own method for five shared defects. Decision focus also split, with surgeons stressing age and growth room and intervention doctors stressing body state and complications. Shared teams must bridge those lenses case by case. The survey gives managers a map of where talks stall.
pmc-13478024:
Shihshuan Fang and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review comparing clotting risk between two ways of giving immunoglobulin therapy. Intravenous treatment creates high peak antibody levels and is tied to vein clots, lung clots, stroke, and heart attack. Under-skin treatment produces lower peaks, which may lower that risk. The team searched six databases through December 2024.

Thirty-four studies covering roughly 12,800 patient-years met the review rules. Clotting events occurred at a pooled rate of about 1.8 per 100 patient-years with intravenous therapy. The under-skin rate was about 0.14 per 100 patient-years, with only three events, each in a patient who already had clotting risk factors. No study directly randomized patients between the two routes, which limits firm conclusions about the size of the difference.
pmc-13478224:
Yang and colleagues studied eye surgery outcomes in Marfan syndrome in 2026, a genetic condition that weakens connective tissue and often slips the eye's lens out of place. Surgeons replace the lens and add a capsular tension ring, a tiny spring-like loop that steadies the implant. The team measured the angle between the ring's force line and the implant's long axis in 15 patients covering 25 eyes treated in Wuhan between 2020 and 2024.

Patients were 68 percent male, and the measured angle proved to be a significant driver of leftover astigmatism, the blur caused by uneven focusing power. When the angle fell below 50 degrees, residual astigmatism rose in a direct relationship with how small the angle got in the eyes analyzed. At 50 degrees or more that relationship vanished, suggesting a practical threshold surgeons can aim for when seating the ring and lens.
pmc-13481324:
Takeshita and colleagues reported in 2026 a minimally invasive fix for a rare kidney blood-vessel malformation in a man in his forties. A renal arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal direct link between an artery and a vein. His lesion had one feeding artery, one draining vein, and a ballooned vein segment with a narrowed outflow, a type I layout. The goal was to seal the shunt while sparing healthy kidney tissue.

Through catheters, the team blocked flow with a balloon and injected warmed, diluted medical glue using a triple-layer catheter system. Coils were then placed to reinforce the block. The shunt disappeared completely, with no kidney dysfunction or complications. The authors suggest this balloon-occluded glue technique is a useful option for selected fistulas of this shape.
pmc-13481424:
Darja Popkova and co-authors offer a 2026 scoping review of why valproic acid, a mainstay drug for seizures and mood care, so often adds weight. The team searched four databases and mapped fifteen studies with 1,339 adults in total. Study types ranged from snapshots and follow-ups to gene studies, and quality checks used a standard scale.

Proof clustered into three lanes. Hormone shifts led, covering raised insulin, raised leptin, and insulin resistance. Fat measures shifted too, with higher total cholesterol and triglycerides plus mixed readings for protective cholesterol. Gene lanes stayed young, pointing to a drug-processing gene variant and a methylation mark, yet small groups demand larger checks. Bipolar patients were scarce in the pool. The map argues for personal watch plans that track weight, hormones, and lipids from the start.
pmc-13482324:
Song and colleagues build an explainable risk model in 2026 for a dangerous turn in intensive care, pneumonia patients who go on to develop bloodstream infections after admission. They trained the model on the MIMIC-IV critical care database and tested it externally on patients from Dazhou Central Hospital in China. Six predictors survived the selection process, mixing illness severity scores with sputum culture results and how long the patient had already spent in intensive care.

The best algorithm scored 0.753 on the discrimination curve in internal testing, respectable but far from perfect for spotting who will develop the infection. On the external hospital's patients it slipped to 0.703 on the same measure, and charts of feature importance showed stay length and culture results driving most predictions. A version restricted to admission-day data fell to 0.632 externally, which the authors read as a warning that early warning, before cultures return, remains genuinely hard.
pmc-13483624:
Ontas, Güçlü, and Aydın Son built in 2026 a cheap web system, named SALGINTR, that lets doctors in Türkiye report their own flu like illness each week. Such crowd reporting can back up the classic sentinel network of clinics. Their tools were free cloud forms and sheets, with a total build cost near one hundred dollars. Doctors joined through peer invites and filed weekly symptom forms through the flu season's first three months.

Of 243 doctors who signed up, 197 gave data fit for study, near fifteen hundred person weeks in all. About half of them caught a flu like illness in the span. Weekly rates from the new system rose and fell in step with the national sentinel figures, and matched them most tightly before the peak weeks. Alarm tools in both systems fired in fair accord, and neither led the other in time.
pmc-13483724:
Pin-Jui Kung and co-authors map tiny protective RNAs in developing human germ cells and find a surprising address pattern. Their 2026 study collects fetal testes from weeks 12 to 22 of gestation in Taiwan and compares profiles with United States material. These piRNAs normally guard the genome against jumping genetic elements while the germline resets its marks.

Many of the human fetal piRNAs matched enhancers, the DNA switches that boost gene activity, including both super-enhancers and ordinary enhancers. The same enhancer link appeared in mice and chickens, marking it as deeply conserved across warm-blooded vertebrates. Notably, many switches involved normally serve body tissues rather than germ cells. The authors propose that piRNAs police those switches, dampening body-program genes at the wrong moment to protect germ cell identity.
pmc-13483824:
Stephina Adjoa Yanney measures how strongly malaria mosquitoes in Ghana now resist the insecticides used to control them. Published in 2026, the study raises mosquitoes from larvae collected at eight sites across coastal and northern savannah zones. Standard intensity tests, species identification, and resistance gene checks are paired with a household survey on home and farm pesticide use.

Coastal mosquitoes showed high-intensity resistance to pyrethroid sprays, surviving even tenfold test doses at notable rates, while northern samples showed only moderate resistance. One organophosphate also met high resistance at two coastal sites. A key nerve-channel mutation sat near fixation at every site sampled. pmc-13486424:
Gregorich and colleagues reviewed how protein-level studies are rewriting the story of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a disease where heart muscle thickens dangerously. The condition was long blamed on single gene defects in the sarcomere, the heart cell's contracting engine. Yet only about one third of patients carry a known defect, and severity varies wildly among those who do. Their 2026 mini-review gathers recent work using mass spectrometry, which weighs proteins to identify and count them.

The protein surveys show broad remodeling far beyond the sarcomere, touching energy factories, the cell's skeleton, calcium stores, and the nucleus. Different genetic causes seem to converge on similar protein-level end states inside the heart muscle. That convergence hints at shared drug targets downstream of the varied genes. Gregorich argues protein profiling can reveal disease modifiers that gene tests alone will never show.
pmc-13486824:
Yang and co-authors tackled resource waste in blockchain-secured federated learning, where phones and sensors train shared models without sending raw data. Adding blockchain removes the single central server that could fail or cheat, but consensus and training compete for scarce wireless resources. Their 2026 framework splits work among client devices, a consensus step, and edge servers, and picks which clients join each round while allocating computing power and bandwidth jointly.

Simulations showed the scheme improved final model accuracy while cutting delay compared with the baselines examined. Screening out low-quality clients protected training from devices with poor data or weak connections. The joint allocation beat schemes that set client choice and resources separately in the scenarios tested. Yang presents the approach as practical groundwork for trustworthy learning on crowded wireless edge networks.
pmc-13487324:
Notaristefano and a French led team ran in 2026 a pilot test of a new heart catheter for persistent atrial fibrillation, a lasting faulty heart rhythm. The tool can switch between two burn types: heat based radiofrequency and pulsed field, a newer electric pulse method. Forty patients got vein isolation plus burn lines across the heart's upper chamber. Half had heat alone, and half had the switchable tool.

First try success for the full burn set came far more often in the mixed group than in the heat only group. By the end of each case, though, block rates were close in both arms, and total time in the lab was much the same. One patient in the pulse group had a brief spasm of a heart artery. The team notes the pulse mode shone on the back wall, but shared heat's limits at one tough line.
pmc-13487924:
Andrea J. Chow leads a large Canadian team describing family care for children with inherited metabolic diseases in a 2026 survey. These rare conditions often need strict diets, medicines, and close daily management at home. Seventy-one caregivers of children aged twelve or younger answered an online questionnaire about supports used, time spent, missed work, and quality of life for child and caregiver.

Dietary supports were the most common help reported. Many families gave several extra hours each week to care tasks, and many caregivers missed work days in the past year. Every respondent reported some fulfillment, yet most also reported mental strain. Children with progressive, multisystem disease fared worst, and the authors call relief for families a policy priority.
pmc-13488224:
Xiuli Zhang and co-authors review a shortened chemotherapy schedule for malignant ovarian germ cell tumors in a 2026 single-center study covering 2004 to 2024. These rare tumors strike mostly teenagers and young women and respond very well to the three-drug BEP combination. The modified plan packs the drugs into three days instead of five, repeated every four weeks, aiming to cut side effects and hospital time. After a median follow-up beyond nine years, five-year freedom from progression reached about ninety-eight percent in the reported figures, with no treatment-related deaths. Lung irritation from one drug affected a few patients and settled with supportive care. Most patients kept fertility, and nine in ten of those trying conceived.
pmc-13490024:
Mubarek Tuna and colleagues measure satisfaction with psychiatric outpatient care in public hospitals of Ethiopia's Harari Region in a 2026 multicenter survey. The team interviewed 422 outpatients chosen by systematic random sampling with a structured questionnaire and standard tools. Satisfaction matters in mental health care because it tracks with staying in treatment and using services again, yet eastern Ethiopian data were scarce before this work.

Just over half of participants said they were satisfied with the care received. Satisfaction ran higher among patients with major depression, strong social support, reliable access to prescribed medicines, and insurance payment in adjusted models. Waits under thirty minutes also linked with higher satisfaction. The authors urge steadier drug supply and shorter waits.
pmc-13490424:
Jillian L. King and colleagues challenge a standard mouse test for psychedelic activity in a 2026 pharmacology study. The head-twitch response, a rapid head shake in mice, is widely used to flag hallucinogenic potential through a serotonin receptor. LSD caused strong head twitches with little effect elsewhere. Blocking the serotonin receptor changed neither drug's wider profile. The authors argue the twitch test alone cannot judge psychoactivity.
pmc-13490524:
Sanjana Dutt and colleagues link satellite images to forest ecology in Poland's Tuchola Forest in a 2026 study. The reserve was divided into structural zones using a foreground density measure that captures how fragmented the canopy is. Sentinel-2 satellite images from 2016, 2020, and 2024 supplied seventeen vegetation indices. Cluster checks showed heavy overlap, so the indices were pruned to a distinct few. They were then fed to interpretable tree-based learning models alongside field records.

Prediction errors stayed under one degradation class, with stand age the loosest target in the reported test results. One red-edge index predicted most consistently across outcomes, while rare zones showed stronger stress signals and wobblier moisture patterns than stable core zones. The authors offer the recipe for open-data monitoring of fragmented forests.
pmc-13491724:
Jiaye Du and four colleagues grade in 2026 the quality of snakebite first-aid videos circulating on TikTok and Bilibili, two major Chinese short-video platforms. Most videos explained causes, symptoms, and treatment, while prevention and basic disease patterns were rarely covered. Overall quality landed in the middle range, with trustworthiness scores lower still. Videos from health professionals and nonprofit groups scored clearly higher than those from individual users. Popularity signals such as likes and shares barely tracked quality, so the authors urge platforms to surface professional content more prominently.
pmc-13491824:
Kohei Ikeda and Tsunehisa Tsubokawa evaluate in 2026 an on-screen alert meant to stop blood pressure checks from lapsing during surgery. Adjusted models confirmed lower odds of long gaps, slightly shorter worst intervals, and fewer large pressure swings across the longest gap. The authors conclude that a simple vendor-built reminder measurably tightened monitoring discipline.
pmc-13493824:
Osuna-Mascaró and co-authors asked whether Goffin's cockatoos can learn that something is permanently broken, not just temporarily unrewarding. The cockatoos learned to skip the dead icons and treated them as a lasting category rather than re-testing them hopefully. They adjusted after a single negative event with each one. Performance improved markedly across sessions at group level, though individuals varied a lot, which the authors link to differences such as age and personality. They call the patterns preliminary, since the sample was small, and propose larger studies.
pmc-13493924:
Debkumar Chakraborty leads a seven-author team studying in 2026 how to ferment mixed kitchen waste into hydrogen and useful acids without chemical crutches. pmc-13494624:

The authors read the snowstorm pattern as a sign that pockets of sperm production survive, worth flagging in counselling.
pmc-13495224:

Stress also ran higher in clinical-stage students, women, smokers, and those living away from family or not exercising. The authors note stress management may deserve a place in dental training, while the one-time survey cannot prove which came first.
pmc-13495324:

pmc-13495524:

pmc-13495624:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a leg wound infected with Wohlfahrtiimonas chitiniclastica, an emerging bacterium carried by flies that can pass to humans. Lab pathogen detection confirmed the culprit, which matters because rare germs are easily missed by routine assumptions. The authors warn the bacterium can cause severe local and body-wide infection in diabetic patients. pmc-13498524:

More patients on the combined plan reached sugar regression during treatment, yet remission rates after stopping drugs were similar in both groups, at roughly two in five patients. The authors conclude the combined plan was not superior, and any true advantage would be modest at most.
pmc-13498724:

The team linked the condition to long-standing care problems, chiefly a badly unbalanced diet and too little sunlight in captivity. The case shows how scans ordered for one problem can expose hidden nutrition and housing failures in zoo animals.
pmc-13500824:

The authors propose the extract as an add-on that could let clinicians use lower steroid doses for inflammatory pain.
pmc-13501724:

The two experts agreed almost perfectly, with kappa values from 0 point 84 to 0 point 94 across regions. ChatGPT matched the trunk at a kappa of 0 point 85 and the knee at 0 point 83 in the reported statistics, and it reached substantial agreement on head and neck position. Agreement sagged to moderate for the scapula, shoulder girdle, pelvis, and feet, where angular judgement matters. Percentage agreement ran from about 64 to about 92 percent. The authors see a support tool, not a replacement.
pmc-13501824:

Children were grouped by age: three to six, seven to ten, and eleven to fourteen years.

The links changed with age. In the youngest group, mouth breathing scores rose alongside steeper jaw angles and taller faces, and every symptom tracked with front height. In the middle group, longer symptoms tied to jaw and tooth angles in mixed directions. In the oldest group, only an apnoea-to-lower-tooth link stood out. The authors identify ages three to ten as the sensitive window and urge age-tailored assessment.
pmc-13502924:

Enrolled between May 2021 and October 2022, they had sheath measurements and Glasgow Coma Scale scores recorded at diagnosis, 24 and 72 hours, day five, and any deterioration.

Twelve patients, 15 percent, died within 28 days. The authors label the signal exploratory.
pmc-13503824:

The authors say the design suits live plant use where loads and speeds shift.
pmc-13504824:

Parents stressed barriers: drug side effects, late diagnosis, and the grind of keeping to schedules. They also praised better focus and trust in their providers. Teens weighed gains like sharper concentration against harms like stigma and tiredness. Both sides valued combined care, though teens prized independence while parents prized system support. The authors call for care shaped to each family and culture.
pmc-13505024:
