Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines led regional output, but the region still supplies under 2.5 percent of world papers on the topic. Only a fifth of papers reported funding. Topics clustered on diagnosis, surgery, registries, and blood-thinning care. Themes like social drivers, cost value, and patient-centered care were thin. Output tracked with country wealth measures and foreign co-authorship, which the authors say deserves investment.
pmc-13505124:
Samet Can Demirci and co-authors studied 226 young inpatients treated for substance use disorders, asking whether remembered childhood ADHD symptoms relate to how severe their addiction had become. They also tested whether time perspective, meaning how people view past, present, and future, helps explain that link. Participants were aged eighteen to twenty-five.

The team measured childhood and adult ADHD symptoms, five time-perspective scales, distress, and addiction severity with standard questionnaires. Patients whose main problem was stimulants scored higher on childhood ADHD measures and on addiction severity than the cannabis or pregabalin groups. In their models, four time-perspective scales carried part of the link, and the model explained a large share of severity differences. Because all measures came from one point in time, the authors caution against reading the pattern as cause and effect.
pmc-13505324:
Floriane Etheve and colleagues describe a 56-year-old woman with widespread melanoma who developed a rare immune side effect one week after her first combined immunotherapy cycle. She arrived with fever, an itchy rash, and loss of vision in both eyes. Eye examination showed fluid lifting the retina in both eyes, matching a Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada-like syndrome, where the immune system attacks pigment-bearing cells.

Spinal fluid testing confirmed inflammation around the brain, and a skin sample showed the rash pattern with fewer pigment cells than normal. Doctors stopped the immunotherapy and gave high-dose steroids followed by methotrexate, and she improved quickly. Over two and a half years later her scans still show cancer remission with no further immunotherapy. The authors use the case to stress fast, joint care across specialties to protect sight, and they note such pigment-directed reactions may mark a strong anti-cancer response.
pmc-13507024:
Jung-Eun Kim, Byoung-Cheol Lee, and Byung-Chang Suh study, in 2026 cell work, how a membrane protein called TMEM16E helps cells survive in acid conditions. The protein shuffles membrane fats and also acts as an ion channel. The team tracked a cell drinking process, macropinocytosis, where cells gulp fluid and membrane in large bubbles.

At a strongly acid level, uptake tied to the marker annexin V rose, while total bubble counts stayed flat across acid levels. Sudden acid exposure quickly shut down protein activity, and calcium inside cells cleared faster. Cells with the protein grew and survived better under acid stress. The pathway may protect membrane health in tumors and muscle disease.
pmc-13508124:
Gil and co-authors reported a 2026 food allergy study on making cow's milk proteins less allergenic by binding them to plant polyphenols. Casein, the main milk protein, triggers IgE antibodies in allergic patients and can cause life threatening reactions. Changing casein's shape could hide the spots those antibodies grab.

Gil tested the bonded formula against blood serum from patients allergic to cow's milk proteins in preclinical assays. IgE binding fell significantly, though the size of the drop varied between patients. Computer modelling showed polyphenols sitting on antibody binding spots across three casein types, with fewer such spots on the fourth type. A related milk protein also responded well, and the authors argue the approach could support personalised oral immunotherapy.
pmc-13508224:
Michael Gonzalez leads a ten-author team hunting the gene locus that sets potassium levels inside sheep red blood cells, in 2026 work. Some sheep carry low potassium cells and others high, and the trait passes down as if controlled by one locus. Genome scans across sheep pointed to a large repeated stretch of a gene family called MYADM. The repeat appears in sheep, goats, cattle, and pigs, but not in horses.

Closer mapping in more sheep tied the trait most strongly to a handful of genes within that repeat. Protein models suggest one family member can grip a potassium transporter and hold its control section in the off position. That offers a route by which the repeat could set cell potassium. The same gene has been linked to human blood pressure, which widens the interest in this sheep finding.
pmc-13508324:
Tsung-Yang Lee and six co-authors hunt factors that predict long hospital stays and sickness after weight-loss surgery, in 2026 work. The study reviewed 476 patients who had one of two operations, a gastric band or a gastric bypass, between 2022 and 2023. A stay over three days counted as prolonged. Statistical models weighed patient traits and care details together to find independent predictors.

Just under a quarter of patients stayed beyond three days, and the typical stay was exactly three days. Longer anesthesia time was the strongest predictor of a long stay. Higher fluid rates during surgery, asthma, and post-surgery sickness each added independent risk. The type of operation itself did not predict stay length once other factors counted. Sickness struck nearly half of patients, more often women and younger patients. The authors advise tightening anesthesia time, fluids, and sickness control to speed discharge.
pmc-13514924:
Aliki Karkala leads a ten-author team investigating morning headaches in obstructive sleep apnoea, in a 2026 retrospective study of 3,227 adults treated at a sleep clinic between 2013 and 2023. Waking headaches are a recognised apnoea symptom. The researchers split patients by headache frequency, comparing those with at least one episode weekly against the rest.

About thirty-five percent reported frequent morning headaches. Simple comparisons tied them to female sex, larger waist size, worse oxygen dips, sleepiness, and insomnia complaints. A tighter analysis of patients with complete sleep-study data reshaped the picture. Being female, waist size, and the rate of brief brain arousals during sleep predicted frequent headaches, while standard breathing-severity measures did not. Karkala's team argues that fragmented sleep, more than apnoea severity itself, drives these headaches, especially in women.
pmc-13515824:
Madalina-Ianca Suba leads a nine-author team asking whether past COVID-19 leaves a lasting inflammatory mark in people living with HIV, in a 2026 retrospective study. Modern therapy holds HIV undetectable, yet low-grade inflammation often persists and drives later illness. The team reviewed 286 adults on treatment at one centre from 2023 to 2025. They compared those with and without a documented past SARS-CoV-2 infection, and repeated the check in the 231 patients whose virus stayed fully suppressed.

Patients with past COVID-19 carried clearly higher levels of several inflammation markers, from C-reactive protein to interleukin-6 and cell-ratio scores. Among the suppressed group, high inflammation also tracked lower CD4 counts, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and fatty liver. Past infection stayed an independent predictor after adjustment. Suba's team stresses that a records study shows association, not cause. They point to long-term host and metabolic factors as the deeper drivers worth prospective study.
pmc-13516324:
Li and colleagues report a 2026 study of nanoparticles that both burn tumors with light and block their spread, tested in bowel cancer models.  The team linked a light-sensitive dye to a peptide that blocks uPA, an enzyme cancers use to invade tissue, and the linked molecules assembled themselves into nanoparticles.

The particles gathered in tumors, produced reactive oxygen under light, and kept the enzyme-blocking action of the peptide, which normally clears from the body too fast to help. In mice, they shrank implanted tumors and curbed lung spread, the pattern this cancer follows when it travels.  Packaging a short-lived peptide with a light drug makes the pair attack growth and spread together.
pmc-13517224:
Noszczyk-Nowak and colleagues published a 2026 report on heart rhythm ablation in dogs in Poland. Fast, stubborn heart rhythms can weaken a dog's heart muscle over time. Catheter ablation burns the tiny faulty spot through a vessel, sparing open surgery. The procedure remains rare in veterinary care, offered at few centers.

The center performed fourteen ablations across dogs of many breeds and sizes. Half the dogs arrived with heart muscle weakened by the fast rhythm. Three dogs needed a second procedure to finish the job fully. No major or lasting complications followed any of the cases treated. Newer three-dimensional mapping systems joined the toolkit over the years covered. The cases span both upper and lower heart chamber rhythm faults.
pmc-13517424:
Kate S Rawlings, Olga Kim, and Anne Huvos argue in a 2026 article that one flu treaty already solves the vaccine-equity problem COVID-19 exposed. Rich countries bought early and deep while poorer nations waited months, and the delay prolonged spread and bred variants. The Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework works differently: binding advance deals hand the World Health Organization a real-time slice of world flu vaccine output.

Allocation then follows public-health risk and need, not wealth. The authors say this design attacks both axes of unfairness at once, who gets doses and when. No country queues behind richer buyers, so vaccine reaches the hotspots where it cuts transmission fastest. Equity and efficiency, usually traded off, here point the same way. Rawlings and colleagues offer the framework as a working model for future pandemic deals beyond influenza, having operated quietly since long before COVID-19.
pmc-13517524:
Roa Al-Osaimi leads a ten-author study of drug resistance in newly diagnosed HIV patients in Saudi Arabia in a 2026 paper. Resistance passed on at infection can blunt first-line therapy, so baseline gene testing guides drug choice. Three hospitals contributed six hundred fourteen untreated patients diagnosed in 2023 and 2024, whose viral genes for three drug targets were sequenced and checked against a standard database.

The patients were mostly men aged twenty-five to forty-four, and most arrived with high virus levels. The virus itself was strikingly diverse, led by subtype C and two recombinant and G forms. Raw mutation counts looked alarming, above eighty percent in some genes, yet nearly all were harmless subtype quirks. Mutations that truly matter sat near three percent overall, and none touched the newest drug class. Al-Osaimi's team backs continued baseline testing to catch any rise early.
pmc-13518924:
Mingfu Tian and a large team explain in 2026 why interferon drugs, stars in lab antiviral tests, fall short once a real infection is underway. Given before infection, interferons protected well. Given later, they failed to help while causing harsh side effects, and the team's sleuthing points at lactic acid made by the host itself.

Lactic acid blunted interferon signaling through a SIRT1 route, helped viruses evade, and teamed with interferon to overactivate the NF-kB inflammation switch, feeding cytokine storms. Pairing interferon with a licensed lactate-blocking drug undid the suppression and calmed inflammation, working even in late-stage infection. Tian's team frames lactic acid as a broad-spectrum antiviral target.
pmc-13519024:
Yongqiang Zhang and four colleagues rank five coastal marine pollution monitoring systems in 2026 using expert judgment and robust decision methods. Choosing among underwater sensor networks, cabled observatories, mobile platforms, and satellites means weighing detection power, coverage, cost, sturdiness, and energy limits at once. A panel of 120 experts supplied judgments, with 110 responses passing consistency checks.

Detection capability earned the highest weight at 0.29, followed by coverage at 0.24. The underwater sensor network ranked first with a closeness score of 0.56, ahead of the cabled observatory and mobile platforms. Shifting weights by 20 percent barely moved the order, and score-jitter simulations stayed tight, supporting a stable verdict.
pmc-13520224:
Cevher İlhan Cevheri leads a ten-author field trial in 2026 pitting organic against chemical fertilizers on cotton under semi-arid conditions at Harran University. Cotton supports the textile industry worldwide, and growers lean on both fertilizer families. Plots drawn by lot got differing doses, and leaves were checked for pigments, protein, carbohydrates, and antioxidant defenses.

The top chemical dose, 300 kilograms of DAP per hectare, gave the highest chlorophyll and protein values. Heavy farmyard manure, at 100 tonnes per hectare, led instead on carbohydrates and antioxidants. Signs of membrane damage stayed fairly stable across treatments. Cevheri's team advises blending organic amendments with targeted mineral fertilizer for healthier plants and steadier yield.
pmc-13520424:
Ayşe Sena Şişman and colleagues chart in 2026 yeast bloodstream infections in intensive care by their likely source, a view missing from earlier literature. Breakthrough infections that appear despite antifungal treatment received special attention.

The study included 141 adults whose blood grew Candida more than two days after intensive care admission. Abdominal sources and primary infections each made up roughly four in ten cases, while line-related cases made up about one quarter. Feeding and steroid patterns differed by source, whereas death rates at two and four weeks did not. Breakthrough cases clustered in the abdominal group and arrived with higher severity scores.
pmc-13521024:
Monika Lamba Saini and colleagues compare in 2026 digital slide file formats from two scanner brands for cancer tissue images, asking whether format conversion alone changes image analysis results. Hospitals mix scanner brands, so hidden format effects could undermine automated readings.

Ten colon cancer and ten lung cancer slides were scanned on both systems at the stated magnification. Converted files stayed highly similar to their native versions in pixels, colour and algorithm predictions. Native files from the rival scanner differed widely in size and colour, reflecting hardware plus format together. Small numbers make findings exploratory, while the authors anticipate a shared enterprise standard for pathology images.
pmc-13521924:
Yuki Ashino and Noriyuki Kida follow in 2026 the careers of 179 Japanese college decathletes from 2000 to 2024. Each athlete held scores for at least three school years. The study tests a trade-off rule. Gains in some skills may cost gains in others over time.

Path groups split athletes into high, upper-middle, lower-middle and low total score bands. Speed, jump and throw scores rose with total points in gaining groups. Running stamina showed little tie with total growth. A repeat check on cleaner data matched that pattern. Coaches may gain more from speed and power work when total score is the goal.
pmc-13522024:
Hung Chang and colleagues test in 2026 a blood protein as a risk flag for lymphoma patients with low standard scores. The protein is beta2-microglobulin. The rival flags are tumour bulk and a liver enzyme. Cohort data came from one hospital for diagnoses in 2015 to 2019.

The full cohort held 523 patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. A total of 238 patients sat in the low score band. Full data allowed class calls for 234 of them. Median age was 64 years. High risk meant tumours over the size cut-off or enzyme over its limit. Survival splits then judge which flag finds true poor outlook in a low-risk group.
pmc-13522424:
Biruk Shalmeno Tusa, Rosa Alati, Getinet Ayano, and Berihun Dachew investigate depression in mothers around pregnancy and birth in a 2026 study. They ask whether it relates to how the children later perform at school. Linked health and education records from New South Wales supplied the data. National literacy and numeracy results in grades three, five, and seven were checked against minimum standards.

Children whose mothers had a perinatal depressive disorder were more likely to fall below the standard in reading, spelling, writing, and grammar, though no clear link appeared for numeracy. Patterns were strongest for depression during pregnancy, while depression after birth related mainly to reading and writing. The authors argue for earlier identification and treatment during pregnancy to support later learning.
pmc-13522524:
Sinan Wang and co-authors build a drought prediction system for the Ordos region of Inner Mongolia in a 2026 study. Ordos is an important mining and economic area that suffers frequent drought. A regional comprehensive drought index was first constructed for 2001 to 2020 from temperature, rainfall, vegetation, soil moisture, land use, and elevation, using an established drought measure as the reference.

Three deep learning models were then trained to forecast the new index, using data through 2016 for training and later years for testing. A hybrid model combining convolutional and memory networks performed best, with clearly lower errors than either model alone. The index matched known drought conditions and tracked standard measures closely. The work offers a technical reference for drought monitoring in the region.
pmc-13522624:
Joyonta Kumar Nath and colleagues compare deep learning models for reading sign language alphabets from images in a 2026 study. Recognizing single-letter hand signs is a basic step toward accessible communication tools for people with hearing or speech impairment. Four pretrained image networks were tested under one protocol on a benchmark American Sign Language alphabet dataset.

The largest modern network reached the highest accuracy, just under ninety-nine point nine percent, with the other three close behind. Transfer learning, meaning reuse of networks pretrained on general images, proved effective at capturing fine hand shape differences. The comparison offers practical guidance for choosing models when building reliable, scalable sign language interpretation systems for real-world use.
pmc-13523224:
Li-bing Liang and co-authors pool trial evidence on exercise for type 2 diabetes in a 2026 systematic review with network and dose-response analyses. One hundred twenty-seven randomized trials with nearly nine thousand people compared eight exercise types for their effect on glycated hemoglobin, a long-term blood sugar marker. Blood factors released during exercise, called exerkines, were studied as well.

A combined mind-body and resistance program ranked highest for lowering the marker, followed closely by high-intensity interval training. Benefit rose steeply up to a moderate weekly dose and then plateaued, with most gain reached well before the plateau. Exercise types showed distinct exerkine patterns, with interval training raising one protective factor and resistance work tending to lower inflammatory factors. The authors advise aiming for the effective dose rather than ever more exercise.
pmc-13523324:
Martha M Lyke leads a team tracking how colony management changed the genetics of captive rhesus macaques in a 2026 study. Macaques are central to biomedical research, and mixing between Indian and Chinese origins can affect study suitability. Whole exome sequencing covered four hundred eighty-eight founding and colony-born animals at a large United States primate center, alongside targeted sequencing of immune genes in more than a thousand animals.

Founder analysis found one Chinese-origin animal and several dozen admixed animals, with structure reflecting their source centers. Chinese ancestry in the colony fell over time, while overall diversity stayed high. Immune gene management reduced a virus-protective variant that can distort research, without sacrificing immune diversity. Genome scans also found many regions where allele frequencies shifted, suggesting short-term adaptation under captive conditions.
pmc-13523424:
Faris Alotaibi and co-authors examine how frailty interacts with patient traits to shape hospital safety incidents in older adults in a 2026 study. More than one hundred fifty-eight thousand acute admissions with a recorded frailty score were analyzed. Safety incidents were defined as staff-reported events with potential to cause harm, and frailty was scored at the emergency department with a standard clinical scale.

Risk of at least one incident rose with frailty. Statistical interactions appeared between frailty and age, emergency waiting time, and length of stay. In the final multivariable model, only the interaction with length of stay improved the fit. The authors conclude that frailty assessment can help flag patients at higher risk of reported incidents, while stressing that the length-of-stay interaction does not prove causation.
pmc-13523524:
Omer Boshra Mohamedsalih Shmed and Waleed Abdelateif Hussein present a 2026 pilot case-control study in Sudan on immune gene variants in patients with end-stage kidney disease and hepatitis B infection. People on maintenance dialysis face higher risk of lasting hepatitis B infection. Variants in two cytokine genes, one promoting and one restraining inflammation, might influence that course.

The study compared 31 patients with both kidney failure and hepatitis B against 37 with hepatitis B alone. Genotyping used a primer-based PCR method, and blood cytokine levels were measured by ELISA. Genotype frequencies for both genes did not differ significantly between groups, nor did levels of the first cytokine. Levels of the second, IL-10, were higher in the kidney group, and within that group one genotype carried higher levels. Small size limits firm conclusions.
pmc-13524424:
Francesco Cecere and others present, in a 2026 methods paper, scGraphVerse, a software workflow for mapping gene networks in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Such data are sparse, wide, and noisy, making network reconstruction hard. Tools rarely combine several data sets or support thorough follow-up.

The R package joins five algorithms with shared inputs and outputs, plus tools for group detection, pathway enrichment, and mining of past papers. It supports early, late, and joint ways for merging data sets. Benchmarks on test data showed model-based methods doing well with small samples, while a joint forest method did best as networks and data sets grew. A blood cell case study found regulatory groups backed by past papers across donors. The package is shared through Bioconductor.
pmc-13525024:
Martin Korpan leads a large Austrian team in a 2026 real-world analysis of treatment for resectable stomach and esophagus junction cancers with a DNA repair defect called mismatch-repair deficiency. These tumors carry a favorable prognosis yet gain little from standard chemotherapy, while immune checkpoint drugs looked promising in early studies. Optimal combinations and nonoperative paths were unclear.

The multicenter study included 55 patients split among chemotherapy, combined chemo-immunotherapy, immunotherapy alone, or surgery first, and 82 percent ultimately had resection. Complete disappearance of tumor in removed tissue occurred in about a quarter of chemotherapy-based groups but in all five resected patients given dual immunotherapy. Among patients managed without surgery, one third reached clinical complete response. Responses clustered with a high PD-L1 score.
pmc-13526524:
Cheon and colleagues find the sensor that lets a worm taste and reject a green tea compound. Their 2026 paper studies epigallocatechin gallate, the main catechin in green tea, and shows the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans actively avoids it. The work identifies both the receptor and the nerve cells involved, answering how plant chemicals shape nematode behaviour at molecular level.

Only catechins carrying a galloyl group triggered strong avoidance. The response ran through the ASH pain-sensing neurons and depended on a receptor called SRXA-7. Worms lacking it showed specific avoidance defects and blunted calcium responses in those neurons. Restoring the receptor just in ASH rescued both. Avoidance also varied across species and wild strains, and shifted with feeding state and prior experience. The authors identify SRXA-7 as a dedicated sensory receptor for this class of plant compounds.
pmc-13527924:
C. Vanlalhriata and nine colleagues document a 2026 shift in malaria patterns in Mizoram, a state in northeast India bordering Bangladesh and Myanmar. Using national program data plus health-center records from Mamit district for 2021 to 2025, the team mapped cases over time and place against environmental factors.

The share of infections caused by Plasmodium vivax climbed from 23 percent in 2021 to 47 percent in 2024, overtaking the historically dominant falciparum species. In Mamit district vivax caused most cases in 2025, including the great majority among children under five, and it circulated all year rather than peaking with the monsoon. Because drug-resistant vivax has been reported in Myanmar, the authors urge urgent drug efficacy testing.
pmc-13528024:
Husein Mufaddal Hassanali and six colleagues recount a 2026 case from Tanzania of many complications in a row after heart bypass surgery. The patient was a 63-year-old man with triple-vessel heart disease. He also had diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, and asthma. His chest wound split open after a fall on day six. Emergency surgery reclosed the sternum with a reinforced technique.

He then developed severe nerve and muscle weakness from critical illness. Later a deep chest infection with Pseudomonas bacteria set in. Care included long antibiotics, repeated washouts, suction wound therapy, wire removal, and a chest muscle flap. Heart rhythm trouble, kidney injury, and fluid on the lung also appeared. After eight months of team care and rehab, he healed fully and regained function. The authors stress early action and teamwork.
pmc-13528524:
Daniël W. Groefsema and five colleagues watch catalyst heat from inside a methane reaction in a 2026 study. The reaction joins methane into ethylene, a prized building block. It runs hot and gives off fierce heat, which has stalled factory use. The team used glowing particles as tiny thermometers during operation. The method is called luminescence thermometry.

Even without reactive gas flowing, catalyst spots ran nearly 250 degrees Celsius above the oven setting. Heat from the reaction itself pushed local readings further. Airflow, bed size, and catalyst amount all swayed the readings strongly. Oven dials, in short, hide the real working heat. The authors say such inside views are vital for taming the process. Better heat control could finally make methane coupling practical at scale.
pmc-13530224:
Fazle Rabbi Chowdhury leads a 2026 study of specialist immune cells in acute melioidosis, a severe tropical infection common in Thailand. These MAIT cells help fight bacteria, yet their role in this illness was unknown. Lab cultures and blood from 120 patients and local controls supplied the data.

The bacterium did trigger the cells to release a key defense signal in culture. During acute illness, circulating cells were fewer, highly activated, and poor at responding, with recovery restoring their function. Patients who died showed weaker responses, while diabetes deepened the deficit, hinting these cells guard against severe disease.
pmc-13530524:
Haskell and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 157, a validation study of the Universal Pain and Function score. This two-question outcome measure, built from a pain rating and a single function rating, is meant to replace long questionnaires that burden patients and clinics after common sports surgeries.

Scores were collected prospectively from 1,648 patients before and after rotator cuff repair, meniscus trimming, or ligament reconstruction, alongside the standard long instruments. The two-question score tracked the shoulder and knee gold standards closely. Its correlations ran from the low seventies up to the low nineties in the study's own reporting of its convergent validity checks. It barely correlated with mental health scores, as a physical measure should not, and it matched the long forms' ability to detect change after surgery. The authors conclude two questions deliver valid, responsive measurement.
pmc-13530924:
Ahsein Addloli and co-authors examine in 2026 how low thyroid hormone reshapes fat-burning organelles called peroxisomes inside rat fat tissue. A drug induced the hormone shortage for 7, 15, or 21 days. Fat pads from under the skin and three belly sites were compared by microscopy and protein measurement.

Peroxisome numbers rose gradually everywhere, yet the timing differed by depot. Production pathways shifted from the standard route toward building fresh organelles. Belly fat alone sprouted odd finger-like structures reaching into fat droplets, possibly from unbalanced fat burning. Under-skin fat never showed them, revealing sharp regional differences.
pmc-13531824:
Gordon Abekah-Nkrumah leads a 2026 study of whether health facilities in Ghana will keep using a digital medicine supply platform called Med4All. Surveys from 124 staff plus 56 interviews measured usefulness, ease, approval, and intention to continue. The system orders medicines and offers interest-free loans to facilities.

Intention to continue scored high, near four on a five-point scale. Usefulness, ease, and positive attitude each fed that intention, while fast deals and the loans stood out as prized features. Delivery delays, weak supplier contact, payment snags, and some staff holding back threatens long-term survival.
pmc-13531924:
Mathieu Megevet and colleagues report in 2026 a rare lung reaction to the myeloma drug pomalidomide in a 67-year-old man. He was receiving a three-drug regimen for relapsed blood cancer when breathlessness, cough, sweating, and chills built over a week. Symptoms had first flickered three months earlier, weeks after the regimen began.

Washing fluid from the lungs was rich in eosinophils, a hallmark white cell of allergic-type lung injury. Antibiotics failed to help, while stopping the drug and starting steroids brought fast clinical and scan improvement. Lung function stayed recovered at twelve months.
pmc-13532324:
Sylvain Meyer, Thomas Lafon, and Olivier Barraud present two cases from 2026 where gene tests missed key facts in Staphylococcus aureus blood infections. In one case at Limoges, a rapid test found no sign of the germ in a man with septic shock. Culture still grew the germ, and full gene reading showed a small loss in the target gene.

In the second case the rapid test called the germ drug resistant, while culture tests showed it was drug sensitive. Gene reading found a small loss that stopped a resistance protein early. The cases show why culture and drug tests still matter beside fast gene tests.
pmc-13534424:
Ewelina Lange and colleagues propose in 2026 a quantum battery design where light-driven jumps help rather than hurt charging. In most designs, random jumps drain stored energy and blur the stored state. Their battery uses groups of three-level atoms that hold energy in a long-lived middle state.

When jumps are limited to fall from the excited state into that middle state, with decay to the ground state blocked, jumps drive the battery to full charge. All stored energy stays extractable, and the second charging stage runs faster. Readers see a route to turn a loss channel into a charging aid.
pmc-13534724:
Jianxi Liu and colleagues develop in 2026 an electronic trigger system to flag sedative-hypnotic drug misuse in a large hospital. Such drugs carry dependence risk, yet passive reporting misses most cases. The team first reviewed over 16,000 outpatient prescriptions, then ran a ten-day live pilot.

A trigger dictionary inside the hospital system produced 200 automated alerts during the pilot. Phone screening of high-risk patients found 17 meeting criteria for suspected dependence, while the passive system found none in the same span. Benzodiazepine use, older age, and longer therapy stood out. Pharmacists can use the alerts to triage cases and curb diversion risks in busy clinics.
pmc-13536724:
Melike Buşra Atar and co-authors examine what raises the chance of newborn eye inflammation in a 2026 case-control study at a referral center. Records for babies born between 2022 and 2024 were reviewed, comparing 203 newborns who developed conjunctivitis in the first 28 days with 355 newborns who did not. Maternal, birth, newborn, and lab details were tested together to find independent links.

Affected newborns were more often male and born slightly earlier, with lower health scores at birth. Mothers of affected babies were older on average and showed higher diabetes rates and higher inflammation marker levels. After adjustment, older maternal age, maternal diabetes, higher inflammation levels, and male sex each stayed linked to the condition. The authors suggest closer early eye checks for babies with these features.
pmc-13536824:
Xingyu Sun and colleagues develop a prediction tool for urinary infection after surgery in older adults in a 2026 study at a teaching hospital in southwest China. Infections after surgery prolong stays and raise costs, yet early flagging is hard. Patients aged 65 years or older who had inpatient surgery between 2019 and 2024 supplied routine care data. Cases were split into training and validation groups, and a chart for personal risk estimates was built.

About one in five training patients developed a urinary infection after surgery. Six factors formed the final model, covering diabetes, intensive care stay, catheter time, repeat catheter use, hospital stay length, and return within a month. Accuracy stayed good in validation, and risk estimates matched observed rates well. The authors frame the tool as ongoing risk tracking during recovery, not a pre-surgery forecast.
pmc-13538224:
Ahmed Mohamed and colleagues review nanoparticle strategies for diffuse midline glioma in a 2026 synthesis. These deep brain tumors mostly strike children and teens, spread through tissue, resist drugs, and sit behind a tight blood-brain barrier. Survival past five years stays extremely low. The review covers current care and then sorts tiny carrier designs by material and targeting method, including paired imaging and therapy options.

Carriers can cross or bypass the barrier through receptor shuttles or local delivery, concentrating drugs at tumors while sparing the body. Metal particles can also boost radiation damage inside tumors. Imaging-linked carriers promise live tracking of treatment. Lab results look strong, yet barrier entry, spread inside tumors, and large-scale making still block patient use. The authors set four research priorities.
pmc-13538524:
Jian Yun and Tao Liu propose a blockchain framework for asynchronous federated learning in a 2026 design study. Federated learning trains shared models without moving private data, yet waiting for slow nodes stalls sync versions and ledgers add storage strain. The design stores bulky parameters off-chain, boosts local adaptation while compressing updates, verifies updates by shared information while discounting stale ones, and elects committees by stake-weighted chance.

Simulations showed steady global accuracy with lower communication load than rival schemes. Oscillations from delayed updates were damped, and poisoning plus Byzantine attacks were resisted. Scaling to three hundred nodes brought no sharp rise in agreement delay. The authors present the stack as a secure, efficient base for decentralized learning among uneven devices.
pmc-13538724:
Angela Zanfardino and colleagues report first real-world results for a tubeless automated insulin system in young people with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 observational study. Seventy-six children and adolescents starting the patch pump with its adaptive learning algorithm were followed for six months across centers. Glucose monitor metrics and blood sugar averages were tracked at one, three, and six months.

Time spent in the target glucose range jumped within the first month and stayed higher through six months. Time above range fell while low time held steady, and average glucose plus variability declined. Blood sugar averages dropped meaningfully by three months and held. Over half the group met the international target range goal at six months. No severe low events or acid crises occurred, supporting safety in routine care.
pmc-13540824:
Li Xiaonan and colleagues search health records from northern China in a 2026 study. They wanted the ages when three health risks start to climb fast. The risks were high blood pressure and raised fasting blood sugar. Abnormal blood lipids were the third. Sharp turning points could guide screening by age and sex.

The records numbered 263,824 health examinations. They spanned January 2020 to May 2025. Blood pressure turned upward near age forty. It turned earlier in men than in women. Blood sugar turned later, above all in women. Lipid problems turned strikingly early in men, near age thirty-one. Having several risks at once predicted more than any one alone.
pmc-13541624:
Linda L Magnusson Hanson and five colleagues review, in a 2026 systematic review, longitudinal evidence on whether working conditions raise the risk of suicidal behaviour. Research on employment as a mental health determinant had never been gathered this comprehensively.

Searches across four databases for studies from 1995 to 2024 found twenty-seven eligible papers, fourteen fit for pooling. Part-time work, job loss, job insecurity, high demands, low control, job strain, and workplace bullying each associated significantly with suicide, with job loss more than doubling relative risk. Certainty was moderate only for job loss and low for insecurity, and evidence on suicide attempts was thin. The authors call for many more studies.
pmc-13542124:
Reshmi Debbarma and colleagues test a natural powder in a 2026 study. The powder comes from de-oiled moringa seeds. It serves as a clumping agent for biofloc fish farming. In biofloc systems, microbial flocs clean the water. Synthetic clumping chemicals work, yet they cost more. They also sit poorly with green production.

Lab checks showed strong clumping by the powder. It removed over ninety percent of suspended solids at its best dose. A forty-five-day trial used young Clarias magur catfish. Tanks held eighty fish each. One dose stood clearly ahead of the rest. Ammonia and nitrite fell, while nitrate rose. Fish gained more biomass, with better survival and feed use.
pmc-13543324:
Nayeli Gonzalez-Gomez and colleagues report a proof-of-concept study adapting low-cost parent-child activity packs, first made in the United Kingdom, for vulnerable families in Argentina. Early childhood is a key window for language, thinking, and social development, and parents in economic hardship lack access to rich activities. The packs were reworked for local culture, materials, and daily routines with help from a local health worker, then given to 73 families at early childhood centres.

Parents filled in surveys and joined feedback sessions, while infants were checked with the Bayley-III developmental scales. Families said they did more varied activities, and the home learning setting improved. Parents spoke of enjoyment, stronger bonds, and greater confidence in playing with purpose. Developmental scores did not change, as foreseen in a short pilot. The authors present the packs as a welcome way to support early learning in poorer settings.
pmc-13543424:
Liming Shi and colleagues reported in 2026 on building a scorecard for judging the quality of lung cancer diagnosis and treatment. Lung cancer is China's commonest and deadliest cancer, yet hospitals lacked a shared, weighted set of quality indicators. The team used the Donabedian model, which splits quality into structure, process, and outcome, and ran two rounds of a Delphi consultation, where experts rate items until they converge. An analytic hierarchy process then converted expert judgements into weights.

The finished system holds three top-level indicators, fifteen secondary ones, and fifty-five detailed measures. Structure covers staff, rules, and facilities; process runs from diagnosis and team review through surgery, drugs, radiation, and follow-up; outcomes cover effectiveness, safety, and timeliness. Expert participation stayed above ninety-six percent across rounds, and their agreement strengthened. The authors offer the weighted system as a credible shared yardstick for hospitals.
pmc-13543524:
Maria Paes and co-authors asked in 2026 whether grapevine cells grown in flasks can stand in for whole leaves when studying defence chemistry. Cell cultures are tidy and repeatable, but disease research in the end concerns real plants. Cells from two vine types, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chambourcin, were dosed with jasmonic acid, a plant stress hormone. Their chemistry was read two and five days later with an ultra-precise mass spectrometer, side by side with detached leaves.

Cultures and leaves kept clearly unlike chemical profiles, and responses varied by type and time in both systems. Yet on chosen ground the two met, above all in oxidative-stress defence, stress signalling, and secondary metabolite output. Flask cells can thus serve as a partner platform for switch-on responses, the authors conclude. Findings still need checking in intact plants, with key chemicals firmly named, before the stand-in is trusted.
pmc-13545124:
Jen-Hao Wu and colleagues published a 2026 population pharmacokinetic study of bosutinib, a targeted leukaemia drug, in children with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukaemia. Dosing children by shrinking adult rules is unreliable, and the phase one dose-finding trial behind this work enrolled only twenty-six young patients. The team therefore borrowed strength from a published adult model, using its knowledge as a prior while fitting 235 blood samples from the children.

A two-compartment model with a brief absorption lag described the children's data well. Clearance, scaled to body size, ran higher in children than the reported adult value, a difference that matters for keeping blood levels in range. Simulations from the fitted model were used to judge the recommended phase two dose for children. Sparse paediatric data, the authors show, can still yield firm dosing science when adult knowledge is formally folded in.
pmc-13546724:
Rakhmad Perkasa Harahap and colleagues tested in 2026 whether chitosan, a compound made from shrimp shells, can preserve mixed livestock rations and improve how rumen microbes handle them. Rations were stored for 30 days with no additive, raw shell, chitin, or chitosan, under conditions with and without air. Afterward the team measured storage losses and ran laboratory rumen fermentations.

Storage without air preserved feed better overall, and chitosan gave the strongest protection, with the least dry matter loss and the best appearance and smell scores. Chitosan rations also digested best in the laboratory and produced the least methane. The authors present shrimp shell waste as a useful feed additive that turns a disposal problem into a benefit.
pmc-13547324:
Panpan He, Shouyang Yu, and Jingjing Wang proposed in 2026 a system that reads college students' facial expressions and then learns, by trial and feedback, which support strategy to offer each person. Questionnaires and manual counseling are slow and subjective, the authors argue. Their pipeline cleans and aligns face images and extracts texture features tied to states like stress and anxiety. Those features feed a reinforcement learning agent that picks relaxation exercises, cognitive prompts, or motivational messages.

Tested on a public dataset of about ten thousand records, the combined system beat traditional techniques on accuracy and related scores, all landing near or above ninety percent. The authors offer the design as a framework for adaptive, personal mental health support on campus.
pmc-13547424:
Saini, Fidler, Boffito, and colleagues ask why people on HIV prevention pills still seroconvert. Their 2026 paper reviews new HIV diagnoses at a London clinic. The clinic, 56 Dean Street, serves many PrEP users. PrEP is medication taken beforehand to block HIV infection. Records covered diagnoses from 2017 through 2024.

Among 1,080 newly diagnosed people, 210 had used PrEP before. That share climbed steeply across the study years. It rose from about four percent in 2017 to sixty percent in 2024. Prior users tested more often and caught infections earlier. Over a third of them had stopped PrEP entirely. Among those still nominally on it, most reported poor adherence. Running out of pills was the top reason for stopping. Monogamy and stomach side effects followed behind. One resistance mutation, M184I/V, appeared far more in PrEP-exposed patients. Support for staying on PrEP is the clear unmet need.
pmc-13548624:
Marie Emilie Hjorth Lutambi and colleagues review what is known about intoxication among injured patients arriving at emergency departments, in a 2026 systematic review. Alcohol and other psychoactive drugs alter judgment and behavior, so they may change both how badly people get hurt and how they fare afterward. The team searched two major databases and kept eighteen prospective studies of patients aged fifteen and older.

Intoxication was common but varied enormously: alcohol involvement ranged from under ten percent to nearly two thirds of patients across studies. Nine studies found worse injury severity scores among intoxicated patients, while others found no difference or even milder injuries. Hospital stays and death rates also swung between studies. Intoxicated patients were consistently younger and mostly male. The authors call the severity evidence inconsistent and point prevention efforts at those groups.
pmc-13551924:
Sivan Cukerman and Orli Grinstein-Cohen published a 2026 survey of emergency nurses in Israel. The topic was forensic nursing, the work of saving evidence from injured patients. An online survey reached 438 nurses from November 2023 to April 2024. It asked how often they do set forensic tasks. It also asked how important they judge those tasks.

Nurses said they do such tasks rarely. Yet they rated the tasks as highly important. Few had any forensic training in their studies. Close to nine in ten wanted such training. Older nurses and those with a master's degree rated the tasks higher. So did nurses with more years on the job. The pair urge schools to add forensic content and hospitals to back the role.
pmc-13554024:
Xiang Shi and three colleagues check how well a thin-needle test sorts swollen lymph nodes in a 2026 single-centre study. Needle sampling is quick and gentle, yet final proof still comes from surgery. The team reviewed 133 cases from 2023 and 2024 where both tests were done. Four kinds of disease were covered: harmless overgrowth, two forms of lymph cancer, and cancer spread from elsewhere.

The needle test matched the surgical answer in close to nine cases out of ten. It was sharpest for spread cancer, catching most cases, and never falsely named the rarer lymph cancer. Cell shapes and patterns differed clearly between the four groups. The authors call the test a sound first screen that helps doctors plan next steps.
pmc-13555724:
Andrew S Handel leads a four-author team reporting a lone star tick rash illness in an eight-year-old New York girl in a 2026 case report. The illness, called STARI, mimics Lyme disease with an expanding round rash after a tick bite. Two weeks before her visit she had developed a five-centimetre ring with a central bump on her upper back. Fever, swollen neck glands, and muscle aches came with it.

The tick, removed from the very spot and kept, tested positive for Borrelia lonestari, a disputed suspect for this illness. Suspecting early Lyme disease, her doctor prescribed two weeks of amoxicillin. Rash and symptoms cleared within one week, and she stayed well at follow-up. Lone star ticks are spreading north, sharpening the Lyme look-alike problem.
pmc-13555924:
Xueying Bai leads a seven-author team stress-testing two collagen membranes used in jaw bone rebuilding in a 2026 lab study. Guided bone regeneration lays a membrane over graft material to hold space for new bone. One membrane comes from cow heart sac tissue, the other from pig skin. Wet tests stretched, inflated, and compressed both materials.

The cow-derived membrane proved far stiffer and stronger under pulling and compression loads. The pig-derived membrane stretched much further before failing and expanded slightly wider under air pressure. Surgeons thus face a trade-off: strength and load bearing against flexibility and give. The authors frame the results as a mechanical basis for choosing membranes in horizontal bone rebuilding around implants.
pmc-13556024:
Shengnan Kong and six colleagues examined in 2026 whether a simple nutrition score predicts death in patients whose severe infection brings on delirium. The prognostic nutritional index combines blood albumin with a white cell count, and its value in sepsis-associated delirium was unclear. Using the MIMIC-IV intensive care database, they split 2,160 patients into low and high score groups and tracked survival to one year.

Patients with low scores died far more often at three, six, and twelve months than patients with high scores. The link held after statistical adjustment and after weighting methods that balance the groups, and the score predicted death about as well as a standard organ failure score. The relationship was curved rather than straight. Clinicians could use this cheap, routine measure to spot high-risk patients early.
pmc-13558624:
Konosuke Takashima and four colleagues proposed in 2026 a damage detector for structures that computes with the structure itself. Physical reservoir computing treats a physical system's response as the computer, needing only a thin trained readout. Their version splits a structure's vibration into frequency bands. Each band passes through a nonlinear function. The results are summed and fed back into the structure, creating virtual nodes from one sensor and one actuator pair.

Tests used a thin plate plus a thin-walled tube, in simulation and in the laboratory, classified damage about as accurately as ordinary neural networks. Training and running costs fell sharply by comparison, since only the small readout layer learns. The authors present the scheme as a cheap route to continuous structural health monitoring for bridges, pipes, and similar assets where many sensors are impractical.
pmc-13558724:
Yang Yu and six colleagues traced in 2026 how liver cancers escape lenvatinib, a first-line targeted drug whose benefit usually fades as resistance grows. A ubiquitin-trimming enzyme, USP32, turned up overactive in these tumours and tied to aggressive spread and drug failure. Silencing it in cells and in mouse grafts slowed growth and movement and restored the drug's bite, while forcing it higher did the opposite.

The enzyme protects a partner protein, a helicase called DDX17, by snipping off the tags that mark it for destruction. Stabilised DDX17 silences a small tumour-suppressing RNA, which unleashes a growth signalling pathway at the heart of the resistance. Adding a blocker of that pathway to lenvatinib overcame resistance in grafts from already resistant tumours. The authors propose the whole chain as a target sequence for refractory liver cancer.
pmc-13559124:
Liqin Ke and three colleagues present two cases of endobronchial inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor in children, a rare growth inside the airway that is often mistaken for asthma or a swallowed foreign body. Their 2026 report shows treatment guided jointly by where the tumor sat and by its molecular profile, especially ALK status, a gene change that can drive growth.

One boy, aged eight, had an ALK-negative tumor in the right lower lobe bronchus and received a robot-assisted sleeve resection that spared working lung tissue. The other boy, aged six, had an ALK-positive tumor at the airway fork that badly narrowed breathing. He had endoscopic removal followed by crizotinib, a drug aimed at ALK. Neither child showed recurrence at follow-up, though those checks came at only six and three months. The authors urge early molecular testing in children with unexplained airway blockage.
pmc-13560124:
Ümit Karabulut and colleagues investigate duodenogastric reflux, the backward flow of intestinal contents into the stomach, in patients with indigestion. Their 2026 retrospective case-control study covers 524 patients who had upper endoscopy between January 2017 and December 2022. Endoscopic signs such as bile pooling sorted 287 patients into the reflux group, with 237 serving as controls.

Chemical gastropathy, stomach lining injury from bile exposure, appeared significantly more often in the reflux group. Intestinal metaplasia and Helicobacter pylori rates, however, did not differ between the groups. Reflux patients showed higher bilirubin and lower albumin in blood tests. Gallbladder removal and gallstones stood out as strong independent risk factors, while age added a modest effect. The authors describe the condition as multifactorial and leave open whether reflux itself drives precancerous change, calling for prospective research.
pmc-13560824:
Julia Marie Stewart and colleagues present the chromosomal genome of the maze coral, Meandrina meandrites, together with sequences from its microbial partners. Their 2026 genome note describes a stony coral of the western Atlantic, ranging from Bermuda and Florida through the Caribbean to Brazil in shallow water. Its ridged, valleyed surface gives the species its maze and brain coral names.

The assembly spans 551.16 megabases, with 99.25 percent arranged into fourteen chromosomal pseudomolecules, plus a mitochondrial genome of 17.2 kilobases. Annotation by Ensembl identified over thirty thousand protein-coding genes. The team also recovered two bins from the specimen's metagenome, capturing symbiont microbes. The coral grows slowly, laying calcium bands by day, and reproduces both by broadcast spawning and asexually. The authors offer the resource for reef biology and symbiosis research.
pmc-13562224:
Alejandro Lopez-Bezanilla and colleagues use frustrated magnets shaped like fullerene cages to stress-test quantum annealers. Their 2026 study builds Ising models on these closed carbon-like shapes, where magnetic moments cannot all please their neighbors at once, leaving a huge set of equally good layouts. Quantum fluctuations must do the choosing.

The team saw quantum swings lift that tie, favoring certain coherent setups through tunneling between states. Since the models have no edges and high symmetry, they make clean test cases for quantum hardware. Scores rose sharply across successive generations of superconducting annealers on these problems. The authors argue that hitting the shared ground state exactly is where quantum rigs prove themselves. Frustrated cages, they conclude, offer a sharp benchmark for the young field.
pmc-13562924: The full genome of common heather — Calluna vulgaris — sequenced and published. Vladimir Krivtsov, Peter M. Hollingsworth, and others deliver it. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is plant genomics. It presents the genome sequence of the iconic moorland shrub, a resource for ecology and conservation.
pmc-13569824:
Feifei Huang, Zhongyi Tong, and Yi Jiang review, in a 2026 retrospective study, 265 patients with invasive breast cancer tested for inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene variants. These variants raise cancer risk and open the door to targeted PARP inhibitor drugs. Tumor features, immune markers, and outcomes were compared by variant status.

Inherited faulty variants clustered with distinct tumor traits, enrichment for triple-negative breast cancer, and worse outlook. Adding standard tissue markers, including an immune marker used in triple-negative disease, may sharpen risk grouping. The authors argue that pairing genetic testing with routine marker panels can guide more personal treatment choices for patients carrying these inherited variants.
pmc-13572524:
Constance Denoyelle, with 16 colleagues, reports a 2026 survey of a gut protozoan in French broiler chickens. Blastocystis is the most common such organism found in people, and birds may pass it to humans. No French farm survey had been done, so the team sampled birds at one slaughterhouse from 66 farms.

A total of 967 gut samples covered three farm systems, from free-range label birds to standard indoor flocks. The organism turned up in 49.7 percent of samples and on 83.3 percent of farms. Farm type and season shaped how often it appeared. Subtype 7 led by far, with subtype 6 next, and near a fifth of positive birds carried two or more subtypes. Gene reads showed wide variety within subtype 7. The authors flag flocks as a real source of human exposure.
pmc-13575124:
Narek Abelyan introduces PocketMaster, a 2026 software tool for comparing the pockets in protein structures where molecules bind. Small shape changes in these pockets can alter how a protein works and how a drug fits. Comparing many structures by hand is slow, so the tool automates lining up, grouping, and charting pockets.

Two case studies show its range. For the TYK2 protein, the tool separated kinase and pseudokinase pocket shapes and found subtypes within each. For the estrogen receptor, it caught a known shift in one helix between active and inactive states. Results come with automatic reports and visuals. Abelyan positions the tool for early drug design, with code shared openly online.
pmc-13576124:
Wu Weiwei and five colleagues test a spiral form of arc radiotherapy for bulky tumours in a 2026 planning study. GRID therapy aims high dose at peaks inside a tumour while keeping valleys between them low. Standard linear accelerator methods struggle to keep that contrast sharp.

Twenty patients' plans were rebuilt three ways: the spiral method, standard arc therapy, and helical tomotherapy. The spiral approach pairs couch movement with gantry rotation to trace a helical path. It produced the steepest dose fall-off and the highest peak-to-valley ratios under both measures used. Healthy organ limits were met by all three methods with no meaningful gaps. Beam time for the spiral method sat between the other two. The authors judge the spiral method dosimetrically strongest for single-session GRID work.
pmc-13576224:
Szymon Kuliś and three colleagues test whether brief targeted cooling calms the tremor that follows hard exercise in young swimmers, in a 2026 crossover trial. Tremor rises after intense effort as muscles tire. Cold therapy is common in sports medicine, yet its effect on exercise tremor had not been directly tested.

Thirty-four competitive teenage swimmers each completed both conditions: 60 seconds of localised cooling on tender muscle trigger points, and a no-treatment control. Tremor in both legs was recorded before and after a 30-second maximal tethered swim, with a set recovery gap. Exercise raised tremor power as expected. Cooling blunted that rise in the 9 to 14 hertz band, the frequency range tied to nerve-driven tremor. Frequency shifts were less tidy. The authors note the value for actual performance is still unknown.
pmc-13576324:
Andrea Stašek leads a 2026 study mapping how problem gaming and problem social media use connect to teenage wellbeing across ten European countries. Most past work scored each habit as a single total. This team used symptom networks on survey data from 33,586 adolescents aged 11 to 15, gathered in 2021 and 2022.

One symptom sat at the centre of both habits: escapism, using games or feeds to dodge feelings. It was the most common symptom and the main bridge to loneliness in both sexes, and to overall wellbeing and nervousness in girls. Symptoms reflecting fallout, such as conflict, deception, and trouble with others, linked tightly across the two habits, hinting at a shared condition rather than separate ones. The authors argue prevention should target single symptoms, starting with escapism.
pmc-13577924:
Ximing Ran leads a 2026 study hunting blood proteins that foretell when a healthy carrier of an ALS gene fault will develop the disease. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal nerve disease, and prevention trials are blocked by not knowing who will convert, or when. The team used a high-throughput protein platform on stored blood samples.

The collection held 516 samples from 33 people who later developed ALS, 35 patients, 10 symptom-free carriers, and 59 controls. Ninety-two proteins shifted in level before symptoms began. A core panel of 19 predicted conversion with ranking scores between 0.80 and 0.89 across half-year to five-year windows, and estimated the timing to within a mean of 1.6 years. Checks in UK Biobank data backed several of the signals. The authors say the panel beats the single best-known marker used alone.
pmc-13578324:

Vessel diseases grow from long term injury and oxidative stress, a state where reactive oxygen overwhelms cell defenses. The team stressed human vein cells with peroxide, then added hemoglobin and watched stress and inflammation markers.

Hemoglobin lowered three key inflammatory signals and cut cell death, along with the waste markers of oxidative damage. The gain ran through a defense pathway that switches on protective genes. Blocking that pathway largely erased the benefit, which ties the effect to the pathway itself. Since the anti-inflammatory effect followed the drop in stress, the authors frame stress control as the root of the gain.
pmc-13578424:
Temesgen Debas Awoke, Semu Mitiku Kassa, and Gizaw Mengistu Tsidu model short, sharp control bursts against visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly parasite disease spread by sandflies, in a 2026 study. Heat and rain drive sandfly numbers, so spread swings with the seasons. Steady year round control is too costly for many poor regions, which pushed the team toward brief, well timed pushes.

Their model folds weather into the spread math and tests spray rounds, breeding site clearing, and culling of infected host animals. Sandfly linked factors drove cases far more than host factors, so fly control won priority. Two one week pushes a year cut human cases by about ninety five percent in the model. Starting six weeks after the infection peak worked best, and pairing fly control with culling beat either alone.
pmc-13578724:
Haelim Yoon and colleagues test an old drug, emetine, against liver cancer cells that learn to spread, in a 2026 lab study. Spread starts when cancer cells loosen their neat sheet form and gain a wandering form, a shift driven by a protein called Twist1. The drug, long used for other ills, had never been checked for this anti-spread role.

At doses that spared cell life, the drug slowed migration and invasion across five liver cancer cell lines. Twist1 levels fell, sheet markers rose, and wandering markers dropped. Rescue tests showed the drug shortens the life of the Twist1 protein itself. A mutant form that cannot take a key chemical tag resisted the drop. Two stress pathways that place that tag went quiet under the drug, tying the pieces together.
pmc-13579824:

A 58 year old woman past menopause carried a large belly and pelvis tumor of a clear cell type. Scans showed odd patches in the gut lining membrane, and a blood marker ran high, both hinting that cancer had seeded widely.

Surgery told another story. The membrane patches were one blood filled cyst, not spread at all. Lab work confirmed the ovarian tumor was still early stage, and the cyst was harmless. Twelve months after surgery she remained free of disease. The authors warn that scans and markers alone can overstage such cases, and that eyes in the operating room plus lab proof should settle the stage.
pmc-13584424:

Long-term pain often brings both sharp sensitivity and foggy memory, yet the shared wiring was unclear. The team used a nerve injury model and tested the animals on mazes and object tasks while recording activity in a front brain region called the prelimbic cortex.

One set of calming nerve cells in that region stayed overactive after injury, which threw off the balance between go and stop signals and dulled memory. Quieting those cells eased both pain sensitivity and memory faults. Switching them on in healthy mice created the same faults. A protein named ATF4 sat upstream of the shift, which gives drug hunters a concrete target to test.
pmc-13587324:
Benjamin Wee Y and colleagues map gene networks that help hemp cope when phosphorus runs short. Phosphorus is a core plant nutrient, and hemp, shaped by centuries of human selection for fiber and seed, handles poor soils better than many crops. Their 2026 study grew hemp under rich and poor phosphate supply and read gene activity across roots, leaves, and other organs, then grouped genes that rose and fell together.

Twelve gene groups appeared, tied to jobs such as root growth, fiber making, and flowering. Two groups, one in leaves and one in roots, tracked the plant's phosphorus state closely, and both overlapped with genes marked by domestication. A gene called SPX3 sat at the hub of the leaf response, while root shape changes ran through known regulator families. Hormones called strigolactones also steered the root response.
pmc-13587824:

Closures and distressed hospitals stretch care thin across the United States, yet the standing public scores were designed for narrow hospital types or demand complete data, which shaky hospitals often lack. Their 2026 measure, the integrated vulnerability measure, extends a rural model to every general acute-care hospital filing Medicare cost reports between 2017 and 2022.

The index sorted checked hospitals into four risk bands, with about half called low risk and under one in ten high risk. Higher bands were far more likely to land in real financial distress within two years. Because the model stays readable and forgiving of missing data, the authors pitch it for targeting help and oversight before a closure is on the table.
pmc-13589924:
Yilun Qu heads a large team in a 2026 study of a kidney disease marked by fast growth of cells in the filters of the kidney. That growth, driven by swelling and irritation, can end in kidney failure. The team tested chlorogenic acid, a natural plant compound, and asked how it protects the kidney. Their work used a rat model of the disease plus lab tests on the compound.

Qu and the team found that the acid binds a protein called RAC1 and blocks its action. That step lowered signals that spur cell growth and calmed immune cells called macrophages. Levels of key irritant signals fell as well. The authors propose the acid as a lead for a new drug, though human tests lie ahead.
pmc-13592324:
Xiao Wang leads a 2026 team building a flow battery with no membrane at all, pairing lithium metal with an organic liquid cathode. Membranes usually keep the two fluids apart yet add cost and resistance. Their cell stacks two liquids that refuse to mix. A deep eutectic lithium fluid sits below, while a chlorine solvent floats above it. The upper fluid holds a sulfur nitrogen dye that stores charge and stays in its own layer.

The stack reached about 3.6 volts, high for this class. After 100 cycles it kept most of its charge with near perfect charge recovery, and a flowing version ran ten days with little self drain. Cost estimates undercut vanadium systems, and both fluids resist flame. Wang and the team credit the eutectic lithium mix for the wide, stable window.
